atlasmch engine — a guided tutorial

mch engine — a guided tutorial

commit ff4135bc · excerpts pulled from the live tree at render time · drift-checked per excerpt

A tutorial, not a reference: chapters are ordered so each one only needs what came before, and together they take you from zero to being able to read, verify, and extend the mch C++ engine. Every code block is pulled from the real tree at render time and drift-checked against the hash recorded when it was annotated — what you see IS the code. Captured-output blocks show real engine runs you can reproduce. Each chapter ends with the in-scope files that were deliberately NOT annotated (with reasons), so you always know what remains for your own reading. The ABI/tolk side gets its own tutorial later; chapter 6 previews the boundary.

The pipeline you will understand by chapter 8
flowchart LR
  T["trace fixture (.lz4)"] --> L[TraceLoader] --> E[EventNode tree] --> B["Block tree (init spine)"] --> W["Walker: matchers from IR"] --> BP["build programs -> captures"] --> A["ActionBuild -> Action rows"]
  IR["mch_ir.json (compiled .mch specs)"] --> W
  P["parse registry (ch.6)"] -.-> BP
  TW["Python twins (ch.9)"] -. byte-diff .- A

Reading order

2

3

4

5
5 · Matching — Walker, try_build, prefilter
6
6 · Parse layer — 3 parser sources, 2 value universes
7
7 · Build programs — expressions, captures, host seam
8
8 · From blocks to Action rows
9

10
10 · The production path (Phase G)

Global "read yourself" list

  • ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/main.cpp — PARTIAL: the dispatch region is excerpted. The remainder is the option-parser table (one add_option per mode — read it as the mode index), the two print_* helpers behind mode 1's tree dump, and the actor-scheduler fall-through (~355 LOC) (big-picture)
  • ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/ClassifyCore.h — PARTIAL: the entry points and result types are excerpted. Not shown: the file's header comment (the core/harness contract, paraphrased in prose) and the FailureCategory enum, whose comment argues carefully about which failures can and cannot be a trace-terminal value — worth reading before adding one (~117 LOC) (big-picture)
  • ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/ClassifyCore.cpp — PARTIAL: classify_trace's loop and commit are excerpted. The rest is prepare_classify (table pairing + prefilter precompute), try_build's merge/shape/auto-append tail, the ported post-process passes, and the basic-actions fallback — all owned by later chapters (~534 LOC) (big-picture)
  • ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/Classify.cpp — PARTIAL: the adapter contract, the fixture loop and the render fork are excerpted. The remainder is render_action (the fixed ~35-key key order — a gate artifact, not logic), emit_action, and the thin run_* wrappers (~218 LOC) (big-picture)
  • ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/Classify.h — declarations for the six run_* dump entry points plus the loader/lookup-factory typedefs the -schema/-prod variants inject; no logic (~82 LOC) (big-picture)
  • ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/TraceLoader.h — PARTIAL: the Message struct is excerpted. Transaction and Trace are the same kind of decode-only shape; the one comment worth reading there is on Trace::interfaces, which documents the msgpack->Value scalar mapping (~86 LOC) (big-picture)
  • ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/TraceLoader.cpp — the LZ4-frame decompressor plus the msgpack walk. Mechanical and defensive (unknown keys ignored by design); read it only if a fixture fails to load (~266 LOC) (big-picture)
  • ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/BlockTree.h — PARTIAL: EventNode, the Block head and the TraceContext bundle are excerpted. Not shown: the file's header comment listing four deliberate deviations from the Python substrate (read it — find_frontier dedup is called out as suspect #1 for diamond-shape diffs), and the merge/connect/insert_between API that block-tree owns (~219 LOC) (big-picture)
  • ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/BlockTree.cpp — the implementations: to_tree's msg_hash linkage, init_block's iterative classification, and merge_blocks. Entirely block-tree's subject (~430 LOC) (big-picture)
  • ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/ActionBuild.h — PARTIAL: the Action struct is excerpted; only the build_action declaration and its "returns false for an unported btype" contract are left (~39 LOC) (big-picture)
  • ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/ActionBuild.cpp — PARTIAL: one fill_* is excerpted. The other ~30 are the same shape per action type, plus the base fields (id/tx_hashes/accounts/lt window) and the btype dispatch — actions (~560 LOC) (big-picture)
  • ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/ir/mch_ir.json — PARTIAL: one matcher row, its two match-tree nodes, and one output field are excerpted. The other ~11.4k lines are 32 more matchers and 327 more nodes in the same format — read it with a JSON tool, not an editor (ir-artifact) (big-picture)
  • ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/IrLoader.{h,cpp} — turns the JSON document into LoadedIr / CompiledMatcher, computes the source sha the build table is paired against, and decides build_skip_reason. Directly next in ir-artifact (~700 LOC) (big-picture)
  • ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/Walker.{h,cpp} — the match-phase engine: node-kind dispatch, reachability, capture binding. This chapter treats a match as atomic; matcher-runtime does not (~600 LOC) (big-picture)
  • ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/BuildRuntime.{h,cpp} — BuildEnv/BuildOutcome and the rt_* runtime functions the generated build code calls (rt_parse, rt_access_build, rt_builtin_*). Named in this chapter's captured output only; build-programs (~800 LOC) (big-picture)
  • ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/GenBuilds.h — the three generated build tables (ir / vectors / testbed) and their per-document sha guards. Its header comment explains why the pairing is correct by construction — read it if prepare_classify ever exits 2 on you (~55 LOC) (big-picture)
  • ton-index-worker/cmake-build-debug-visual-studio/ton-mch-engine/generated/builds_ir_generated.cpp — the generated build functions, shown here as captured output because it is a BUILD-TREE file, not committed — it is regenerated by a CMake step from mch_ir.json and must never be edited (~5k LOC) (big-picture)
  • ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/Value.{h,cpp} — the value type every capture, data field and Action column is made of, plus the rendering that makes dumps comparable. It is chapter 2 (value) precisely because everything here assumes it (big-picture)
  • ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/parse/ParseVesting.cpp — the parser behind parse send as VestingSendMessage — it fully deserializes an inner int_msg_info header. Its header comment states its one documented deviation; parse-layer (~79 LOC) (big-picture)
  • ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/twins/py_classify.py — the Python twin whose output this chapter diffs against. It runs the REAL Python IR engine plus a thin re-implementation of the dump format; gates (~400 LOC) (big-picture)
  • indexer/indexer/events/mch/btypes.py — the Block-class -> btype table the frontend uses to turn produces VestingSendMessageBlock into "vesting_send_message". A flat dict; the only reason to open it is to add a row (big-picture)
  • ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/{SchemaTraceLoader,ParsedBlockLookupSource,MchClassifierActor}.cpp — the production-side loader, lookup source and actor that the --schema/--prod modes dispatch into. Named in this chapter's dispatch excerpt, owned by prod-path (big-picture)
  • ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/Value.cpp — partial · PARTIAL: the 18 make_* factories (lines 15-138) are one-liners that set t plus one member — read them as a table; the only three with semantics are make_amount_none (leaves num null), make_amount_float (sets the flag) and the Asset pair (TON = is_ton, jetton = has_jetton + str). Also unannotated: td_boc_serialize (a thin vm::std_boc_serialize wrapper, discussed in prose) and describe() (lines 347-394 — diagnostic rendering, reached by --parse-dump only through ParseDump's default: branch). ~185 LOC of the 396 (value)

Note it says "currently 32 matchers" — stale by one since dedust_v2_claim_reward landed (~98 LOC) (ir-artifact)

The one non-obvious rule there is that a non-name callee is rejected outright because the evaluator only ever calls bare builtins (~70 LOC) (ir-artifact)
  • indexer/indexer/events/mch_ir/loader.py — the Python twin loader. The C++ loader is a subset by design — it trusts an artifact the Python side already accepted (~335 LOC) (ir-artifact)

It never runs a build program — no Block or parse state (~53 + ~220 LOC) (build-programs)

1 · The engine in one pass — a trace becomes an action

After this chapter you can take any fixture in tests/traces, run it through the C++ engine, and say which matcher fired, why, and where every field of the resulting Action row came from. We follow ONE real trace — 03RZCW7mu3eJp-FWifVzKsRHafUrqQNu4E6YwZxvXJ0=.lz4, 5 transactions, 5 leaf blocks, exactly 1 action — end to end: LZ4+msgpack fixture -> Trace -> EventNode tree -> Block spine -> the one matcher whose anchor opcode is present -> captures -> a 6-field build output -> an Action row. You also see the same matcher in its two committed forms, the .mch source a human writes and the compiled row the runtime actually executes, and you learn the one discipline that holds the whole port together: the C++ dump and the Python twin must be byte-identical. Everything here is deliberately shallow — each stage is one chapter later on, and this page is the map you hang them on.

Lab setup — three commands

Keep a shell open at S:/Dev/ton-indexer-clear/indexer for the rest of the tutorial. Two paths never change, so export them once: the engine binary …/cmake-build-debug-visual-studio/ton-mch-engine/ton-mch-engine.exe and the IR artifact …/ton-mch-engine/ir/mch_ir.json. -T takes either a single .lz4 or a directory (which it walks sorted, .lz4 only).

The three commands you will use constantly:

1. ton-mch-engine -T <fixture> — no mode flag. Decodes the fixture and prints the transaction list plus the initialized block tree. This is the ONLY mode that spins up a TON actor scheduler; every --… mode returns from main before reaching it, single-threaded and deterministic, because their stdout is a compared artifact. 2. ton-mch-engine --classify -I <ir> -T <fixture|dir> — the whole match+build+merge pipeline, one ACTION line per produced block. 3. ton-mch-engine --actions -I <ir> -T <fixture|dir> — the same pipeline, but each produced block is serialized into a database Action row before printing.

Everything on stdout is byte-compared against a Python twin; anything advisory (orphan-node warnings, registry complaints) goes to stderr. When you pipe engine output anywhere, 2>/dev/null is usually what you want.

The fixture, and why this one

The corpus is 148 .lz4 fixtures producing 199 actions. Most are jetton/DEX traces with 20+ transactions and several interacting matchers — bad for a first read. 03RZCW7mu3eJp-FWifVzKsRHafUrqQNu4E6YwZxvXJ0=.lz4 is the smallest trace in the corpus that still exercises a genuinely non-trivial matcher: 5 transactions, 5 leaf blocks, exactly one action, and the matcher that produces it (vesting_send_message) is a two-node chain with a real message-body parse and a fully declarative 6-field build. Nothing about it is a special case — no lookups, no host shapers, no post-processing, no merge of a composite into another composite — so every mechanism you see is the general one.

A .lz4 fixture is LZ4-frame-compressed msgpack, written by the Python indexer's recorder.py and read by tests/utils/trace_deserializer.py on the Python side. It is a whole trace: transactions, their in/out messages, base64 message bodies, and a root interfaces section — the per-account interface data that TestInterfaceRepository serves. The C++ loader decodes only the fields structural matching needs and ignores unknown keys, so fixtures recorded by a newer recorder still load.

29struct Message {
30 std::string msg_hash;
31 std::string tx_hash;
32 std::int64_t tx_lt{0};
33 std::string direction; // "in" | "out"
34 std::optional<std::string> source;
35 std::optional<std::string> destination;
361 std::optional<std::int64_t> opcode; // stored SIGNED (int32)
37 std::optional<std::int64_t> value;
38 std::optional<std::int64_t> created_lt;
39 std::optional<std::int64_t> created_at;
40 std::optional<bool> bounce;
41 bool bounced{false};
422 bool has_extra_currencies{false}; // value_extra_currencies map is non-empty
433 std::optional<MsgContent> content;
44 
454 // Owning transaction, wired after decode (Python Message.transaction).
46 Transaction *tx{nullptr};
47 
48 // Opcode masked to 32 bits (matches Python EventNode.get_opcode).
49 std::optional<std::uint32_t> opcode32() const {
50 if (!opcode) {
51 return std::nullopt;
52 }
53 return static_cast<std::uint32_t>(*opcode & 0xFFFFFFFF);
54 }
55};
1L36The trap in this struct: opcode is stored SIGNED, because msgpack carries Python's int and the indexer writes opcodes as int32. 0xA7733ACD round-trips as a negative number here. Never compare *msg->opcode against a hex literal — use opcode32() at the bottom, which is the exact port of Python's EventNode.get_opcode.
2L42A derived flag, not a decoded field: the fixture carries a value_extra_currencies map and the loader collapses it to "non-empty?". That is all any ported matcher asks, and keeping the map would mean owning a second value universe for no reader.
3L43content is optional and its absence is NORMAL, not an error — a message whose body was not indexed simply has nothing to parse. Downstream that becomes a failed parse alternative rather than a fault; see parse-layer.
4L45–46The back-pointer is wired AFTER decode, mirroring Python's Message.transaction. It is why Trace must outlive everything built on it — a moved-from Trace dangles every EventNode and every Block.

EventNode tree, then the Block init spine

Two structural steps happen before any matching, and both are straight ports of the Python substrate you already know: to_tree (from blocks/utils/tree_utils.py) links transactions into a message tree, and init_block (from event_processing.py) turns every node into exactly one leaf Block — ton_transfer, call_contract, or tick_tock — connected in the same shape.

Our fixture's tree, from the lab run above: the ext-in wallet tx becomes call_contract 0xcfc2d330, its child is call_contract 0xa7733acd (owner -> vesting request), and that node has two children — the outgoing ton_transfer the vesting contract forwards, and call_contract 0xf7733acd, the response callback. Five leaves, one root. The deep dive on ordering, merging and the deliberate deviations from Python lives in block-tree.

ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/BlockTree.h:38–64EventNode — the sentence that explains the whole treecpp8e6a5c17
381// A node in the message tree. For a normal transaction the node's msg is the
39// incoming message; for a notification/log leaf it is the destination-less
40// outgoing message.
41struct EventNode {
42 const Message *msg{nullptr};
43 const Transaction *tx{nullptr};
44 bool is_tick_tock{false};
453 EventNode *parent{nullptr};
46 std::vector<EventNode *> children;
47 
48 std::optional<std::uint32_t> opcode() const {
49 return msg != nullptr ? msg->opcode32() : std::nullopt;
50 }
51 
522 // Mirrors EventNode.get_lt.
53 std::int64_t lt() const {
54 if (is_tick_tock && tx != nullptr) {
55 return tx->lt;
56 }
57 if (msg != nullptr && msg->created_lt) {
58 return *msg->created_lt;
59 }
60 if (msg != nullptr) {
61 return msg->tx_lt;
62 }
63 return 0;
64 }
1L38–40Read this comment twice. A node's msg is normally the INCOMING message, but a log/notification leaf (an outgoing message with no destination) gets its own node whose msg is that outgoing message. That is why an event-log opcode can be a matcher anchor at all — it is a first-class node, not a field of its parent.
2L52–63lt() is the sort key for the entire spine (next_blocks is kept in min_lt-ascending order), so its fallback chain is load-bearing: tick-tock uses the transaction's lt, everything else prefers created_lt and only falls back to tx_lt. Get this wrong and blocks reorder, which changes which candidate a matcher meets first.
3L45–46Raw pointers into EventTree's arena — no ownership here. Python's GC hides this chain; in C++ the lifetime Trace -> EventTree -> BlockArena is what TraceContext (below) exists to keep intact.

3L102A deliberate deviation from Python: the order invariant is maintained at construction and after every merge, instead of Python's sort-at-every-walk-site. Same observable semantics, but it means C++ code may read next_blocks raw — and it means a mutation that forgets to re-sort is a real bug class.

The one matcher that fires — spec form

Only one matcher in the artifact can possibly match this trace: the anchor prefilter keeps a matcher whose anchor is an opcode set only if one of its opcodes appears on the spine, and 0xA7733ACD appears exactly once. Here is the whole matcher, in the form a human writes and commits.

Thirty lines, and every one of them shows up in the output you already saw. Two opcode constants, a two-node chain, a parse, and six output fields. The --match run below stops after the match phase, so you can see the captures before any building happens.

indexer/indexer/events/mch/specs/vesting.mch:1–30specs/vesting.mch — the entire matchertext1cd0bd52
1# Vesting send-message matcher — ported from blocks/vesting.py
21# VestingSendMessageBlockMatcher. Linear two-node chain (M1 shape): the
3# owner->vesting request plus its required response callback. The response is
4# consumed (legacy child_matcher optional=False) but only the request feeds the
5# build. VestingAddWhiteListBlockMatcher stays hand-written (out of scope).
6#
7# Fully declarative build (M4 §9): field-for-field parity with
8# build_vesting_send_message_core in blocks/vesting.py. `message_boc_str` uses
9# the b64 builtin over the parsed `message_cell` — b64 BOC-encodes a raw Cell
10# before base64 (mirrors the legacy `message_cell.to_boc()`).
11 
122opcode VestingSendMessage = 0xA7733ACD
13opcode VestingSendMessageResponse = 0xF7733ACD
14 
15matcher vesting_send_message {
163 produces VestingSendMessageBlock
17 entry @send
18 
194 op VestingSendMessage @send -> op VestingSendMessageResponse @response
20 
215 parse send as VestingSendMessage
22 out {
23 sender: account(send.msg.source)
24 vesting: account(send.msg.destination)
25 query_id: send.body.query_id
26 message_boc_str: b64(send.body.message_cell)
27 message_destination: account(send.body.message_destination)
28 message_value: amount(send.body.message_value)
29 }
30}
1L2–5"The response is consumed … but only the request feeds the build" is the single most important invariant on this page. Matching a block does two independent things: it may bind a capture the build reads, AND it removes the block from the spine so no later matcher can claim it. The response capture exists purely for the second effect.
2L12–13opcode declarations are spec-local names. Nothing downstream knows the identifier — the compiled artifact carries only the number, in decimal. Grepping mch_ir.json for A7733ACD finds nothing; grep 2809346765.
3L16–17produces names a Python Block CLASS, but the emitted btype is vesting_send_message — the frontend maps class -> btype through indexer/events/mch/btypes.py. The btype is what the serializer dispatches on, so that table is a real part of the contract, not a naming convenience.
4L19The chain arrow walks the BLOCK tree's next_blocks, not the message tree. In this fixture 0xf7733acd happens to be a direct child of the anchor, but the walker's reachability rules (matcher-runtime) are what actually decide, and they are not simply "is a child".
5L21–29send.msg.* reads the message envelope and is available immediately; send.body.* is null until the parse statement on line 21 has run. Both are attribute accesses on the same capture, and nothing in the syntax marks the difference — the ordering of statements is the only thing that makes body non-null (parse-layer, build-programs).
captured output
$ ton-mch-engine.exe --match -I <ir> -T "tests/traces/03RZCW7mu3eJp-FWifVzKsRHafUrqQNu4E6YwZxvXJ0=.lz4"
=== 03RZCW7mu3eJp-FWifVzKsRHafUrqQNu4E6YwZxvXJ0=.lz4
MATCH vesting_send_message anchor=call_contract#a7733acd@45769974000002 consumed=[call_contract#a7733acd@45769974000002,call_contract#f7733acd@45769974000005] captures={send=call_contract#a7733acd@45769974000002,response=call_contract#f7733acd@45769974000005}
Match phase only — no build, no merge. block_key is btype#opcode@lt, the identity used in every dump. Note consumed has two entries while the build reads only one: the response is claimed and removed from the spine regardless.

…and the same matcher, compiled

ir/mch_ir.json is the committed compilation of every .mch file — one JSON document, 11.5k lines, produced by the Python frontend (indexer/events/mch/) and consumed by both engines. It has three top-level parts that matter here: matchers (one row per matcher), nodes (a FLAT array of match-tree nodes shared by all matchers and referenced by index), and registration_order (the priority order matchers run in). Our matcher is matchers[32].

Read the row next to the spec above and the mapping is one-to-one. The point of showing both is that they are the same object: nothing is inferred at runtime, and if you ever wonder what the engine will actually do, this file — not the spec — is the answer. ir-artifact covers the format properly.

1L9293–92982809346765 is 0xA7733ACD. This set is also the runtime prefilter key: classify_trace collects the trace's opcode inventory once and skips a matcher's entire BFS when the intersection is empty. On this trace 32 of 33 matchers are skipped without ever touching a block.
2L9299root is an INDEX into the document-level nodes array, not an inline subtree. Match trees are pooled across all matchers, so node indices are global and a node can in principle be shared.
3L9303–9312Captures are declared with cardinality (one vs a list form) and in spec order — and that order is their SLOT order. The generated build function addresses them positionally as env.slots[0], never by name, so reordering captures in a spec silently changes the compiled program.
4L9313–9314Both default to true: after a successful match the anchor's remaining excess/bounce children are auto-appended to the consumed set. That is the auto=[] field in the --classify line — empty here, because this trace has neither.
5L9315–9322build_program is an ordered STATEMENT list, not an expression tree. parse is a statement with a side effect: it fills slots[0].body. That is why spec statement order is semantically significant, as flagged on the spec excerpt above.

BuildOutcome build_32_vesting_send_message(BuildEnv &env) {
  (void)env;
  BuildOutcome o = BuildOutcome::accepted();
  Value pt0 = env.slots[0];
  EvalResult sp0 = rt_parse(env, pt0, std::vector<std::string>{"VestingSendMessage"});
  if (sp0.faulted) return BuildOutcome::rejected(std::move(sp0.message));
  Value::Fields fs1;
  const Value &v2 = env.slots[0];
  EvalResult r3 = rt_access_build(env, v2, "msg");
  if (r3.faulted) return BuildOutcome::rejected(std::move(r3.message));
  Value v3 = std::move(r3.value);
  EvalResult r4 = rt_access_build(env, v3, "source");
  if (r4.faulted) return BuildOutcome::rejected(std::move(r4.message));
A third representation of the same matcher: the build program is COMPILED to C++ at build time by mch-codegen (a CMake step), not interpreted. This file lives in the build tree and is not in git — which is why it is shown as captured output rather than an excerpt. Note env.slots[0] and the positional capture access, and that every step can reject the whole match. Full story in build-programs.

Mode dispatch and the core/harness split

main.cpp is a flat option parser followed by a chain of early returns. Every mode is a run_* free function that owns its own lifecycle; nothing is shared but the parsed -I / -T values and one startup check (validate_registries(), placed ahead of dispatch so even the self-test modes get it — see parse-layer).

Underneath, the code is split in two on a hard line. ClassifyCore.{h,cpp} is the PURE pipeline: (TraceContext + LoadedIr + LookupSource + generated build table) -> a buffered per-trace result, with no stdout, no filesystem, no fixture knowledge and no rendering. Classify.cpp is the harness that prints. That split is what lets the production actor reuse the identical pipeline (prod-path) and, more immediately, it is why a diff between --classify and --classify-prod can only come from the loader or the lookup source, never from the matching.

1L297–311The -schema and -prod variants are not different pipelines: they run the SAME ClassifyCore with a different trace loader and a different lookup source. They exist to be A/B-diffed against the plain modes, which is how the production ingestion path is proven equivalent to the fixture path.
2L313–321--classify and --actions are the same run; they diverge at one boolean deep inside the shared adapter (below). If the two dumps ever disagree about WHICH actions exist, the cause is the serializer's fill table, not the engine.
3L314"no scheduler needed" repeats on every dump mode and is a real constraint, not a note: all of these return before the td::actor::Scheduler at the bottom of main. Single-threaded, deterministic, no actor context — required, because their stdout is compared byte-for-byte against Python.

112// semantics) + Phase E post-process passes, buffered. `arena` is the caller's
113// (usually ctx.arena) — the pipeline allocates produced/proxy blocks from it.
114ClassifyResult classify_trace(TraceContext &ctx, const LoadedIr &ir,
115 const ClassifySetup &setup, const LookupSource &src);
1L94–95"Trace-independent" is the whole point: matcher selection, the build-fn table, the lookup kinds and the anchor prefilters are computed ONCE per process. Anything you see recomputed per trace in the loop below is there because it genuinely depends on the trace.
2L99The build table is a map from artifact matcher index to a plain function pointer, selected by the ARTIFACT's sha256. A mismatched artifact/binary pair cannot run silently — prepare_classify reports and the adapter exits 2.
3L109No I/O in either signature. prepare_classify takes an already-loaded LoadedIr; classify_trace takes an already-loaded TraceContext. Reading files is the caller's job, which is exactly what makes both callable from an actor that gets its rows from Postgres instead.
4L111–115arena is the CALLER's (ctx.arena): produced and proxy blocks are allocated into the same arena as the leaves, so the whole block graph shares one lifetime and pointers stay valid for as long as the caller holds the context.
ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/ClassifyCore.h:44–71The result: rendering-agnostic and atomiccpp5c70ffae
441// One produced action, RENDERING-AGNOSTIC: raw block pointers + fire-time aux.
45// The adapter renders block_key(anchor)/data/consumed/aux or builds an Action
46// row from `produced`. Pointers reference the caller's arena (TraceContext),
47// valid for as long as the caller keeps it alive.
48struct CoreAction {
49 std::string matcher_name;
50 Block *anchor;
51 Block *produced;
52 std::vector<Block *> aux; // fire-time excess/bounce auto-append (anchor)
53};
54 
55// Buffered ATOMIC per-trace result: on a mid-trace throw the pipeline sets
562// `failure` (+ reason) and returns whatever was collected — NOTHING is emitted
57// by the core; the adapter decides (a dump reproduces today's TRACE_FAIL line,
58// production commits only on success).
59struct ClassifyResult {
60 std::vector<CoreAction> actions; // surviving post-pass, in fire order
61 bool failure = false;
62 std::string failure_reason;
63 // Trace-terminal failure category (additive telemetry; none unless `failure`).
643 FailureCategory failure_category = FailureCategory::none;
65 // Step 2c basic-actions fallback (try_classify_basic_actions): populated ONLY
66 // when `failure` — a fresh leaf-only classify (no matchers) + the
67 // post-processor chain, one CoreAction per surviving spine block of a basic
68 // btype (call_contract / contract_deploy / ton_transfer). Production commits
69 // these when classification fails. Ungated (corpus has no failing traces).
70 std::vector<CoreAction> fallback_actions;
71};
1L44–53A CoreAction is three block pointers, not data: anchor (where the matcher fired, used as the dump's identity), produced (the composite whose data holds the build output), and aux (the fire-time excess/bounce auto-append). Rendering — or building an Action row — happens strictly in the adapter.
2L56–58"ATOMIC" and "NOTHING is emitted by the core" together: a mid-trace throw does not leave a half-emitted trace. The core buffers, sets failure, and hands the decision to the adapter — a dump prints TRACE_FAIL, production commits nothing. This is the C++ image of the Python classifier's per-trace try/except boundary.
3L64–70The fallback mirrors Python's try_classify_basic_actions: on failure, reclassify with NO matchers and keep the surviving ton_transfer / call_contract / contract_deploy leaves. Note the honesty in the comment — no corpus trace fails, so this path is ungated, i.e. untested by the twins.

118// per surviving action either the classify line (emit_action) or the serialized

121int run_dump(const std::string &artifact_path, const std::vector<std::string> &paths,
122 bool actions_mode, const TraceContextLoader &load_ctx,
123 const LookupSourceFactory &lookup_factory) {
124 auto r_ir = load_ir(artifact_path);

126 std::fprintf(stderr, "failed to load IR artifact: %s\n", r_ir.error().message().c_str());
127 return 2;
128 }
129 LoadedIr ir = r_ir.move_as_ok();
1302 warn_missing_artifact_parsers(ir);

1323 ClassifySetup setup = prepare_classify(ir);
133 if (setup.table_missing || setup.fn_missing) {
134 std::fprintf(stderr, "%s\n", setup.error.c_str());

136 }

1L115–120The contract of the whole dump surface in one comment, ending with the line that matters: the two modes differ ONLY in the per-action render. Any structural difference between --classify and --actions output is therefore a serializer fact, never a harness fact.
2L130A preflight, not an assertion: a matcher referencing a message type nobody registered is warned about on stderr and build-skipped, so a half-wired protocol degrades into "this matcher never fires" instead of a crash (parse-layer).
3L132–136prepare_classify runs once, before the fixture loop — and a table/fn mismatch exits 2 rather than running with a stale generated build table. That guard is what makes "rebuild the C++ after regenerating the IR" a hard failure instead of a mysterious diff.
4L137–139SKIP lines are part of the compared stdout, sorted for stability: which matchers the engine refuses to run is itself a gate artifact. Our corpus run prints zero of them — every matcher in the committed artifact is runnable today.

The loop that actually runs it

classify_trace is a port of the Python event_processing outer loop, and its shape is worth memorizing because every later chapter plugs into it: FOR EACH matcher in priority order, do a full BFS over the spine and try to build at every block. Not the other way around. That ordering is why the global matcher list order matters in the Python engine and matters identically here — an earlier matcher consumes blocks a later one would have wanted.

After every matcher has had its pass, host-side post-processing runs over a flat snapshot of the spine. Those passes are not expressible in the DSL (they merge across matcher results), so they stay hand-written on both sides.

ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/ClassifyCore.cpp:465–492The matcher loopcppa11f473c
4651 std::vector<CoreAction> pending;
466 try {
4672 for (const IncludedMatcher &im : setup.included) {
468 if (!anchor_can_match(im.filter)) {
469 continue; // B1: no spine op/btype can satisfy this anchor — skip traversal
470 }
471 const CompiledMatcher &m = ir.matchers[im.matcher_index];
472 auto fn = setup.build_fns.at(m.artifact_index);
473 std::size_t produced_from = pending.size();
474 // Python bfs_iter port: FIFO; cur's next_blocks are read AFTER try_build
475 // ran on cur (generator resume order) — merges mutate the tree mid-walk.
476 std::deque<Block *> queue{wrapper};
477 while (!queue.empty()) {
478 Block *cur = queue.front();
479 queue.pop_front();
4803 if (cur->parent == nullptr) {
481 try_build(m, fn, cur, ctx.arena, setup.kinds, src, pending);
482 }
4834 for (Block *n : cur->next_blocks) {
484 queue.push_back(n);
485 }
486 }
4875 // Fold this matcher's produced btypes into the inventory so a later
488 // btype-anchored matcher composing on them is not wrongly skipped.
489 for (std::size_t j = produced_from; j < pending.size(); j++) {
490 if (pending[j].produced != nullptr) inv_btypes.insert(pending[j].produced->btype);
491 }
492 }
1L465–466One try around the ENTIRE matcher loop, and every result accumulates in a local pending. Nothing escapes on the failure path — this is the buffering promised by ClassifyResult, and it is the reason a spec bug can never produce a partially classified trace.
2L467–471The prefilter short-circuit: with an opcode anchor and no matching opcode on the spine, the matcher's whole traversal is skipped. On our fixture this eliminates every matcher but one — and it is safe precisely because consumed blocks are never REMOVED from the inventory, so the set is a conservative superset.
3L480–482cur->parent == nullptr is the consumed guard. A block absorbed into a composite gets a parent, so later BFS passes still walk it but never attempt a build on it. This one line is the C++ equivalent of Python's parent check and the reason double-classification cannot happen.
4L483–485The subtle one: next_blocks is read AFTER try_build ran on cur, because a successful build MERGES blocks and mutates the tree mid-walk. Python gets this for free from generator resume order; here it is a deliberate statement ordering, and swapping the two lines would change which blocks the walk reaches.
5L487–491btypes grow, opcodes do not. A matcher anchored on a btype like jetton_transfer can only match blocks a previous matcher produced, so produced btypes are folded back into the inventory after each matcher — otherwise the prefilter would wrongly skip every composing matcher.

495 std::vector<Block *> spine;
496 {
497 std::deque<Block *> q{wrapper};
498 while (!q.empty()) {
499 Block *cur = q.front();
500 q.pop_front();
501 spine.push_back(cur);
502 for (Block *n : cur->next_blocks) q.push_back(n);
503 }

5052 std::set<Block *> removed;
506 post_process_dedust_liquidity(spine, removed);

Our matcher performs no lookups at all, which is part of why it makes a clean first example.

From captures to an Action row

--classify stops at the produced block. --actions takes one more step: build_action serializes that block into the wide Action schema the database actually stores — the C++ port of block_tree_serializer.py. The dispatch is a btype switch onto a fill_* function, exactly like the Python match block.btype you know.

This is where the fixed directional columns (source, destination, destination_secondary, amount, …) get filled and where anything left over goes into a per-type composite. Our matcher's six build fields split four/two. actions takes this apart properly.

2L199A produced btype with no fill_* is silently skipped in --actions but still printed by --classify, so the two dumps can legitimately have different line counts. That is a coverage signal, not a bug: it tells you which btypes are matched but not yet serializable.

diff-0 — the discipline behind every claim on this page

The C++ engine is a PORT, and the thing that makes a port trustworthy is not tests of the port's own opinions — it is running the same artifact through the original and demanding identical bytes. twins/py_classify.py runs the real Python IR engine (the same build_matchers + event_processing outer loop) and prints the exact same line format. So the correctness statement for the entire pipeline is a diff returning nothing.

One fixture is shown below because it fits on the page; the real gate is the same command over the whole 148-fixture corpus, plus the same treatment for --actions, --match, --parse-dump, and the schema/prod loader variants. gates is the full story, including how to run all of them and what each one actually protects.

captured output
$ diff <(ton-mch-engine.exe --classify -I "$IR" -T "$F" 2>/dev/null) <(venv0/python.exe twins/py_classify.py "$IR" "$F" 2>/dev/null) && echo "OK: cpp == python, 0 diff lines"
OK: cpp == python, 0 diff lines
Both sides consume the SAME mch_ir.json. That is the point: the artifact is the shared contract, and a divergence is always in an engine's execution of it, never in two independent readings of a spec.

Check yourself

Four things you can verify right now. If any of them surprises you, that is the chapter to read next.

1. **Know the corpus baseline.** The run below is the first thing to check after any change: 148 fixtures, 199 actions, and zero SKIP lines. Any page — including this one — that quotes different numbers is out of date.

2. **Prove the response capture is consumed but never read.** Read specs/vesting.mch line 19 next to the --match output above, then confirm in mch_ir.json that nodes[328] (line 11510) has no child and that response appears nowhere in matchers[32]'s build_program. A capture can be bound purely to remove a block from the spine — which is exactly why matcher ORDER changes results.

3. **Find your own anchor fixture.** Run --classify over tests/traces, pick any single-action line, take its anchor=btype#opcode@lt, convert the opcode to DECIMAL and grep it in mch_ir.json to find the matcher, then open the matching .mch in indexer/indexer/events/mch/specs/. You should be able to predict the data={…} keys from the spec's out block before you look at the dump. If you can, you have the loop.

4. **Test the claim that --classify and --actions are the same run.** Run both over the whole corpus and compare the anchor= values line by line. They may differ ONLY where a produced btype has no fill_* — the set you would get by listing the btypes absent from build_action's dispatch in src/ActionBuild.cpp (around line 543). Any other difference means the harness is doing something the comment on run_dump claims it does not.

captured output
$ ton-mch-engine.exe --classify -I <ir> -T tests/traces 2>/dev/null | grep -c "^ACTION " # then the same with: grep -c "^=== "
199
148
199 actions over 148 fixtures, and the --classify run prints no SKIP lines at all — every matcher in the committed artifact is runnable against the committed build table.
Connected scopes
  • value — every data field, capture and Action column on this page is an mch::Value; its kinds and rendering rules are what make the dumps comparable
  • block-tree — to_tree / init_block / merge semantics — the substrate this chapter only sketches, including the deliberate deviations from the Python tree
  • ir-artifact — the full format of mch_ir.json: node kinds, capture cardinality, registration order, and how IrLoader turns rows into CompiledMatcher
  • matcher-runtime — what op X @cap -> op Y @cap actually walks, how try_build accepts or rejects, and the prefilter this chapter uses without explaining
  • parse-layer — the parse send as VestingSendMessage statement resolves a name against the message-parser registry; a failed parse is a null body, not an error
  • build-programs — statements, expression nodes, host builtins like account/amount/b64, and the generated build functions shown here only as captured output
  • actions — build_action's full fill table, the post-process passes that can remove an action, and how accounts/tx_hashes are assembled
  • gates — the diff-0 run at the end of this page is one of ~8 gates; that chapter runs them all and says what each protects
  • prod-path — --classify-schema / --classify-prod are the same ClassifyCore with a production loader and lookup source; that is where the split introduced here pays off

  • ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/GenBuilds.h — the three generated build tables (ir / vectors / testbed) and their per-document sha guards. Its header comment explains why the pairing is correct by construction — read it if prepare_classify ever exits 2 on you (~55 LOC)
  • ton-index-worker/cmake-build-debug-visual-studio/ton-mch-engine/generated/builds_ir_generated.cpp — the generated build functions, shown here as captured output because it is a BUILD-TREE file, not committed — it is regenerated by a CMake step from mch_ir.json and must never be edited (~5k LOC)
  • ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/Value.{h,cpp} — the value type every capture, data field and Action column is made of, plus the rendering that makes dumps comparable. It is chapter 2 (value) precisely because everything here assumes it
  • ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/parse/ParseVesting.cpp — the parser behind parse send as VestingSendMessage — it fully deserializes an inner int_msg_info header. Its header comment states its one documented deviation; parse-layer (~79 LOC)
  • ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/twins/py_classify.py — the Python twin whose output this chapter diffs against. It runs the REAL Python IR engine plus a thin re-implementation of the dump format; gates (~400 LOC)
  • indexer/indexer/events/mch/btypes.py — the Block-class -> btype table the frontend uses to turn produces VestingSendMessageBlock into "vesting_send_message". A flat dict; the only reason to open it is to add a row
  • ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/{SchemaTraceLoader,ParsedBlockLookupSource,MchClassifierActor}.cpp — the production-side loader, lookup source and actor that the --schema/--prod modes dispatch into. Named in this chapter's dispatch excerpt, owned by prod-path

Value — the engine's currency

Everything downstream of the trace loader speaks one type: mch::Value. A matcher's where expression, a parsed message body, a build program's capture, a host function's return, an Action column — all of them are Values, and every equality, render and null-check in this tutorial is a rule about this one struct. It is a hand-discriminated tagged union of 14 kinds with a deliberately Python-shaped semantics: unbounded integers (RefInt256, because jetton amounts overflow int64), an Amount wrapper that can be present-but-empty (Amount(None)), an Account that can be present-but-addr_none, and two different map kinds that differ only in attribute-access rules. Read this chapter for four things you will otherwise re-derive painfully later: why null and addr_none are not the same value (and why the two parser universes disagree about which one a missing address becomes), why Cell-derived fields are compared by root hash instead of bytes, why there are two equality functions rather than one, and why the VType enum may only ever be appended to.

What a Value is, and why the enum only grows

Value.h opens with the only design rationale you get for the whole model, and it is worth reading as a spec rather than as a comment: each bullet is a Python behaviour that had to be imported rather than improved on. The C++ side is a mirror of what indexer/events/mch/expr_eval.py produces, and the twin gates compare RENDERED values (gates) — so every place the two could disagree had to be decided deliberately, once, here.

The VType enum carries an unwritten rule that the design docs state explicitly: it is APPEND-ONLY. W12-BRIDGE-DESIGN.md §3 rejects a native external-address kind on exactly this ground — "Value.h VType enum is append-only and adding a member forces a clean engine-obj rebuild". The hazard is mechanical, not stylistic: several translation units in this engine are GENERATED into the build tree (wheres_generated.cpp, builds_ir_generated.cpp, …) and ninja will happily reuse their stale object files after a Value layout or enum change, producing a binary whose halves disagree about the struct — which shows up as heap corruption at runtime, not as a link error. Inserting a member in the middle of the enum is the worse version of the same bug, because generated code stores kind tags.

ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/Value.h:1–29Value.h — the four decisions everything else inheritscpp1a6db5af
1// Runtime value model for the MCH expression VM (docs/mch-ir-spec.md §7, §12).
2//
3// This is the C++ mirror of the Python reference values (blocks/utils AccountId
4// / Amount / Asset, plus plain int/str/bytes/list/dict) that the expression
5// evaluators in indexer/events/mch/expr_eval.py and mch_ir/expr.py produce and
6// consume. Only the semantics the conformance vectors exercise are modelled;
7// design decisions and deliberate deviations are documented per-member below.
8//
91// Key decisions:
10// - Integers are td::RefInt256 for EVERY expression integer (Int and Amount
11// value). Python ints are unbounded and jetton amounts overflow int64, so a
12// fixed 256-bit big-int is the faithful carrier. int64 inputs (JSON numbers,
13// host fields) are widened on entry.
142// - AccountId carries a distinct addr_none state (present-but-empty address),
15// separate from a null Value — mirrors AccountId(None): repr "addr_none",
16// as_str() -> null. Addresses are normalized to the raw "wc:HEX" form with
17// UPPERCASE hex (matches AccountId.as_str()); only the raw form is parsed
18// (the vectors never use user-friendly base64 addresses).
193// - Asset == string is JETTON-ONLY: a case-insensitive compare of the jetton
20// master's raw string (Asset.__eq__ lowercases both sides without
21// re-normalizing `other`). A TON asset vs a string FAULTS — __eq__ reads the
22// jetton master before the is_ton branch, so the "ton"-string match is dead.
234// - Dict vs Obj are two distinct map kinds: Dict is pure key lookup (Python
24// dict / block data map / record literal), Obj is attribute access with the
25// special `.exit_code` envelope accessor (Python SimpleNamespace, the $obj
26// decode of a message envelope / body / lookup record). They differ only in
27// attribute-access semantics (§7.2).
285// - List/Dict/Obj payloads are held behind shared_ptr so a Value stays cheaply
29// copyable (values are immutable once built; sharing is safe).
1L9–13Every expression integer is a 256-bit big-int, not an int64, and that is a correctness requirement rather than caution: Python ints are unbounded and a jetton amount routinely exceeds int64. Widening happens on entry (JSON numbers, host fields), so no arithmetic path in the engine ever has to think about overflow — but it also means num is a refcounted handle that can be NULL, and a null num is meaningful (see the Amount line in the kind list below, and make_amount_none).
2L14–18The distinction the rest of this chapter keeps returning to: Account has a third state besides "has an address" and "is absent" — present-but-empty (addr_none). It mirrors AccountId(None), whose repr is addr_none but whose as_str() is None. A null Value and an addr_none Account are different values and compare unequal.
3L19–22A parity bug faithfully preserved: Python's Asset.__eq__ reads the jetton master's string BEFORE it checks the is_ton branch, so comparing a TON asset with a string raises instead of matching "ton". The C++ side reproduces the raise as a fault, and the dead "ton" branch stays dead. Fixing this would be an A/B diff, not a bug fix (gates).
4L23–27Dict and Obj carry the same payload and differ ONLY in attribute-access semantics — Obj is a SimpleNamespace (message envelope, parsed body, lookup record) and gets the .exit_code envelope accessor; Dict is a plain map (block data, record literal). Because they are distinct kinds, a Dict never compares equal to an Obj with identical fields.
5L28–29Containers are shared, never copied — which is only safe because a Value is immutable once built. There is no mutating API on Value anywhere in the engine; a "changed" object is a new make_obj over rebuilt fields.

533 Amount, // td::RefInt256 nanoton-style amount; null num == Python Amount(None)

1L45A Value can point at a matched Block — the tree from block-tree — through a raw non-owning pointer. That works because blocks live in an arena that outlives every Value derived from it, per trace. It also means Block-valued equality is pointer identity (mirroring Python's default __eq__), not structural.
2L47–49APPEND-ONLY. Adding Foo at the end costs a clean rebuild of the engine objects; inserting it in the middle silently renumbers every kind tag baked into already-compiled generated TUs. When the ABI bridge needed a representation for external addresses it built an Obj{bits,value} rather than pay this (parse-layer).
3L53–55Amount is not a synonym for Int: it is a wrapper kind whose payload may be null (Amount(None)), and Account is not a synonym for Str. Both exist so that Python's wrapper types survive the round trip into the dumps — collapsing either one would make the twin comparison lossy.
4L61Float exists only because fixture data contains one (a GetGems price). The language has no floats — but the fault is narrower than "any use": a float-backed AMOUNT (same dnum, amount_float set) faults on ==, on arithmetic and on .value, the three pinned vectors; a BARE Float faults on arithmetic and attribute access, yet an == against it merely returns false, because the guard tests t == Amount && amount_float and a Float slips past it into container_eq. Rendering is split too: BuildDriver prints float:<%.17g> (the line's "bare -> unrenderable" comment predates that), while describe() and --parse-dump still print ?. A dead end by design either way, not an escape hatch.

The struct: one flat bag, hand-discriminated

There is no std::variant here. Every kind's payload is a named member of one struct, and only the members relevant to t are meaningful. That is a deliberate trade — it keeps the type trivially copyable-ish and cheap to pass around, at the cost that nothing prevents you from reading str off an Int. When you read engine code, always check t first; v.str on the wrong kind is empty rather than wrong-looking.

The factories below are the ONLY sanctioned way to build a Value (plus the default-constructed null()), and several of them encode a contract that the struct itself cannot: make_account_raw takes an ALREADY-normalized string, make_amount_none deliberately leaves num null, make_amount_float sets a flag that makes the value un-usable in expressions.

1L91Amount(None): a present Amount carrying nothing. Its documented behaviour — "== only to itself" — is what a spec relies on when a protocol legitimately has no amount yet; it is NOT null, so x == null is false for it.
2L93"caller normalized" is a real contract with no enforcement: pass a lowercase or malformed address here and it silently becomes a value that will never compare equal to a properly built one. Every call site pairs this with normalize_raw_address (below) — that pairing IS the invariant.
3L102–105The entire read API: an is_null predicate and one field lookup. There are no getters per kind — consumers switch on t and read the member directly, which is why the members above are public and why reading the wrong one is possible.
4L107–108describe() is diagnostic-first (FAIL lines, fault messages) — it is not the PRIMARY dump rendering. The comparable renders live in ParseDump.cpp and BuildDriver.cpp and are deliberately different formats. One caveat: ParseDump's render_value ends in default: return v.describe();, so for the kinds it does not case on — List, Block, Float — describe() IS the de-facto --parse-dump render (and, having no Float case, it prints ? for one of them).

Field access: Dict, Obj, and the .exit_code hop

Both map kinds store a vector<pair<string, Value>>, not a std::map. The reason is size, not order: field counts are tiny, so a linear scan beats a node-per-key tree and the whole Fields vector is a single allocation.

Insertion order is PRESERVED but almost nowhere observable. Every comparable render sorts keys — render_fields_sorted in ParseDump.cpp, the explicit key sort in BuildDriver.cpp, and sorted(...) in both Python twins — and neither equality function is order-sensitive (structural_equal and container_eq both compare key SETS). What genuinely sees insertion order is describe(), the positional assertions in DexRecordsTest.cpp (key_at(d, 0, "asset") and friends), and the ABI bridge's rule that "$" is emitted FIRST so a consumer can switch on .$ (W12-BRIDGE-DESIGN.md §3, Struct row).

The lookup itself is trivial; the interesting behaviour is one level up, in the expression runtime's rt_access, which is where the Dict/Obj distinction finally pays for itself.

2L144–148First match wins, so a Fields vector with a duplicate key is not an error — it shadows. Nothing in the engine builds one today, but a parser that emplace_backs the same name twice would produce a value whose second entry is unreachable by lookup yet still counted by every size-based comparison (see structural_equal and container_eq below, both of which compare size() first).

323EvalResult rt_access(const Value &obj, const std::string &field) {

338 return rt_ok(ec != nullptr ? *ec : Value::null());

1L324–326Null PROPAGATES through attribute access — x.a.b on a null x is null, never a fault. This is the single most load-bearing null rule in the language: it is why an unparsed body (.body null after a failed parse, parse-layer) makes a whole guard expression evaluate to null rather than blow up.
2L331–341The one accessor that is not a lookup: .exit_code on an Obj hops through the envelope's transaction sub-object to compute_exit_code. Note the asymmetry — a missing transaction FAULTS (you asked a message-envelope question of a non-envelope), but a transaction without the field yields null (the transaction genuinely had no compute phase).
3L342–353A MISSING field is a fault, not null — the opposite of the null-propagation rule two lines above. Absent-key means the spec is wrong about the shape; null-object means the data was absent. Keeping those distinguishable is why Value::field returns a pointer instead of an optional-Value.
4L348–353Dict and Obj reach identical code here — only the fault MESSAGE differs ("object" vs "data"). The kinds are kept distinct for equality and for the .exit_code envelope rule, not because plain lookup behaves differently.

Accounts, and the two meanings of nothing

An address enters the engine as text from three directions — a transaction account off the trace loader, a parsed message field, an address literal in a spec — and all three funnel through normalize_raw_address before becoming an Account. Canonical form is raw wc:HEX with UPPERCASE hex, matching Python's AccountId.as_str(). User-friendly base64 addresses are simply not a thing in this engine.

The important part is what happens to a MISSING address, because the two parser universes answer differently. On the pytoniq-parity path an addr_none in a message body becomes a NULL Value; on the ABI path it becomes Value::make_account_none() — a present Account with addr_none set (parse-layer). Both are correct for their own twin, and the run below shows the pytoniq answer landing in a real dump. A spec that null-tests an address field is therefore asking a question whose meaning depends on which parser produced it.

One more asymmetry worth internalising: the account() builtin FAULTS on a string it cannot normalize (and maps the literal string "addr_none" to make_account_none()), while the trace-side helper passes a non-normalizable address through unchanged rather than failing the trace.

ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/Value.cpp:225–259normalize_raw_address — the canonicalization every comparison depends oncppd3850aa4
225std::optional<std::string> normalize_raw_address(const std::string &s) {
2261 auto colon = s.find(':');
227 if (colon == std::string::npos || colon == 0) {
228 return std::nullopt;
229 }
230 const std::string wc_part = s.substr(0, colon);
231 const std::string hex_part = s.substr(colon + 1);
2324 
233 // Workchain: optional leading '-', then digits.
234 std::size_t p = 0;
235 if (wc_part[p] == '-') {
236 p++;
237 }
238 if (p >= wc_part.size()) {
239 return std::nullopt;
240 }
241 for (; p < wc_part.size(); p++) {
242 if (!std::isdigit(static_cast<unsigned char>(wc_part[p]))) {
243 return std::nullopt;
244 }
245 }
2462 // 256-bit account id == exactly 64 hex digits.
247 if (hex_part.size() != 64) {
248 return std::nullopt;
249 }
2503 std::string up;
251 up.reserve(64);
252 for (char c : hex_part) {
253 if (!std::isxdigit(static_cast<unsigned char>(c))) {
254 return std::nullopt;
255 }
256 up.push_back(static_cast<char>(std::toupper(static_cast<unsigned char>(c))));
257 }
258 return wc_part + ":" + up;
259}
1L226–229Parsing is deliberately narrow: exactly one colon-separated raw form. There is no base64 branch, no bounce-flag handling, no testnet variant — the vectors never use them, and adding one would silently change what compares equal.
2L246–249Exactly 64 hex digits — no zero-padding of a short account id, no truncation of a long one. A 63-digit address is rejected rather than repaired, so a malformed address becomes a visible fault (via the builtin) instead of a value that quietly matches nothing.
3L250–258Uppercasing is the whole point of the function: Account equality is a plain str == (no case folding anywhere), so canonicalization at construction is what makes two addresses from different sources comparable at all. Contrast Asset-vs-string equality, which DOES lowercase both sides at compare time — an inconsistency inherited from Python, not a choice made here.
4L232–245The workchain is validated as an optional - plus digits and then carried through as TEXT, not parsed to an int: -1:AB.. and -01:AB.. normalize to different strings and will not compare equal. Nothing produces the padded form today, which is why this has never bitten.

Both halves of this chapter in two real dump lines. response_address=null is an addr_none in the wire body that the pytoniq path turned into a NULL Value (the ABI path would have rendered addr_none here). from_address / destination show the canonical uppercase raw form. And forward_payload=cellhash:… versus custom_payload=null is the next section: a present cell rendered by root hash, an absent one rendered as null.

Cells: the root hash is the currency

A Cell Value is a td::Ref<vm::Cell> and compares by root hash everywhere. The subtler rule is about cell-derived STRINGS and BYTES: a forward_payload that a parser serialized to BOC bytes, or a b64() builtin output, cannot be compared bytewise between the two engines — pytoniq and td produce different BOC containers (ordering, CRC provenance) for the same cell tree. Plan §12 resolves this by rendering such fields as cellhash:<HEX-UPPER> in every comparable dump.

The gate is by FIELD NAME, not by value type — is_boc_field("forward_payload") is true, is_boc_field("comment") is false — because comment, bitcoin_txid and pubkey are raw non-BOC bytes whose exact bytes ARE the data. That set is small, hand-curated, and exported to the Python twins through --surface so a name can never be in the set on one side only.

(td_boc_serialize, just above the excerpt, is the other half of the same decision: once dumps compare by root hash, container byte order stops mattering, so the engine uses td's deterministic native writer everywhere. The former pytoniq-order writer — and a P3 exponential-re-walk DoS in it — went away with that change.)

179std::string boc_field_cellhash(const Value &v) {
180 auto hash_of = [](const td::Ref<vm::Cell> &cell) -> std::string {
1815 auto h = cell->get_hash();
182 static const char *hexd = "0123456789ABCDEF";
183 std::string out;
184 const unsigned char *p = h.as_slice().ubegin();
185 for (std::size_t i = 0; i < h.as_slice().size(); i++) {
186 out.push_back(hexd[p[i] >> 4]);
187 out.push_back(hexd[p[i] & 0xF]);
188 }
189 return "cellhash:" + out;
190 };
191 // Decode-fail marker (never throws — the dump must not abort/trace-fail on a
192 // bad BOC field). A short deterministic prefix aids diagnosis; both engines
193 // compute it identically from the same value type (str → the b64 string;
194 // bytes → base64 of the raw), so a fail-case would still be A/B-comparable.
195 // Never fires over the corpus (all BOC fields decode) — defensive only.
1963 auto decode_fail = [](const std::string &enc_prefix_src) {
197 return "cellhash:DECODE_FAIL:" + enc_prefix_src.substr(0, 12);
198 };
1992 if (v.t == VType::Cell) {
2004 return v.cell.is_null() ? std::string() : hash_of(v.cell); // null cell → fall back
201 }
202 std::string raw;
203 if (v.t == VType::Bytes) {
204 raw = v.str; // raw BOC bytes (MsgParse payload)
205 auto r_cell = vm::std_boc_deserialize(td::Slice(raw));
206 if (r_cell.is_error() || r_cell.ok().is_null()) {
207 return decode_fail(td::base64_encode(td::Slice(raw)));
208 }
209 return hash_of(r_cell.move_as_ok());
210 }
211 if (v.t == VType::Str) {
212 auto r = td::base64_decode(v.str); // b64() builtin output
213 if (r.is_error()) {
214 return decode_fail(v.str);
215 }
216 auto r_cell = vm::std_boc_deserialize(td::Slice(r.ok()));
217 if (r_cell.is_error() || r_cell.ok().is_null()) {
218 return decode_fail(v.str);
219 }
220 return hash_of(r_cell.move_as_ok());
221 }
222 return std::string(); // null / other type → fall back to normal render
223}
1L170–173The whole set: seven names, all of them fields whose value is a serialized cell tree. The exclusions in the comment are the interesting part — comment is UTF-8 text bytes and bitcoin_txid / pubkey are fixed-width binary, so hashing them would destroy the very content the twins are trying to compare.
2L199–210Three accepted input shapes for the same logical thing: an actual Cell, raw BOC Bytes (what a pytoniq-path parser produces for a payload), and a base64 Str (what the b64() builtin produces). All three collapse to the same hash — which is exactly the point, since the two engines choose different ones for the same field.
3L196–198The failure marker is itself designed to be A/B-comparable: both engines derive the 12-char prefix from the same source (the b64 string, or base64 of the raw bytes), so even a corrupt BOC field would diff cleanly instead of producing engine-specific noise. It has never fired over the corpus.
4L200An empty return means "not renderable as a cellhash — fall back to the normal render", and it is used for a null cell and for any other kind. That protocol is why every call site is the two-line if (rendered.empty()) pattern rather than a single expression.
5L181–189Hex is uppercased by hand rather than via to_hex — the render string is compared bytewise against Python's v.hash.hex().upper(), so case is data, not formatting.

Two equalities, on purpose

There are two deep-equality functions over Value and they are kept apart deliberately. structural_equal (in Value.cpp) is the HARNESS comparator: it answers "does this actual value match the expected value from a conformance vector", and it is asymmetric — the EXPECTED value's type drives the switch. rt_eq → raw_eq → container_eq (in ExprRuntime.cpp) is the LANGUAGE's ==: symmetric, with cross-type rules (Account vs Str, Asset vs Str) that a harness comparator has no business having.

The file comment states the reasoning plainly: "the runtime owns its own container == instead of borrowing the harness comparator… The two are behaviourally equivalent for the value model today — this is a separation of concerns so structural_equal stays harness-only." Read that claim narrowly, because it is scoped to the CONTAINER walks — and those do agree. The GUARDS in front of them do not: eq_result faults on a float-backed Amount, and on TON-asset-vs-string, before raw_eq is ever reached, whereas structural_equal quietly accepts the first of those pairings. The separation is what lets a change to what a spec's == means avoid silently changing what a vector accepts. If you are reading match/build behaviour, rt_eq is the one you want (build-programs); if you are reading a FAIL line from --vectors, it came from structural_equal (gates).

ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/ExprRuntime.cpp:126–153container_eq — the runtime's own deep equalitycpp239fc6ae
126// Symmetric `==` on containers, recursing through raw_eq (so nested scalars use
127// the language's typed equality). List: same length, element-wise. Dict/Obj:
128// same map kind + exact key-set + per-key equal. Cell: root-hash equal. Any
129// other/mismatched pairing is unequal. Mirrors Python list/dict `==`.
1301bool container_eq(const Value &l, const Value &r) {
131 if (l.t == VType::List && r.t == VType::List) {
132 const auto &xs = *l.items;
133 const auto &ys = *r.items;
134 if (xs.size() != ys.size()) return false;
135 for (std::size_t i = 0; i < xs.size(); i++) {
136 if (!raw_eq(xs[i], ys[i])) return false;
137 }
138 return true;
139 }
1402 if ((l.t == VType::Dict || l.t == VType::Obj) && l.t == r.t) {
141 if (!l.fields || !r.fields || l.fields->size() != r.fields->size()) return false;
142 for (const auto &kv : *l.fields) {
143 const Value *rv = r.field(kv.first);
144 if (rv == nullptr || !raw_eq(kv.second, *rv)) return false;
145 }
146 return true;
147 }
1483 if (l.t == VType::Cell && r.t == VType::Cell) {
149 if (l.cell.is_null() || r.cell.is_null()) return l.cell.is_null() && r.cell.is_null();
150 return l.cell->get_hash() == r.cell->get_hash();
151 }
1524 return false; // mismatched types / non-container
153}
1L130–139Mutual recursion with raw_eq, not with itself: nested SCALARS therefore get the language's typed equality (including the Account-vs-Str and Asset-vs-Str cross-type rules), which is precisely what structural_equal's self-recursion does NOT do.
2L140–147l.t == r.t means a Dict never equals an Obj even with identical fields, and the size check plus per-key lookup means the key SETS must match exactly while their order need not. Order is observable in neither comparator AND in neither dump — both renderers sort keys. Only describe() and the positional assertions in DexRecordsTest.cpp ever see it.
3L148–151Cells compare by root hash on this path too, so a spec's == on two cells is a hash compare and never a byte compare — the same decision as the dump's cellhash rendering, taken independently in the runtime.
4L152The catch-all: any mismatched pairing that reached here is simply unequal, never a fault. Faults in == come from two specific places above this (float-backed Amount, TON-asset vs string) — everything else degrades to false, which is what keeps a wrong-shaped guard from killing a match.

Truthiness: there isn't any

Python's "empty list is false" has NO analogue in this engine. A matcher's where expression must evaluate to a genuine Bool that is true; the Walker's check is !r.faulted && r.value.t == VType::Bool && r.value.boolean, so a null, a zero Int, an empty List, or a faulted evaluation are all equally "did not match" (matcher-runtime). That single line is why null-propagation is safe: an expression that silently became null just fails the guard instead of throwing.

The one place a Python-ish truthiness is reproduced is inside a host function, over a block's data dict — and it is narrow on purpose.

ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/host/BlockViews.cpp:53–57data_truthy — the only truthiness in the engine, and it is a host-side viewcppd4f65eb7
53bool data_truthy(const Block *b, const char *field) {
542 Value v = data_field(b, field);
551 return (v.t == VType::Bool && v.boolean) ||
56 (v.t == VType::Int && !v.num.is_null() && v.num->sgn() != 0);

1L55–56Only two kinds can be truthy: a true Bool and a non-zero Int. A missing field, a null, an empty string, an empty list — all false. It exists to mirror Python host code writing if block.data.get("has_internal_transfer") and is used by exactly one family of callers (the StonFi hosts), which is why it lives in host/BlockViews.h rather than in Value.h.
2L54It goes through data_field, which returns a null Value for an absent field — so "absent" and "present but null" collapse here. That collapse is fine for a host predicate and would be wrong in the expression language, where a missing field faults (block-tree covers Block::data).

Check yourself

Four things you can verify in a few minutes; each one pins a claim from this page.

1. THE NULL/ADDR_NONE SPLIT IS REAL, AND VISIBLE. Re-run the parse-dump command from the accounts section and grep for both spellings: --parse-dump -T tests\traces | Select-String 'addr_none' returns NOTHING over this corpus, while response_address=null and response=null are common. That is the pytoniq universe's answer to a missing address. Now read AbiBridge.cpp's adapt_address (parse-layer) and confirm the ABI path would have printed addr_none for the same wire bytes.

2. THE BOC SET REALLY IS NAME-GATED, AND SHARED. boc_field_names() in Value.cpp lists seven names; --surface prints the same seven; twins/cpp_surface.py reads them as BOC_FIELDS out of the committed cpp_surface.json. Add a name to boc_field_names(), rebuild, then regenerate cpp_surface.json — both dumps change together. Skip the regen and the A/B gate goes red, which is the enforcement (nothing stops you from skipping it). Then confirm the exclusion: comment is a Bytes field and renders as b64:… in the dump, never as a cellhash.

3. THE TWO EQUALITIES ARE WIRED TO DIFFERENT CALLERS. grep -rn structural_equal ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src returns the declaration, the definition plus its two internal recursions, and exactly two external call sites — VectorRunner.cpp:169 and BuildVectorRunner.cpp:193, both harness. rt_eq is called from ExprEval.cpp:208 and ClassifyCore.cpp:100. Neither function ever calls the other.

4. FLOAT-BACKED AMOUNTS FAULT RATHER THAN COMPARE. The conformance vectors pin all three use sites (below). If you ever "fix" one of them to return null instead, expect amount_float_eq_fault to fail and the getgems A/B twin to diverge.

Connected scopes
  • block-tree — Block::data is a Dict Value and a Block-kind Value points into the block arena — the lifetime rule behind Value::block lives there
  • parse-layer — the two parser universes disagree about addr_none-vs-null and about how an external address is shaped; both produce this same Value type
  • build-programs — rt_eq / rt_access / the builtins that construct Account, Amount and Asset values are the expression runtime built on this model
  • gates — structural_equal is the conformance-vector comparator, and the cellhash render rule exists purely so the A/B twin dumps can be byte-compared
  • actions — Action columns are filled from these values; the Amount/Account wrappers survive until the row is serialized
Not annotated in this scope — read directly

3 · From trace to Block tree — the structure matchers walk

Chapter 1 showed a trace turning into an action; chapter 2 showed the Value that travels through it. This chapter is the substrate in between: the four plain structs a fixture decodes into, the EventNode tree that reassembles the message graph from flat rows, and the Block spine that init_block lays over it. By the end you can read any block-tree dump and say exactly which C++ line produced each node, predict what failed will be for a given transaction, and know precisely what a merge inherits and what it destroys. This layer is a port of the Python indexer's tree_utils.to_tree / core.Block / event_processing.init_block, and it is the one layer that was verified byte-identical against Python across the whole fixture corpus — so most of what is worth saying here is about the places where the C++ deliberately does NOT copy Python (determinism) and the places where it copies Python bug-for-bug (failed semantics, ContractDeploy children). Nothing in this file matches anything: it only builds the shape that matcher-runtime walks.

Fixture to spine
flowchart TD
  F[".lz4 fixture (LZ4 frame + msgpack)"] --> L["load_trace -> Trace / Transaction / Message / MsgContent"]
  L --> T["to_tree: sort tx by lt DESC, link child by in-msg hash"]
  T --> R["root = lowest-lt tx, then walk .parent up"]
  R --> I["init_block: iterative DFS over EventNode.children"]
  I --> LB["one leaf Block per node:<br/>tick_tock | ton_transfer | call_contract"]
  LB --> D["+ contract_deploy pushed into children_blocks<br/>(uninit/nonexist -> active)"]
  LB --> C["connect(parent,child) then sort_next_blocks (min_lt asc)"]
  C --> S["Block spine -> walker (ch.5)"]
  L -.-> IF["interfaces section -> LookupSource (ch.7)"]
What merge_blocks does, in order
flowchart TD
  E["produced->merge_blocks(consumed)"] --> Q["dedup, FIRST-SEEN order<br/>(Python uses set() = nondeterministic)"]
  Q --> EC["ensure_earliest_common_block:<br/>sort by (min_lt_without_initiating_tx, direction),<br/>every other block must chain back to the head"]
  EC -->|nullptr| FA["return false -> build rejected,<br/>tree left completely untouched"]
  EC --> M["each merged block: parent = produced,<br/>event_nodes APPENDED, pushed to children_blocks"]
  M --> FR["find_frontier(earliest): BFS through the merged set,<br/>first non-member on each path -> new next_blocks (deduped)"]
  FR --> PR["previous_block = earliest->previous_block<br/>initiating_event_node = earliest's"]
  PR --> LT["calculate_min_max_lt, then sort_next_blocks"]
  LT --> CC["earliest->previous_block->compact_connections()"]

The fixture loader — msgpack in, four structs out

TraceLoader.{h,cpp} is the FIXTURE path only: it reads one tests/traces/*.lz4 (an LZ4 frame wrapping msgpack, written by the Python recorder) and produces Trace -> Transaction -> Message -> MsgContent. The production loader that reads the same shape out of Postgres is a different file entirely and is covered in prod-path; everything downstream of these four structs is shared, which is exactly what makes the prod A/B gate meaningful.

The decode is deliberately dumb: every field is fetched by name, a missing or nil key yields the default, and unknown keys are ignored. There is no schema validation because the fixture writer and this reader are pinned together by the twin gates, not by a contract. Two decisions in here have consequences much later — the signed storage of opcode, and the fact that message_content is optional.

45 // Owning transaction, wired after decode (Python Message.transaction).

48 // Opcode masked to 32 bits (matches Python EventNode.get_opcode).
494 std::optional<std::uint32_t> opcode32() const {
50 if (!opcode) {
51 return std::nullopt;

53 return static_cast<std::uint32_t>(*opcode & 0xFFFFFFFF);
54 }
55};
1L36Stored SIGNED because that is how Postgres stores it (int4) and how the msgpack fixture carries it. Every consumer must go through opcode32(); comparing msg->opcode against 0xa7733acd directly would silently fail for any opcode with the high bit set. This is the single most common way to write a wrong condition against this struct.
2L42Only the emptiness of value_extra_currencies is kept, not the map. That is enough because the one place it is read is the call_contract failed-exception rule, which tests Python's not node.message.value_extra_currencies — a truthiness test. Decoding the dict would be dead weight.
3L43Optional: a message with no content row is representable. Python's EventNode.__init__ RAISES NoMessageBodyException in that case and the whole trace falls back to basic classification; the C++ node has no such precondition and the leaf simply gets comment = null. No fixture in the corpus exercises it, so the twins agree — but it is a real asymmetry to remember if you ever feed the engine a hand-built trace.
4L49–54The mask, mirroring Python's EventNode.get_opcode. Note it returns nullopt for an absent opcode, NOT 0 — and init_block treats absent and 0 the same, so the distinction only matters to specs that read data.opcode.

1L129–130bounce is optional<bool> and bounced is a plain bool, and the difference is load-bearing: the ton_transfer failed rule tests msg->bounce && *msg->bounce, i.e. it must distinguish "bounce flag absent" from "bounce == false". bounced has no such consumer, so it collapses to false.

3L134–140body stays as the base64 BOC string — no cell is deserialized here. Every consumer (the comment derivation later in this chapter, the parsers in parse-layer) decodes it itself, which is why a corrupt body is a local parse failure rather than a load failure.

1L240–243A missing transactions array is the ONLY hard error in the decoder. Everything else degrades to defaults, on the principle that a fixture the recorder wrote is trusted and a fixture it did not write should fail loudly at the top rather than subtly three layers down.
2L247–251Back-wiring the owning transaction into each Message (Python's Message.transaction). It has to happen after the whole vector is filled — trace.transactions is a vector of unique_ptr, so the pointers are stable, but the vector itself reallocates while it grows. This is why Message::tx is not set inside parse_message.
3L252–262The interfaces section decodes generically into Value (via msgpack_to_value, just above) rather than into typed structs, because the Python TestInterfaceRepository serves whatever the recorder captured. Note the float branch in that helper: msgpack floats become VType::Float, a kind that deliberately has NO rendering, so a spec that reads a raw float fails exactly where the Python twin's render() raises (value).

to_tree — parent links by message hash

A trace arrives as a flat list of transactions. to_tree rebuilds the message graph with one trick: sort the transactions by lt DESCENDING, so every child transaction is created before the parent that sent to it. By the time a parent enumerates its out-messages, the in-msg-hash -> tx-hash map already contains the child's entry, and the link is a single lookup. This is a direct port of Python's tree_utils.to_tree, sort direction and all.

The node type is deliberately thin — a message pointer, a transaction pointer, a tick-tock flag, and links. Everything derived (lt(), opcode(), tx_hash()) is computed on demand so there is no cached state to get stale when a block absorbs nodes from elsewhere.

ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/BlockTree.h:41–75EventNode — three accessors that all special-case tick_tockcpp9f3365b6

1L41–46For a normal transaction msg is the INCOMING message; for a destination-less out-message (a log/notification) the node's msg is that outgoing message and tx is the sender's transaction. So msg->direction is the only way to tell the two node flavours apart, and Block::direction() in the merge code depends on exactly that.
2L53–64Port of EventNode.get_lt. The precedence is tick_tock first, then created_lt, then tx_lt — and it matters because min_lt derives from it and min_lt decides sibling order everywhere. A tick_tock node has no meaningful message lt at all, hence the first branch.
3L54–56Python synthesises a fake Message(msg_hash=tx.hash, direction='in', transaction=tick_tock_tx) for tick-tock nodes; the C++ leaves msg null and reads tx instead. Same answers from lt(), tx_hash() and is_tick_tock, but any new code that dereferences node->msg unconditionally will crash on a tick-tock node where Python quietly returned a synthetic value.

Python's sorted(txs, key=lt, reverse=True) is stable in the original order for equal lt, and reversing after an ascending sort would flip those ties.
