1L113–117A destination-less out-message becomes its own leaf node under the sending transaction. This is where the engine's log/event leaves come from — every call_contract block whose opcode is an event opcode is one of these, and it shares its tx with its parent.
2L119–126Python assert m.msg_hash in msg_tx here; the C++ skips silently. That is intentional (it matches the Go PoC and keeps the no-abort rule), but silence is the dangerous half — hence unlinked below. An out-message with a destination and no matching child transaction means the trace was captured incomplete.
3L131–135sorted.back() is the LOWEST-lt transaction, and walking .parent up from it lands on the root. Note the trace root is normally the ext-in transaction; picking it by lowest lt rather than by "has no in-message source" is Python's rule, copied verbatim.
4L137–149The reachability sweep that turns the silent skip above into a number. unlinked != 0 prints a warning in the classify drivers, so an incomplete fixture is visible instead of quietly classifying a subset. On the current 148-fixture corpus it is zero for every fixture — see the corpus run at the end of this chapter.

What a Block is

A Block is a node in a second tree laid over the first. Initially there is one block per event node (the "spine"), and matching replaces runs of blocks with produced blocks that own them. Two link families coexist and must not be confused: next_blocks/previous_block is the FLOW (who follows whom in the message graph), and children_blocks/parent is CONSUMPTION (who was absorbed into whom). A matcher walks the first; the serializer in actions reads the second.

The file header is worth reading before the struct, because it enumerates every place the C++ deliberately departs from Python. All four departures are in the same direction: replace a Python set() or an unsorted list with a deterministic order.

ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/BlockTree.h:1–19The four deliberate deviations, stated up frontcpp831d95ad
1// EventNode tree + Block substrate for the MCH engine.
2//
3// Ports the Python indexer's structural machinery (blocks/utils/tree_utils.py
4// to_tree, blocks/core.py Block, event_processing.init_block) following the
5// already-validated Go port (mch-go-poc/tree/tree.go, A/B-verified against the
6// Python engine on real fixtures).
7//
8// Deliberate deviations from the Python substrate (all deterministic):
91// - next_blocks is kept in canonical order (min_lt asc, stable) at all times:
10// after tree construction and after every merge. The Python IR engine
11// instead sorts candidates at every walk site (T21); maintaining the
12// invariant here lets the C++ walker read lists raw with identical
13// observable semantics.
142// - find_frontier dedups its output; Python's find_next can yield the same
15// block twice on diamond shapes and keeps duplicates in next_blocks.
16// Suspect #1 if a matcher A/B diff ever shows up on diamond traces.
173// - compact_connections preserves first-seen order (Python uses set()).
18// - No `transient` flag: only legacy LabelBlock ever set it; the IR engine
19// produces no transient blocks, so the merge filter would filter nothing.
1L9–13The invariant that lets the walker read next_blocks raw. Python's IR engine sorts candidates at every walk site instead; maintaining the order at construction and after every merge is observably identical and strictly cheaper. If you ever add a mutation of next_blocks, re-establishing this is your job — nothing asserts it.
2L14–16The one departure that is NOT provably neutral, and it says so. Python's find_next can yield the same block twice on a diamond and leaves the duplicate in next_blocks; the C++ dedups. Named "suspect #1" because if a matcher A/B diff ever appears on a diamond-shaped trace, this is the first thing to un-dedup and re-run.
3L17–19transient was a Python filter on the merge input, used only by a legacy LabelBlock. The IR engine emits no transient blocks, so the filter would filter nothing — dropping the field is the honest encoding of that, and this comment is the receipt if the assumption ever changes.

1L96–99One data field carries two very different payloads depending on who built the block: for a spine leaf it is the basic_blocks.py constructor dict (a deliberate subset — see leaf_data below), for a produced block it is whatever the build program captured. where_exprs read it through rt_dotfield and cannot tell which, which is why the leaf subset is documented rather than enforced.
2L107–110initiating_event_node is a LEAF's tree-parent — the node that caused this block to exist, not one of its own nodes. It survives a merge (inherited from the earliest merged block) and is read twice by the serializer: to extend tx_hashes and to add the initiating transaction's account. Get it wrong and actions gain or lose an account row with no other symptom.
3L111–114is_ghost_block is permanently false: ghost nodes (an intended-but-never-started operation) exist only in a Python code path the IR engine does not use. It is kept as a field rather than deleted because actions gates the destination-account push on it, and a hard-coded false there would hide the dependency.
4L119–120Two lt fields, and the difference only exists for a leaf: min_lt is the node's message lt, min_lt_without_initiating_tx is the owning transaction's lt. They are the same after calculate_min_max_lt, i.e. after any merge. Sibling ordering uses min_lt; merge-anchor selection uses the other one.

init_block — the leaf spine

init_block walks the event tree and hangs exactly one leaf block off each node. There are four leaf btypes: tick_tock, ton_transfer, call_contract, and contract_deploy — but the fourth is never a spine node, it is a side-effect block pushed into a leaf's children_blocks.

The classification rule is three lines long and the failed rules are longer than the classification. That is the honest shape of this code: what a block IS is trivial, whether it FAILED is a pile of protocol-specific exceptions that the Python engine accumulated over years, and every one of them had to be copied exactly.

ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/BlockTree.cpp:19–61Comment derivation — the only BOC work init_block doescpp28012964
19// TonTransferMessage.encrypted_opcode — an encrypted-comment plain transfer.
20constexpr std::uint32_t kEncryptedTonOpcode = 0x2167da4b;
21 
221// TonTransferBlock.comment/encrypted/comment_encoded (basic_blocks.py): parse
23// the leaf's message body. `comment` is decoded (base64 when encrypted, else
24// utf-8 backslashreplace with U+0000 stripped) exactly as ton_transfer_comment
25// does; `encrypted` is the op == TonTransferMessage.encrypted_opcode flag;
26// `comment_encoded` is set only when a comment is present AND encrypted. Any BOC
27// failure == Python's inner try swallowing -> comment None, encrypted false.
28struct LeafCommentInfo {
29 std::optional<std::string> comment;
30 bool encrypted{false};
31 bool comment_encoded{false};
32};
33 
34LeafCommentInfo leaf_comment_info(const EventNode *node) {
35 LeafCommentInfo info;
36 const Message *msg = node != nullptr ? node->msg : nullptr;
37 if (msg == nullptr || !msg->content) {
38 return info;
39 }
40 auto r_raw = td::base64_decode(td::Slice(msg->content->body));
412 if (r_raw.is_error()) {
42 return info;
43 }
44 auto r_cell = vm::std_boc_deserialize(r_raw.move_as_ok());
45 if (r_cell.is_error()) {
46 return info;
47 }
48 td::Ref<vm::Cell> cell = r_cell.move_as_ok();
49 info.comment = ton_transfer_comment(cell);
503 // TonTransferMessage.encrypted: op == 0x2167da4b (peek the first 32 bits).
51 bool special = false;
52 try {
53 vm::CellSlice cs = vm::load_cell_slice_special(cell, special);
54 if (cs.size() >= 32) {
55 info.encrypted = static_cast<std::uint32_t>(cs.fetch_ulong(32)) == kEncryptedTonOpcode;
56 }
57 } catch (...) {
58 }
59 info.comment_encoded = info.comment.has_value() && info.encrypted;
60 return info;
61}
1L22–27The contract in one comment. comment is base64 of the RAW bytes when the message is encrypted, and utf-8-backslashreplace with U+0000 stripped otherwise — both branches live in ton_transfer_comment (parse-layer). comment_encoded is the AND of the two, and it is a Python attribute on the block rather than a data key; it is promoted into data here because a Value dict is the only channel a spec has.
2L41–47Three early returns, all silent. Python wraps the whole body parse in a try and swallows, so an undecodable body must yield comment = null, encrypted = false — not a failed block, not an error. A stricter reading here would reject traces Python happily classifies.
3L50–58The encrypted flag is a raw 32-bit peek, not a parse: 0x2167da4b is the encrypted-comment opcode. Note this same opcode is treated as a TON transfer by the classifier below, which is the whole reason the flag has to be recovered from the body.

These are log/event leaves: they "fail" only because the transaction that emitted them aborted, and treating them as failed would poison every action built above them.

444Block *init_block(BlockArena &arena, const EventNode *node) {
4453 // Iterative DFS: trace depth is unbounded, recursion is not.
446 Block *root = make_leaf_block(arena, node);
447 std::vector<std::pair<const EventNode *, Block *>> stack{{node, root}};
448 while (!stack.empty()) {
449 auto [cur, block] = stack.back();
450 stack.pop_back();
451 for (const EventNode *c : cur->children) {
452 Block *child = make_leaf_block(arena, c);
453 block->connect(child);
454 stack.emplace_back(c, child);
455 }
4564 block->sort_next_blocks();
457 }
458 return root;
459}
1L429–431The deploy predicate: the transaction ended active and did not start active or frozen. Python attaches this to TonTransferBlock and CallContractBlock but NOT to TickTockBlock — hence the explicit !node->is_tick_tock guard, which is the only reason it is spelled out.
2L432–437The subtle one. The deploy block goes into children_blocks but its parent is left NULL, because Python only sets .parent inside merge_blocks. Consequence: the deploy block is not reachable from the spine at all — it is not in anyone's next_blocks and topmost_parent() returns itself — so it survives independently even when its host leaf is consumed by a matcher, and gets serialized as its own top-level action. The run below shows exactly that.
3L445–447Iterative where Python recurses. Trace depth is attacker-influenced (a long chain of forwards), so recursion depth is not a safe function of input. The stack is LIFO, which visits siblings in reverse — harmless, because connect happens inside the parent's own loop and the order is re-established by the sort below.
4L456The canonical-order invariant established at construction. Every child's min_lt is already final at this point (set by init_leaf inside make_leaf_block), so one stable sort per node is enough and no later pass has to re-sort the spine.

merge_blocks — who inherits what

When a matcher accepts, the produced block calls merge_blocks(consumed) and the spine is rewritten in place. This is the only destructive operation in the substrate, and the header comment states the contract bluntly: it must be called ONLY after a build accepts, because there is no rollback. The false return exists for the one case that can be detected before any mutation — no earliest common block — and in that case the tree is untouched.

Four helpers do the work. ensure_earliest_common_block picks the anchor and validates that the consumed set is actually connected. find_frontier computes what the produced block should now point at. compact_connections repairs the parent's outgoing edges. calculate_min_max_lt re-derives the ordering key. Read them in that order.

2L172–180The repair after a merge: an edge that used to point at a consumed block must now point at whatever swallowed it, hence topmost_parent(). The dedup is by first-seen order — Python writes set(...), whose iteration order is id-based and therefore varies between processes. This is the single largest determinism win in the file, and it is invisible until you diff two Python runs of the same trace.
3L181–182Python's compact_connections does NOT sort; the sort here is what keeps the canonical-order invariant true after a merge. Note the ordering constraint it creates: merge_blocks must finish calculate_min_max_lt on the produced block BEFORE the parent compacts, or the parent would sort on a stale key.

255Block *ensure_earliest_common_block(const std::vector<Block *> &blocks) {
256 std::vector<Block *> sorted = blocks;
2571 std::stable_sort(sorted.begin(), sorted.end(), [](const Block *a, const Block *b) {
258 if (a->min_lt_without_initiating_tx != b->min_lt_without_initiating_tx) {
259 return a->min_lt_without_initiating_tx < b->min_lt_without_initiating_tx;
260 }
261 return a->direction() < b->direction();
262 });
263 if (sorted.empty()) {
264 return nullptr;
265 }
2662 Block *earliest = sorted.front();
267 std::unordered_set<const Block *> connected{earliest};
268 for (Block *block : sorted) {
269 if (connected.count(block) != 0) {
270 continue;
271 }
272 if (block->previous_block != nullptr) {
273 if (connected.count(block->previous_block) != 0) {
274 connected.insert(block);
275 continue;
276 }
2773 return nullptr;
278 }
279 }
280 return earliest;
281}
1L257–262The sort key is (min_lt_without_initiating_tx, direction), i.e. the OWNING TRANSACTION's lt, not the message lt. That is deliberate: an out-message leaf and the transaction that produced it tie on the first key, and direction() (0 = in/anchor, 1 = out, 2 = multi-node) breaks the tie toward the incoming side. Python's tuple sort, reproduced.
2L266–279The connectivity check, and it is weaker than it looks: it only requires each block's IMMEDIATE previous_block to already be in connected, and it iterates in sorted order, so it validates a chain rather than a general reachability. Copied as-is — a stronger check would reject matches Python accepts.
3L277return nullptr here is what becomes merge_blocks returning false. Python raises instead (raise "Earliest common block not found" — a bare string, which would itself be a TypeError), so on the Python side this path is a hard failure caught upstream; on the C++ side it is a clean build rejection with the tree untouched.

2973 for (Block *b : to_merge) {
298 b->parent = this;
299 event_nodes.insert(event_nodes.end(), b->event_nodes.begin(), b->event_nodes.end());
300 children_blocks.push_back(b);
301 }
3024 for (Block *fb : earliest->find_frontier(to_merge)) {
303 next_blocks.push_back(fb);
304 fb->previous_block = this;
305 }
306 previous_block = earliest->previous_block;
307 // core.py merge_blocks: the merged block inherits initiating_event_node from
308 // the earliest merged block (Step 2a). is_ghost_block would OR over ghost
309 // nodes, but the C++ substrate has none, so it stays false.
310 initiating_event_node = earliest->initiating_event_node;
3115 calculate_min_max_lt();
312 sort_next_blocks();
313 if (earliest->previous_block != nullptr) {
314 earliest->previous_block->compact_connections();
315 }
316 return true;
317}
1L284–292Dedup preserving FIRST-SEEN order, against Python's set(blocks). This order then feeds the sort in ensure_earliest_common_block (whose ties are broken by stability) AND the event_nodes append order below — so a nondeterministic set here would produce a nondeterministic anchor and a nondeterministic node order in the same breath.
2L293–296The only pre-mutation exit. Everything after this line mutates the tree irreversibly, which is why the header insists this is called after a build ACCEPTS, never speculatively.
3L297–301What a merge inherits: event_nodes are APPENDED in merged order (so anchor_tx_hash() is the first consumed block's first node), each consumed block gets parent set and lands in children_blocks. Note it does NOT take their data, failed, or opcode — a produced block's data comes entirely from its build program (build-programs).
4L302–310The three link repairs, in Python's order: frontier blocks become the produced block's next_blocks and get their previous_block re-pointed; the produced block takes the anchor's previous_block; initiating_event_node is inherited from the ANCHOR, not from the first consumed block. The is_ghost_block OR that Python does here is unreachable and is documented instead of written.
5L311–315Order matters and differs from Python: calculate_min_max_lt runs BEFORE the parent's compact_connections, because compaction now sorts and would otherwise sort on the produced block's pre-merge min_lt. Python compacts first and never sorts, so both orders are correct in their own engine — but swapping them here would silently reorder siblings.

Reading a block: the view helpers

Host functions need to ask small questions of a block, and host/BlockViews.{h,cpp} is the deliberately tiny vocabulary they are allowed to use. It is not a graph query language — the header says so, and the rule for admitting a new op is that some host already demonstrates it twice. Two of them, data_truthy and acc_str, are the ones you will meet everywhere and both encode a Python semantic rather than a C++ one.

48 blocks.erase(std::unique(blocks.begin(), blocks.end()), blocks.end());
49 std::stable_sort(blocks.begin(), blocks.end(),
50 [](const Block *a, const Block *b) { return a->min_lt < b->min_lt; });
51}

1L47–50Sort by POINTER, unique, then stable-sort by min_lt. The pointer sort is not cosmetic — it is how HostCoffee's original code deduped, and reproducing it (rather than a first-seen dedup) is what keeps peer-swap order byte-identical. This is the one place in the substrate where address order is deliberately observable, and it is safe only because the second sort is stable on a key that ties rarely.
2L53–57bool(block.data[field]) for exactly the two carriers the specs use. Note what is FALSE here: a missing key, a null, a string, an Amount. Python's bool() would say a non-empty string is true — the narrow reading is intentional, because every real call site tests a bool or an int flag and a wider rule would silently change behaviour if a field's type ever moved.
3L59–63AccountId(v).as_str() — and crucially addr_none returns nullopt, not an empty string. Callers gate on the optional, which is how an addr_none address stops a wallet lookup instead of performing one against the empty key. Contrast the ABI universe in parse-layer, where addr_none is a present-but-empty Account for the same TL-B input.

Check yourself

Four things you can verify right now. The first two are the evidence behind this chapter's parity claims; the third exercises the one substrate operation not covered by an excerpt (insert_between, used by shapers); the fourth is a claim about the Python side you should confirm by reading rather than trusting.

All commands run from S:/Dev/ton-indexer-clear/indexer, with $ENGINE = ton-index-worker/cmake-build-debug-visual-studio/ton-mch-engine/ton-mch-engine.exe and $IR = ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/ir/mch_ir.json. The venv python is S:/Dev/H-dump/tonscan-indexator/venv0/Scripts/python.exe.

1. Classify the whole corpus and confirm stderr is EMPTY — that is the unlinked counter reporting that every one of the 148 fixtures has a single-rooted event tree, i.e. to_tree never silently dropped a subtree.

3. Run --shape-test, which drives Block::insert_between directly (parent/proxy/target rewiring, grandchild edge redirection, target back-edge reparenting) plus the getgems shaper that uses it.

4. Open indexer/events/blocks/core.py and read compact_connections (one line, set(...)) and merge_blocks (blocks_to_merge = [b for b in set(blocks) ...]). Then re-read the two C++ dedups in this chapter. Convince yourself that the Python engine's sibling order and merge anchor really are hash-seed dependent, and that the C++ is not — this is the difference the whole "canonical order" invariant exists to buy.

4 · The IR — what the runtime actually executes

The C++ engine contains no matchers. It contains an interpreter for ir/mch_ir.json, a single 272 KB artifact compiled from the .mch specs by the Python frontend. After this chapter you can open that file and read it: you will know why a matcher record has both an anchor and a root, why nodes is one flat global array instead of a tree, what each of the six node kinds and six edge fields means, how maybe / ^ / <- / $rule in a spec turn into JSON keys, and why a key being ABSENT (priority, builder, shape) carries meaning. You will also know what IrLoader refuses to load and why each refusal exists — the loader is written fail-closed on purpose, because a silently-degraded artifact matches MORE blocks than the spec author wrote. The matcher half of what the loader produces is executed in matcher-runtime; the build_program half in build-programs. This chapter stops at "you can read it".

The artifact in one screen

Open ir/mch_ir.json and the first 33 lines tell you almost everything about its shape: a version tag, a provenance block nobody reads, and then two flat arrays. There is no nesting — a matcher points at nodes by integer index, and nodes point at each other by integer index. That is a deliberate wire format, not an accident of serialization: it makes the whole graph addressable by a stable id, which is what lets the C++ build step generate a function per (matcher, node) pair and pair it with the artifact by sha.

The file is regenerated, never edited. ir/README.md documents the one command; everything downstream of it (where_expr codegen, build-fn codegen, table sha pairing) is a CMake custom command.

1L2A strict equality gate on both loaders — no dual-accept, no range. The 1.0 -> 1.1 bump was made deliberately non-additive (docs/mch-w7-handoff.md §1b) so that a stale binary cannot half-read a newer artifact and fail later at eval time. Treating specs/ as the source of truth for what production runs will mislead you; ir/emit_manifest.json is authoritative and this array echoes it verbatim.

1L36–41anchor and root are two representations of the same head test, kept separate on purpose. The anchor is a PREFILTER — the walker only visits blocks whose opcode is in this set — while the root is the pattern's first node. ir_emit._anchor_record derives the anchor from the root when the compiler didn't record a distinct one, so they usually agree; the interesting cases are when they don't (next section).
2L42root: 0 indexes the GLOBAL nodes array. The loader immediately renumbers the reachable subgraph to local ids with root == 0, so the id you read here is not the id the C++ runtime uses — CompiledNode::global_id is what preserves the artifact id for the codegen table.
3L43–45produces is a LIST, not a string. Most matchers produce one btype, but change_dns produces three and tonstakers_withdraw two — the switch build statement chooses which at build time (build-programs). A reader who assumes produces[0] is the answer will be wrong twice.
4L46–59The captures table IS the slot numbering: position in this array is the slot id, and card (one/opt/many) is what the walker enforces on binding. A node's capture key is a NAME; the loader resolves it against this table and stores -1 for an unknown name rather than erroring — a capture typo is a silent no-bind, not a load failure.
5L60–62Absent keys are meaningful and that is the trap of this format. include_excess/include_bounces are always written; priority is written ONLY when it differs from 100; builder and shape only when present. So "no priority key" means 100, and the 30 priority-100 matchers simply omit it — you cannot sort matchers by reading m.priority without a default.

Opcodes are stored as UNSIGNED decimal (260734629 == 0x0f8a7ea5); the emitter masks with 0xFFFFFFFF and the loader masks again, so a spec that wrote a negative literal can never reach the runtime as a signed value.
2L9456child: 1 is the -> edge — "the block produced by this block's message". Chains are a linked list of records, never nesting, which is why reading a matcher means jumping through the array rather than reading a subtree.
3L9464–9468maybe becomes optional: true ON the node, not a wrapper node. Together with card: "opt" in the captures table, that is the entire encoding of an optional leg — there is no separate Maybe node kind in the IR.
4L9452–9469Note what is NOT here: no back-pointer to the owning matcher. A node does not know who owns it; ownership is discoverable only by walking from each matcher's root, which is exactly what the loader does and what the runs block below reproduces.

1L75artifact_index is recorded BEFORE the priority sort, and it is the key into the generated build-fn table. After load_ir returns, matchers[i].artifact_index != i in general — using the vector index to look up a build function is precisely the bug this field exists to prevent.
2L79–83The anchor is decomposed into three parallel members of which exactly one is populated. This is also a performance decision: prepare_classify turns OpcodeSet/BType into a real prefilter and leaves Pred/Mixed as a full scan of the block tree (matcher-runtime).

4L101–102Six ref_* sets, and the header comment above is explicit that they are report-only for MATCHING. Builders, shapers, parsers, lookups and host fns are build-phase bindings; the loader never marks a matcher unrunnable for a missing one. That check lives in build_skip_reason, later on this page.

The node pool: six kinds, six edge fields

Every node record has a kind (one of contract, block_type, pred, any, or, recursive) and may carry up to six edge fields (child, children[], parent, branches[], step, exit) plus the modifiers optional, capture, where, where_expr, exclusive, strategy. In the production artifact the distribution is 208 contract, 64 block_type, 36 or, 11 recursive, 8 pred, 2 any.

Two of those numbers are worth pausing on. Only two nodes are any — and neither is a wildcard, as the first excerpt shows. Only 11 are recursive, but they carry the entire multi-hop-swap machinery.

Build programs and expression nodes — a preview

About 95% of the artifact by volume is not pattern at all: it is build_program, a flat statement list per matcher whose expressions are k-tagged trees. This chapter only teaches you to READ them; execution is build-programs and the parse statement's registry is parse-layer.

Statement tags in the production artifact: 32 let, 31 out, 29 parse, 27 reject, 18 failed, 2 switch. Expression tags: 600 attr, 512 name, 144 call, 107 bin, 98 null, 51 ternary, 17 unary, 13 str, 9 int, 8 lookup, 5 bool, 4 dotfield, and exactly one each of mapc, list, record.

2L65–68The parse EXPRESSION is a different construct from the parse STATEMENT: it evaluates inline and faults on total failure. It is also invisible to the C++ loader's ref_msgtypes scan, which keys on the statement tag s == "parse" — so the first spec that uses the expression form will not get its message types checked against the parse registry. Latent today: zero occurrences in production, and the Python twin has the same shallow rule, so the A/B gate cannot surface it either.
3L69–75map and any/all land on two different tags — mapc, and quant carrying the operator. Both are build-expression only: the Python loader hard-rejects either inside a where_expr, because where_expr composes onto a synchronous test_self and a comprehension can hide an async lookup.

IrLoader: what it refuses to load

IrLoader.cpp is 520 lines and roughly a third of it is refusal. That ratio is the design: the IR spec's §8.1 rule is that an unrecognized or missing field must never degrade into something permissive, because a permissive degrade makes a corrupt artifact match MORE blocks than the spec author wrote — and matching more blocks is silent, whereas failing to load is loud.

The exceptions are documented at their sites and worth memorizing, because they are the places where a corrupt artifact WILL load: priority absent defaults to 100, include_excess/include_bounces absent default to true, and strategy falls back to frontier for any unrecognized string (contrast parse_kind, which errors on an unknown node kind with the explicit comment that a typo must not become the permissive any wildcard).

5L265–268Opcode masked to 32 bits at load, mirroring _unsigned32 on the emit side. Both ends normalize, so the comparison against a block's opcode is unsigned on every path and a spec author cannot create a signed/unsigned mismatch.

Priorities and registration order

Two knobs decide which matcher gets to consume a block first, and they interact. priority (default 100, ascending — lower runs first) is the primary key; registration_order breaks ties. In the production artifact registration_order is the identity permutation, which means ties break on emission order: manifest file order, then source position within each file. That is the whole reason emit_manifest.json lists specs_decl/jettons.mch first and documents it in a comment.

1L486–503registration_order must be a permutation of [0, matchers), checked with a seen bitmap plus a length equality. It would be easy to treat a stray index as harmless — it is not: the sort below indexes compiled[] directly, so an out-of-range entry is out-of-bounds access and a duplicate silently drops a matcher from the run.
2L509–510One stable_sort on priority is the entire ordering rule. Because the input vector is already in the artifact's registration order, stability means ties keep that order — which is what makes an in-spec priority 90 sufficient to run the declarative jetton family first, with no filename tricks.
3L512–514Matchers are MOVED into the output in final order. From this point the vector index no longer equals the artifact index — the reason artifact_index was captured at the top of the load and the reason the generated build table is keyed by it.

What a matcher gets skipped for

Runnability is decided twice. The loader decides the MATCH half (predicates only). build_skip_reason decides the BUILD half by checking the artifact's collected ref_* sets against the live C++ registries — and this is the function that makes an unported protocol a visible SKIP line rather than a crash or, worse, a silently empty result.

A matcher with a non-empty skip reason is dropped from the run entirely, and the reason is printed once, sorted, at the top of every --match / --classify dump. The Python twin computes the same set from the same artifact, so the skip set is itself gate-checked (gates).

2L123–125Two distinct reasons for "no build program": builder means the spec named a registered Python builder function the C++ side does not implement, no_build_program means the spec had neither. Both are empty in the production artifact today — all 33 matchers are declarative, which is what the census run at the top of this page shows as with builder 0.
3L126–131First of four independent surfaces, all checked against the LIVE registries rather than against anything in the artifact: message parsers here (parse-layer), then lookup kinds, host fns and shapers below. A name the artifact references but this binary does not provide degrades that matcher to "never builds" — nothing is rewritten and nothing throws.
4L132–136The lookup check runs against FixtureLookupSource::kinds() — the fixture-backed source used by the dump modes. Production substitutes a different source, so whether a lookup kind is available is a property of the deployment as much as of the artifact (prod-path).
5L138–149Host fns and shapers close the list. Note the asymmetry with the Python engine, which HARD-FAILS at load on an unregistered builder/shaper/fn/message-type; C++ degrades to a skip instead, because a partially-ported engine has to be able to run at all. Same artifact, two different strictness policies — deliberate, and the reason the twin gate compares skip sets rather than assuming both sides ran everything.

The emit side, briefly

You do not need the Python compiler internals to read the artifact, but you do need to know three facts about how it is produced.

First, the source list is ir/emit_manifest.json, and its order IS the registration order; frontend.source_files echoes it. Second, ir_emit.py emits node ids as a per-matcher DFS with a memo keyed on Python object identity — which is why cyclic recursion resolves to a back-edge rather than looping forever, and why node ranges are disjoint per matcher even though the array is global. Third, and most useful in practice: the emitter is byte-deterministic and a pytest holds it to that.

5 · Matching — Walker, try_build, prefilter

This is the heart of the engine: the code that decides WHICH matcher fires on WHICH block. After this chapter you can read a .mch matcher's IR node graph (ir-artifact) and predict, without running anything, which blocks it will consume, which captures will bind, and why running it a minute later in the matcher order would give a different answer. Two loops do all the work: an OUTER loop that walks the block-tree spine once per matcher in priority order, and an INNER recursion (MatchState::match_node) that walks the matcher's node graph against one candidate block. The outer loop mutates the tree (each successful build merges blocks into a composite); the inner walk never does — it is pure, rollbackable, and re-runnable, which is exactly what makes --match a usable debugging tool. Two things trip up readers coming from the Python classifier: the B1 anchor prefilter (a per-trace opcode/btype inventory that skips whole traversals, and that must GROW as matchers produce new btypes or it would silently break composition), and the fact that value_flow does not exist on this side at all — the flow construct was removed from the language, so nothing in the match or build path accumulates account value flows.

Two loops, one tree

Start with the file banner. Walker.h states the contract that everything else on this page depends on: the match phase NEVER mutates the block tree. That is not an implementation detail — it is what makes every matcher in a run see the same tree state as its predecessor left it, and it is what lets --match probe all 33 matchers against every block independently.

Every captured run below was taken from S:/Dev/ton-indexer-clear/indexer with $ENGINE = ../ton-index-worker/cmake-build-debug-visual-studio/ton-mch-engine/ton-mch-engine.exe and $IR = ../ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/ir/mch_ir.json; the corpus is the 148 .lz4 fixtures in tests/traces.

The outer loop is in ClassifyCore.cpp. Read it next to the Python event_processing.py loop you already know: same shape (for each matcher, BFS the spine, try_build on each block), with two additions — the parent == nullptr guard and the B1 prefilter. The tree DOES mutate here, mid-walk, because a successful try_build merges blocks into a composite; the BFS reads cur->next_blocks only AFTER try_build has run on cur, which reproduces Python's generator-resume order exactly.

1L9–10"matching never mutates the tree, so every matcher runs over the same shared block tree with clean A/B". This is the single most useful invariant on the page: a failed match costs you nothing, a successful match costs you nothing either — consumption only becomes real when try_build merges. Everything else in this file is rollback machinery serving that sentence.
2L11–16The determinism argument. Python's engine sorts sibling candidates by min_lt (_canonical); the C++ Block substrate already keeps next_blocks sorted (block-tree), so canonical() is a no-op except where the walker CONCATENATES lists — the recursion frontier. Worth knowing: if you ever see order-sensitivity, the frontier is where to look.
3L18–19Host predicates are a load-time runnability question, not a runtime one: a matcher needing a C++-unavailable predicate is marked unrunnable and never reaches the walker. In the production artifact today that set is EMPTY — --match prints no SKIP lines at all.
4L21–26Two interchangeable where_expr paths over ONE runtime (ExprRuntime). The interpreter walks the loader's JSON tree; the generated path is a table of compiled functions keyed by artifact-global node id. That they agree is a gate, not a hope — --match vs --match-gen over the corpus diffs to zero (see Check yourself).

1L474–476The comment is the whole subtlety: cur->next_blocks is read AFTER try_build(cur) ran. If cur produced a composite, the merge rewired cur's successors, and the BFS enqueues the POST-merge list. Python's bfs_iter is a generator resumed after the body runs, so it has the same behaviour by accident of language; here it had to be reproduced on purpose.
2L480–482The consumption guard, and the reason matcher order changes results. merge_blocks sets parent on every merged block; a block with a parent is inside somebody's composite and can no longer anchor anything. Corpus proof: dedust_deposit_partial MATCHES 14 times but produces only 4 actions — dedust_deposit_final sits earlier in the artifact and eats its anchors first.
3L486–491The fold-back that makes the prefilter safe. jetton_transfer does not exist as a btype until the jetton_transfer matcher fires; five of the six btype-anchored matchers in prod anchor on a btype that ONLY exists after some earlier matcher produced it. Without this loop they would be prefiltered away on every trace.

The anchor: prefilter, test_self, and the conservative-superset argument

matcher_test_self is the cheap "could this block possibly be my anchor" test — the direct port of Python's BlockMatcher.test_self. B1 sits one level above it: instead of asking that question for every (matcher, block) pair, ask it once per (matcher, trace) against an inventory of what the trace contains at all.

The correctness argument has to be airtight, because a wrong skip silently loses actions. It rests on two asymmetries. Opcodes are STATIC: produced composite blocks carry no opcode, so the opcode set can only shrink as matchers consume blocks — and the inventory is never shrunk, making it a superset. Btypes GROW, which is unsafe in the other direction, so produced btypes are folded back after every matcher. Blocks that get consumed are never REMOVED from the inventory, so the worst case is a traversal that runs and finds nothing — never a traversal that was wrongly skipped.

Pred anchors opt out entirely (prefilter = false): their test runs an arbitrary host predicate, not an op/btype comparison, so there is nothing to index. Mixed anchors never run at all — the loader keeps them unrunnable because the branch structure is not stored.

Both hold, and both are what makes a skip provably lossless.
2L438–447The inventory is taken over the SPINE only (blocks reachable via next_blocks from the synthetic root) — not over children_blocks. 3L448–462Linear scans over small sets, not a precomputed intersection — anchor sets are 1-3 elements in practice (see the IR census in ir-artifact). 3L411–412Mixed returns false unconditionally. 4L423–426absorb = false at the ROOT, true everywhere below. This asymmetry is the single most surprising thing in the walker and it is legacy parity: nested nodes swallow excess/bounce siblings into consumed (so they get merged), while the anchor's own excess/bounce siblings are appended to the RESULT list after a successful build — see the aux section below.

Order is the whole game: priority, registration order, consumption

Python's ordering lives in the hand-maintained matchers list in event_processing.py. Here it is data: a priority per matcher plus an optional registration_order permutation in the artifact, resolved once at load.

The resolution is: apply registration_order (default identity), then STABLE-sort by priority ascending. Stability is the tie-break — equal-priority matchers keep artifact order. In the production artifact today only three matchers carry an explicit priority (the jetton trio at 90); everything else defaults to 100 and therefore runs in artifact order. That is the entire ordering story, and it has real consequences you can watch in the dumps below.

1L485–503Fail-closed validation of a field that would otherwise corrupt quietly: an out-of-range index would read compiled[] out of bounds during the sort, a duplicate would drop a matcher entirely. This is the tie-break contract: same priority ⇒ registration (artifact) order preserved. std::sort would be free to permute equal-priority matchers and would silently change which matcher consumes an overlapping anchor first — an ordering bug that only shows up as an A/B diff on some traces.
3L512–514LoadedIr.matchers is stored ALREADY in run order, so nothing downstream re-sorts. artifact_index (set before this move) is what keys the generated build-fn table — it survives the reorder, which is why the build table can be indexed by artifact position while the run walks priority order (build-programs).

Inside match_node

MatchState is one attempt's worth of state: bindings, consumed, visited, recursion frames, current frame, depth. The matcher itself is immutable, so a MatchState is cheap and disposable — matcher_match makes one per anchor and throws it away.

match_node is the whole grammar in 35 lines. Read it as: dispatch the two composite kinds (Or / Recursive) first, then for a plain node do head test → consume → bind → three edge phases → aux absorption. Every one of those steps can fail, and failure just returns false — the CALLER decides whether to roll back, because only the caller knows whether it is inside an optional edge or a branch alternative.

1L20–25The depth cap exists to convert an undefined stack overflow into a clean per-trace failure, mirroring Python's RecursionError hitting the trace-level fallback. 500 vs an observed corpus max of 2 tells you this is a guard against pathological input, not a tuning knob — do not raise it to "fix" a matcher.
2L27–30Frame is the capture SCOPE, not a call frame: (recursive-node id, iteration index) or kExitIdx for the exit attempt. nid == -1 means "outside any recursion". Every bind() records the frame that was current, and that pair is what lets assemble_captures reconstruct per-iteration lists later.
3L39–41A Mark is three sizes. Rollback is resize on three vectors plus erasing the tail from visited_ — O(undone work), no copying, no journal. This cheapness is why the walker can afford to try every branch and every child candidate speculatively.
4L43–48stable_sort by min_lt — stable so equal-lt siblings keep list order. As the header says this is a no-op for a single block's next_blocks (already canonical from block-tree); it earns its keep on the recursion frontier, which is built by concatenating several blocks' successor lists.

1L67–72Or and Recursive are dispatched BEFORE test_head. This is load-bearing for or: test_head's Or case implements the exclusive count rule, and skipping it here is exactly what makes exclusive INERT when an or-node is an edge target — legacy ExclusiveOrMatcher inherits try_build from OrMatcher without consulting test_self. stonfi_v2_swap depends on that inertness.
2L76–79Consume-then-bind happens BEFORE the edges are attempted, so a node's own block is in consumed while its subtree matches. That ordering is what gives consumed its traversal order (anchor first), which builders receive verbatim as _mch_consumed (build-programs).
3L80–88Three edge phases, fixed order, any failure aborts. Note what is NOT here: no rollback. A false return leaves bindings_/consumed_ dirty on purpose — the caller that took a Mark is the one that undoes it, and at the very top matcher_match just drops the whole MatchState.
4L89–91absorb is a parameter, not a matcher flag, and it is false only at the root. Nested nodes ALWAYS absorb excess/bounce regardless of the matcher's include_excess / include_bounces — those flags govern only the root append. This asymmetry is inherited from v1 (nested ContractMatchers were built with default flags) and it is a real trap: nft_transfer sets include_excess = false yet still swallows nested excess messages into consumed.

The head test

test_head answers "does this node's own description fit this block", with no edges involved. It is used in three places: by match_node for plain nodes, by match_recursive as the entry gate on the STEP node, and recursively by itself for nested Or/Recursive kinds.

The exclusive rule lives here and only here. Counting branch head tests and requiring exactly one is a HEAD-test rule — it never gates branch attempts. If you are trying to work out why an exclusive or behaves like a plain or in some position, the answer is that match_node dispatched straight to match_or.

ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/Walker.cpp:127–164test_head — kind dispatchcpp638db6fd
127 bool test_head(int nid, Block *block) const {
128 const CompiledNode &node = m_.nodes[nid];
129 bool ok = false;
130 switch (node.kind) {
1311 case NodeKind::Contract:
132 ok = block->btype == "call_contract" && block->opcode && *block->opcode == node.opcode;
133 break;
134 case NodeKind::BlockType:
135 ok = block->btype == node.btype;
136 break;
137 case NodeKind::Any:
138 ok = true;
139 break;
1402 case NodeKind::Or:
141 if (node.exclusive) {
142 int c = 0;
143 for (int b : node.branches) {
144 if (test_head(b, block)) c++;
145 }
146 ok = c == 1;
147 } else {
148 for (int b : node.branches) {
149 if (test_head(b, block)) {
150 ok = true;
151 break;
152 }
153 }
154 }
155 break;
1563 case NodeKind::Recursive:
157 ok = test_head(node.step, block);
158 break;
1594 case NodeKind::Pred: {
160 auto it = host_predicates().find(node.pred_name);
161 ok = it != host_predicates().end() && it->second(block);
162 break;
163 }

1L131–133The Contract kind is an opcode test AND a btype test. Same pairing as matcher_test_self — an opcode node can only ever match a call_contract block, which is why a produced composite (no opcode, different btype) is unreachable from an opcode node and can only be reached by a block_type node.
2L140–155The exclusive count rule: count how many branch HEADS accept this block, require exactly one. Non-exclusive is a plain any-of with early exit. Both recurse into test_head, never into match_node — so no edges, no consumption, no bindings. Cheap by construction, because this can run inside a recursion entry gate on every frontier candidate.

If you need cross-block conditions, they belong in the build program's reject when (build-programs), which runs after the whole match succeeded.

Edges: child, children-set, parent, or

Four edge forms, four different semantics, and they are easy to conflate. In IR terms: child is a single node id, children is a list of node ids, parent is a single node id, and or is a node kind with a branches list. All four appear on the same node record and are evaluated in the order child → children → parent.

The pair to keep straight is child vs children. child accumulates: it tries the SAME node against EVERY successor and keeps all that match — one matcher node can bind many blocks. children is a bag-assignment: each declared item takes the first successor it fits and REMOVES it from a working copy, so two items can never claim the same block. Overlap between the two phases is legal because consume() dedupes by identity.

Branch order in the spec is the tie-break, and prefix-overlapping branches (stonfi_v2's hop/final arms) resolve first-in-order. No exclusive check anywhere in this function: that is the inertness described above, and it is deliberate parity, not an omission.

Recursion: frontier walk and cyclic descent

Two strategies share one node kind. frontier (9 of 11 recursive nodes in the prod artifact) is an iterative walk: try the exit first on each candidate, else take one step, then rebuild the frontier from what that step consumed. cyclic (2 nodes) is not iterative at all — the node graph itself contains back-edges, so recursion is ordinary match_node descent bounded by tree depth.

The frontier loop has three rules that surprise people. Exit is tried FIRST per candidate (so a pattern whose exit shares a prefix with its step will terminate early — the reason tonco_swap uses cyclic instead). Only ONE step is taken per round, then the frontier is replaced. And frontier exhaustion succeeds iff at least one step landed, REGARDLESS of whether an exit was declared — a declared exit that never fires does not fail the recursion, it just leaves its captures empty.

1L249–259The entry gate runs the recursive node's OWN where clauses against the entry block, before any strategy dispatch — and before the step's head test. So a where on a recursive node is a precondition on entering the recursion at all, not a per-iteration filter.
2L260–262Cyclic: no frame push, no frontier, no exit — just descend into the body, whose subgraph refers back to its own root. frame_ is untouched, which is precisely why the loader REJECTS capture slots anywhere inside a cyclic body: there would be no frame to attribute them to.
3L271–281Exit-first per candidate, with its own frame (kExitIdx). On success it pushes a non-step FrameEntry, restores the outer frame and returns immediately — note it does NOT roll back the step frames already recorded, so the exit's captures land after the accumulated step captures in assembly order.
4L286–295The frontier is rebuilt from the successors of exactly what THIS step consumed (consumed_ beyond the mark), then canonicalised. break after the first successful step is the one-step-per-round rule: sibling candidates that would also have matched are not tried in this round — they reappear only if they are successors of the consumed set.
5L299–302return iter_index > 0: zero iterations is a failure, one or more is a success even with no exit. Combined with optional on the recursive node at the call site, that gives the familiar "zero-or-more hops" shape. The exit's presence is irrelevant to success — pinned by test_walker.py::test_frontier_exhaustion_leaves_exit_captures_empty.

Bookkeeping: consume, rollback, and the absorb asymmetry

Four tiny functions carry the entire transactional model. consume is identity-deduped and append-only within an attempt; mark/rollback are the undo; bind records (slot, current frame, block).

absorb_aux is the nested half of excess/bounce handling — and it is the half that puts blocks into consumed, meaning they get MERGED into the produced composite. The root half (next section) only appends to the result list. Two levels, two different destinations, one flag pair that governs only the second.

2L319–326Rollback must undo visited_ as well as consumed_, and it does it by erasing exactly the tail. Miss this and a rolled-back attempt would leave blocks marked visited, so a later successful attempt would silently omit them from consumed — a bug that would surface as a too-small merge set, not as a match failure.
3L328–332Identity dedup at consume time is what makes overlapping edges safe (child ∩ children, parent re-descent, absorbed aux). The resulting list is traversal order with the anchor first — and that order is observable: builders receive it as consumed, and the classify dump prints it.
4L334bind snapshots the CURRENT frame, not the node. Two bindings of the same slot from different recursion iterations are distinguished only by that frame tuple — the whole per-iteration capture story below rests on this one line.

Capture assembly: slots, frames, gap alignment

Bindings are recorded flat during the walk and folded into captures only at the end. The fold has three modes, keyed by the slot's cardinality and by whether the slot is OWNED by a recursion node.

Scalar (one / opt): first binding wins, unbound is a null. many outside any recursion: every binding in order. many owned by a recursive node R: one element per iteration FRAME of R, in iteration order, with a null for an iteration that bound nothing — that is the gap alignment, and it is what keeps two parallel many captures index-aligned across hops. Iterations that consumed nothing contribute no element at all.

where_expr — the only expressions the match phase runs

Matching evaluates exactly one kind of expression: a node's inline where (expr), against one candidate block. Everything else — parse, lookup, host fn, let, out — is build phase (build-programs).

Two details matter for reading specs. First, a fault is not an error: eval_where collapses faulted, non-bool, and false into a single false, so a where clause that trips over a missing field simply does not match. Second, the interpreter's scope model is a single copied frame per comprehension — map(xs as e => …) binds e into a COPY of the environment, so the element variable shadows for the body only and never leaks. And parse as an expression is explicitly unreachable in the interpreter, which is another way of saying a where clause can never parse a message body.

1L111–118Env local = env_ is copied ONCE outside the lambda, then local[var] is overwritten per element. So the element variable shadows any outer binding for the body only, env_ is never touched, and nested comprehensions each get their own copy. This mirrors the Python engine's scope frame exactly — including the fact that later elements see no residue from earlier ones except through local[var] being reassigned.
2L119–122map and any/all share the binder and differ only in the core they hand it to. Both cores live in ExprRuntime and are shared with the generated code, so a comprehension means the same thing in a where clause and in a compiled build program (value).
3L124–130parse is a build-only expression and faults here. Since a fault in a where clause is just false, a spec that put parse inside where would produce a matcher that never matches — silently. Worth knowing as a debugging shortcut: a where clause that mysteriously never fires is worth checking for build-only constructs.

try_build: produce, merge, aux — and the flow construct that is not here

try_build is where a match becomes permanent. It is also where four different things can decline, all of them cleanly: a structural mismatch, a build-program reject when, a failed merge, and (upstream) an anchor that already has a parent.

One removal deserves a banner, because it is a trap for anyone reading this with the Python classifier in mind. **There is no value_flow here, and no flow statement in the language.** AccountValueFlow is not persisted to the database and the Go API computes flows separately, so the C++ engine never produces them: Phase E does not port AccountValueFlow, the flow statement was dropped from the IR (grep the artifact — zero occurrences), and value_flow was removed from the parity gate. If you are looking for where flows are accumulated during the merge, the answer is nowhere.

And a merge returning false is ALSO a clean rejection: Python's merge_blocks raises when the consumed set has no earliest common ancestor, try_build catches it, and the net effect is the same nothing-happened.

1L293–296ensure_earliest_common_block is the gate: the consumed set must have a single earliest block that dominates the rest. Returning nullptr here is the "merge raises" path — a structurally impossible composite is refused rather than built wrong.
2L297–301b->parent = this on every merged block. This one assignment is what the outer loop's cur->parent == nullptr guard reads, so THIS is the exact moment a block stops being available as an anchor for later matchers. Ordering effects all trace back to this line.
3L302–306The composite splices itself into the spine: it takes the frontier (successors of the merged set that are outside it) as its own next_blocks, and inherits the earliest block's previous_block. That is how a later matcher sees jetton_transfer@… as a spine sibling instead of the three raw calls it replaced.
4L307–312Note what is absent: no flow accumulation, no AccountValueFlow. In the Python Block.merge_blocks this is where value flows would be folded together. Here the merge is purely structural — event nodes, children, lt bounds, connections.

block_key and the --match dump

block_key is the one string that makes all of this observable, and it is shared verbatim by the match dump, the classify dump, the action dump and the Python twins. <btype>[#<opcode-hex8>]@<min_lt>: btype tells you init vs composite, the opcode is present only on call_contract, and min_lt is the identity within a trace.

--match is the debugging mode built directly on matcher_match. It deliberately does NOT run the classify loop: no prefilter, no priority order, no consumption, no builds. Every runnable matcher is probed against every block, so overlapping matches are expected and informative — the difference between the --match output and the --classify output on the same trace IS the ordering/consumption effect.

ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/BuildDriver.cpp:41–50block_keycpp50f14a39
41std::string block_key(const Block *b) {
42 std::string key = b->btype;
431 if (b->opcode) {
44 char buf[16];
45 std::snprintf(buf, sizeof(buf), "#%08x", *b->opcode);
46 key += buf;
47 }
482 key += "@" + std::to_string(b->min_lt);
49 return key;
50}
1L43–47Lowercase %08x, zero-padded, and only when an opcode is present. Both halves are part of the cross-language contract — a produced composite has no opcode, so jetton_transfer@42873104000003 versus call_contract#0f8a7ea5@42873104000003 is how you tell a composite from the raw call it merged, at the same lt.
2L48min_lt is the identity, not a pointer or an index. It is stable across runs and across languages, which is what lets the Python twin emit byte-identical dump lines (gates). Two blocks CAN share a min_lt (a composite and its earliest member), which is why btype is part of the key.

Python-parity trap: the in-leg event_nodes[0] story

Worth knowing because it is the one place where the Python side was genuinely non-deterministic and the C++ port could not simply copy it. build_stonfi_v2_swap_core used to read in_transfer.event_nodes[0].message to describe the incoming leg. On a set-merged composite the node order is hash-seed dependent, so event_nodes[0] flipped between the excess message and the jetton notify across runs on the SAME trace — and with it dex_incoming_transfer, sender, source_asset, peer_swaps[].in.

**Current state, verified in the tree:** fixed. The dual-dispatch wave replaced the message read with a btype gate on both sides, and the fix was proven stable across PYTHONHASHSEED 1/7/999. The C++ trio is registered and 7 stonfi_v2_swap actions fire in the corpus. Older notes calling this a blocker for the stonfi_v2 port are stale. The general lesson survives the fix and is the reason it belongs on this page: a composite's event_nodes list has no defined order, so anything downstream of a merge must read .data, never event_nodes[i].

Check yourself

Four things to try. The first two are captured below; the last two are a read and an experiment.

**3 · Read the two absorb sites side by side.** Walker.cpp:307 (absorb_aux → consumed, merged, ignores both flags) and ClassifyCore.cpp:69 (root append → aux, honours both flags). Confirm for yourself that absorb_aux never mentions include_excess or include_bounces, then look up the one matcher in the artifact that sets include_excess: false (nft_transfer) and satisfy yourself that its NESTED excess messages still land in consumed. If you expected that flag to be global, this is the trap.

**4 · Break the fold-back and watch matchers disappear.** Comment out the produced-btype fold-back loop at ClassifyCore.cpp:489, rebuild, and re-run the ACTION count from step 2. Four matchers anchored on a produced btype — ethena_deposit, jvault_stake, stonfi_v1_swap, stonfi_v2_withdraw — are then prefiltered away on every trace, with no error and no change to the SKIP table; the corpus loses 7 actions (1 + 5 + 1 + 0). That silence is why the conservative-superset argument has to be argued rather than assumed. Revert afterwards. Then ask the harder question the same experiment sets up: getgems_nft_purchase also anchors on a produced btype and its action count does NOT change, because it already runs before its producer — order and the fold-back are two separate preconditions and a matcher needs both.

The match-phase A/B twin (twins/py_match_dump.py vs --match) is the mechanical check behind every claim on this page about candidate ordering, first-wins capture selection and recursion gap alignment — 183 MATCH lines, diff 0 over the 148-trace corpus. Running it, and the fuller py_classify.py gate, belongs to gates.

Parse layer — 3 parser sources, 2 value universes

This layer turns a message body cell into an mch::Value that a build program can read as CAPTURE.body.field. It is a name -> function-pointer registry fed by three independent sources: 7 hand-written parsers, 22 compiled from mch-msgs.schema, and 3 that come out of the Tolk ABI toolchain. The first two sources are pytoniq-parity: they reproduce, deliberately and bug-for-bug, what the Python reference parsers in indexer/events/blocks/messages/ do — including skipping the leading 32 opcode bits WITHOUT checking them. The third source is tolk-faithful: the generated from_slice CHECKS the opcode prefix and models addresses the way @ton/core does. Those two conventions are incompatible in observable ways (a missing address is null in one and a present-but-empty Account in the other), and nothing in the type system keeps them apart — the discipline that does is the op-guard rule at the end of this page. The layer's whole correctness bar is an A/B twin gate: the same corpus through C++ and through the Python engine must produce byte-identical parse dumps.

The registry: three sources, one map, fail-closed

MsgParse.h is short but it is the contract for the entire layer — read its header comment before any code. The registry itself is a lazily-built std::map<std::string, MsgParserFn> where MsgParserFn is a plain function pointer (td::Result<Value>(*)(const td::Ref<vm::Cell>&)), not a std::function. That choice is load-bearing later: it is what lets an ABI parser register as an ordinary row with no closure state and no init API.

Three sources merge in a fixed order. Collisions are possible in principle (all three name-spaces are flat), so they are detected once at build time and refused twice: at startup by validate_registries(), and at every lookup by parse_message_body.

ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/MsgParse.h:1–25MsgParse.h — the semantics contractcpp35c4a704
1// TL-B message-parsing layer: per-family adapters that parse a message body
2// cell into a Value map (VType::Obj) whose keys match EXACTLY the attribute
3// set the Python reference parser exposes (vars(obj) after __init__), so a
4// build program's `CAPTURE.body.field` accesses resolve identically.
5//
61// Semantics contract (mirrors indexer/events/blocks/messages/jettons.py):
7// - no opcode validation: the first 32 bits are skipped unchecked;
8// - a parse failure anywhere (bit underflow, missing ref, bad address)
9// fails the WHOLE parse — the soft-parse machinery then tries the next
10// alternative / yields null (engine's _soft_parse contract);
11// - addr_none parses to a NULL Value (pytoniq load_address returns None),
122// addr_extern to a "extern:<len>:<value>" Str, addr_std to an Account;
13// - Maybe ^Cell payloads become Bytes (BOC with CRC32C, mirroring
14// pytoniq to_boc(hash_crc32=True)); absent -> null;
153// - integers (uint64 / VarUInteger 16) become Int (RefInt256);
16// - conditionally-set Python attributes (JettonTransfer.sum_type) are
17// conditionally-present keys.
18//
194// ONE EXCEPTION, for the ABI-bridge rows (AbiBridge.h): those parsers DO
20// validate the opcode prefix — a generated `from_slice` checks its struct's own
21// prefix and errors on a mismatch — while their Python twins skip the 32 bits
22// unchecked like everything else here. Consequence, and it is a RULE for every
23// future ABI-path protocol: an ABI-path `parse` capture MUST be behind an `op`
24// guard in the .mch spec. Unguarded, the same body gives a C++ parse error and
25// a Python garbage object, and the A/B gate diverges.
1L6–11This is the actual specification of the layer, not a courtesy comment. "no opcode validation: the first 32 bits are skipped unchecked" is what makes the pytoniq universe lenient: a body carrying the wrong opcode does not fail, it produces a plausible object built from the wrong bits. Safety comes entirely from the matcher having already checked op upstream, in the matcher runtime.
2L12–14addr_none becomes a NULL Value — not an empty address. On this path there is no representation for "present but empty"; a spec that wants to detect addr_none tests for null. Remember this line; the ABI path does the opposite.
3L15–17"conditionally-present keys" is a real part of the shape: the Python twin sets some attributes only on some code paths, vars(obj) is what gets compared, so C++ must omit the key rather than emit a null. The jetton sum_type excerpt below is the live case.
4L19–25The one exception, and the rule it forces. Because ABI parsers validate the prefix and their Python twins do not, an unguarded ABI-path parse gives a C++ error and a Python garbage object on the same body — the two sides diverge and the A/B gate fails. Hence: every ABI-path parse capture MUST sit behind an op guard.

951 std::set<std::string> seen;

97 std::vector<std::string> dups;
98 for (const auto *src : sources) {
99 for (const auto &row : *src) {

101 dups.push_back(row.first);
102 }
103 }

Universe 1 — pytoniq parity (PSlice and the hand parsers)

parse/PSlice.{h,cpp} is the leaf layer everything in sources 1 and 2 is built from: address, coins, snake-bytes, to-cell. It is not a thin wrapper over vm::CellSlice — it exists because pytoniq's Slice has behaviours a CellSlice does not, and the twin gate compares rendered output, so those behaviours have to be reproduced rather than corrected.

The rest of PSlice.cpp beyond the excerpt below is the same kind of work: load_snake_bytes (byte-aligned, at most one ref per link), pslice_to_cell, and a byte-level reimplementation of Python's bytes.decode("utf-8", errors="backslashreplace") used for TON-transfer comments. Read those directly if you touch comments; they are mechanical once the principle is clear.

1L32–39The reason a bare vm::CellSlice is not enough: pytoniq tracks the ref list separately from the bit cursor, and copy() does not preserve ref consumption. So refs + off are carried alongside cs and the two cursors are allowed to disagree — reproducing that disagreement is the point.
2L43–44to_cell() means "remaining bits + refs from off", i.e. the pytoniq view of what is left, not a copy of the original cell. This is what a forward_payload Bytes value is serialized from, so getting off wrong changes a payload's root hash.

35// pytoniq Slice.load_address(). Advances `cs`. Error == the Python parser
36// raising (whole message parse fails, or the enclosing try downgrades it).
37td::Result<Value> load_address_py(vm::CellSlice &cs) {
38 if (!cs.have(2)) {
39 return td::Status::Error("address: underflow");
40 }
41 auto tag = cs.fetch_ulong(2);
421 if (tag == 0) {
43 return Value::null(); // pytoniq returns None for addr_none
44 }
45 if (tag == 1) {
46 if (!cs.have(9)) {
47 return td::Status::Error("address: extern underflow");
48 }
492 int len = static_cast<int>(cs.fetch_ulong(9));
50 if (len == 0) {
51 return td::Status::Error("address: extern len 0"); // ba2int('') raises
52 }
53 if (!cs.have(len)) {
54 return td::Status::Error("address: extern underflow");
55 }
563 // pytoniq addr_extern: ba2int(bits, signed=False) — an unsigned big-endian
57 // integer of exactly `len` bits (1..511). fetch_int256(len, false) returns
58 // an invalid-but-non-null RefInt256 for len in 257..511 (renders as NaN),
59 // diverging from Python's exact bigint; build the value by 32-bit chunks so
60 // every length up to 511 is exact. For len <= 256 this yields the identical
61 // decimal fetch_int256 produced.
62 td::RefInt256 acc = td::make_refint(0);
63 for (int rem = len; rem > 0;) {
64 int k = rem < 32 ? rem : 32;
65 acc = (acc << k) + td::make_refint(static_cast<long long>(cs.fetch_ulong(k)));
66 rem -= k;
67 }
68 return Value::make_str("extern:" + std::to_string(len) + ":" + acc->to_dec_string());
69 }
704 if (tag == 3) {
71 return td::Status::Error("address: addr_var unsupported"); // pytoniq raises
72 }
1L42–44addr_none -> null Value. One line, and it is the fork in the road for the whole layer: on this path "no address" and "absent field" are the same value, and a spec cannot tell them apart.
2L49–52A zero-length external address is an error only because pytoniq's ba2int('') raises. Parity means importing the upstream quirk, not fixing it — a "fix" here shows up as an A/B diff, not as a bug fix.
3L56–68Why the hand-rolled 32-bit chunk loop instead of fetch_int256(len,false): for lengths 257..511 that returns an invalid-but-non-null RefInt256 that renders as NaN, diverging from Python's exact bigint. The result is the string extern:<len>:<decimal> — an ordinary Str, so a spec comparing it against an address field gets a plain mismatch rather than a type error.
4L70–71addr_var errors because pytoniq raises on it. Just past this excerpt, anycast is consumed but never APPLIED — the address prefix is left un-rewritten, unlike convert::to_raw_address, so anycast addresses render differently here than elsewhere in the indexer.

Universe 1, continued — the schema-generated middle source

Most registered parsers are not written by hand. mch-msgs.schema is a small declarative file compiled by indexer/events/mch/msgs_gen.py into a committed C++ TU, MsgParsersGenerated.cpp. Two constraints make this safe rather than clever: the generator may only emit calls to leaf helpers that already existed and were already A/B-proven, and regeneration must be byte-stable (a pytest re-runs the generator and diffs the committed file).

The generated code lives in the SAME universe as the hand parsers — same leaves, same unchecked opcode skip. The schema is a compression of hand parsers, not a new semantics.

ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/mch-msgs.schema:19–45mch-msgs.schema — the leaf vocabularytexta6024ac5
191# The leading 32 opcode bits are ALWAYS skipped unchecked (every hand parser
20# advance(32)s without validating — soft-parse leniency). The HEX after `opcode`
21# is documentation + vector filler only; it is never compared. A message with no
22# query_id simply omits the field (e.g. DedustSwapNotification).
23#
242# LEAF TYPES (each maps 1:1 to an existing helper; emitted value in parens):
25# bits N have(N) + advance(N) -> (nothing emitted; a pure skip of
26# N bits — always used with a `_`
27# parsed-and-dropped field name)
28# u32 fetch_ulong(32) -> Int (refint_u64)
29# u64 fetch_ulong(64) -> Int (refint_u64)
30# uint256 fetch_int256(256, false) -> Int
31# coins load_coins_py -> Int (VarUInteger 16; len nibble 0 -> 0)
323# addr_py load_address_py -> Account | Null | "extern:.." Str
33# asset2 2-bit tag (coffee) -> Asset (0=TON, 1=jetton wc:HEX)
34# asset4 4-bit kind (dedust) -> Asset (0=TON, else jetton wc:HEX)
35# ref_cell mandatory fetch_ref -> Cell (kept whole, not descended)
36# maybe_ref_cell Maybe ^Cell -> Cell | Null; bit=1 requires the
37# ref, bit=0 is Null. NO remainder
38# fallback (unlike fwd_cell_*)
39# dict_keys267 HashmapE(267) key walk -> List[Account] (values ignored)
404# fwd_cell_bits maybe-ref-or-remainder -> Cell | Null; remainder taken when
41# unconsumed BITS remain (JettonNotify)
42# fwd_cell_refs maybe-ref-or-remainder -> Cell | Null; remainder taken when
43# unconsumed REFS remain (PTonTransfer)
44#
45# COMPOSITE:
1L19–22"ALWAYS skipped unchecked" and "never compared" — the opcode in a schema line is documentation plus test-vector filler. Contrast the ABI path, where the prefix IS the parse. Two of the three sources treat the opcode as something someone else already checked.
2L24The rule that keeps the generator honest: every leaf maps 1:1 onto a helper that already existed. New protocols get new compositions, never new parse semantics — which is why the generator could not silently introduce a divergence from the Python twins.
3L32addr_py's three possible outputs on one line: Account, Null, or an extern:.. Str. Any spec field fed by an address has to tolerate all three.
4L40–43fwd_cell_bits vs fwd_cell_refs: identical TL-B shape, different rule for "is there a payload in the remainder" — JettonNotify looks at leftover BITS, PTonTransfer at leftover REFS. The two hand predecessors genuinely differed, so the schema kept both leaves instead of unifying them and breaking one twin.

Universe 2 — the ABI bridge (entry to the tolk world)

The third source comes from a completely different toolchain: a .tolk declaration is compiled to dedust_v2.abi.json, which ton-abi-gen turns into C++ structs with from_slice / store / to_abi_value. Those structs know nothing about mch — the dependency runs mch -> ton-abi only, permanently.

AbiBridge is the whole seam: a function template that adapts T::from_slice to a MsgParserFn, plus a total AbiValue -> mch::Value adapter. Both halves are worth reading closely, because this is where the second value universe gets its shape.

33// Parse a message body as the generated ABI struct T, returning an mch::Value.
34// T is a ton-abi-gen type (ton_abi::gen::<contract>::<Decl>) exposing:
35// static td::Result<T> from_slice(vm::CellSlice&); // checks its own prefix
36// td::Result<ton_abi::AbiValue> to_abi_value() const;
37//
382// &abi_parse_body<T> has type td::Result<Value>(*)(const td::Ref<vm::Cell>&) ==
39// MsgParserFn EXACTLY (no closure state -- dispatch is baked into from_slice), so
40// the instantiation registers as an ordinary parser row. Top-level exotic cells
41// are rejected here (W11.5 re-home) with a clean error result -- never an abort.
42template <class T>
43td::Result<Value> abi_parse_body(const td::Ref<vm::Cell> &body) {
44 if (body.is_null()) {
45 return td::Status::Error("abi bridge: null body cell");
46 }
473 bool special = false;
48 vm::CellSlice cs = vm::load_cell_slice_special(body, special);
49 if (special) {
50 return td::Status::Error("abi bridge: exotic cell not supported");
51 }
524 TRY_RESULT(parsed, T::from_slice(cs));
53 TRY_RESULT(av, parsed.to_abi_value());
54 return abi_value_to_mch(av);
55}
1L26–30Stated outright: this adapter is NOT pytoniq. Both universes produce the same C++ Value type, so the compiler will never object to mixing them — the only thing keeping them apart is the op-guard discipline in the next section.
2L38–43The trampoline, and why there is no registration API: &abi_parse_body<T> is a free function-template instantiation, so its address has EXACTLY MsgParserFn's type. No std::function, no closure state, no init step — the type parameter carries the dispatch.
3L47–51Exotic (pruned/library) cells are rejected here rather than deeper: load_cell_slice_special reports specialness, and an exotic body must become a clean Error result. The no-abort rule applies inside parsers as much as anywhere else.
4L52–54Two calls, and the first is the entire divergence from the other two sources: from_slice checks its own prefix. Then to_abi_value() flattens the struct into the ABI's own dynamic value, and only then does mch see anything.

41Value adapt_address(const ton_abi::AbiAddress &a) {

That matters because a throw or error escaping here would be indistinguishable from a parse miss — the adapter is required to be the boring half of the bridge. Same reason cell_from_slice (top of the file) uses append_cellslice_bool: the throwing overload raises vm::CellWriteError, which is neither a vm::VmError nor a std::exception, so parse_message_body's catch list would NOT have caught it.

Why the universes never mix: the op-guard rule

Both universes hand back an mch::Value, and the engine has no way to tell which one produced it. The rule that keeps them from colliding is enforced socially, in spec review: an ABI-path parse capture must be bound to a capture that is already op-guarded.

The reason is asymmetric failure. The C++ ABI parser CHECKS the prefix and errors on a mismatch; the Python twin skips 32 bits unchecked like everything else in the Python engine. On a body with the right opcode both sides agree. On any other body, C++ produces a parse failure (a Null body, silently) and Python produces a garbage object — and the A/B gate diverges, usually somewhere far away from the parse.

How a spec's parse statement actually resolves

The registry has one real consumer: the build runtime's parse statement (build-programs). Its behaviour explains why a mis-wired ABI parse is quiet rather than loud — a failed parse and a not-this-type parse are the same outcome by design.

There is also a preflight: BuildDriver scans every matcher's referenced message types against the registry and build-skips matchers whose types are missing, printing a warning listing them. So a spec referencing a type nobody registered degrades to "this matcher never builds", visible in the skip reasons rather than as a crash (ir-artifact, gates).

ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/BuildRuntime.cpp:27–47soft_parse — first alternative that succeeds winscppf769a178
27// program.py _soft_parse: first type whose parser succeeds wins; a parser
28// failure tries the next alternative; all failed -> Null body. An
29// unregistered type name is an EvalError (fault -> rejection).
30EvalResult soft_parse(const Block *b, const std::vector<std::string> &types, Value &out) {
31 auto r_body = block_body_cell(b);
321 for (const std::string &name : types) {
33 if (message_parsers().find(name) == message_parsers().end()) {
34 return rt_fault("message type '" + name + "' is not registered");
35 }
362 if (r_body.is_error()) {
37 continue; // get_body() raised inside this alternative's try
38 }
39 auto r = parse_message_body(name, r_body.ok());
403 if (r.is_ok()) {
41 out = r.move_as_ok();
42 return rt_ok(Value::null());
43 }
44 }
45 out = Value::null();
46 return rt_ok(Value::null());
47}
1L32–35An unregistered type name is a FAULT (it rejects the whole match), while a failing parser is merely a miss. The distinction is intentional: a typo'd type name is a broken spec, a body that isn't that type is normal traffic.
2L36–38A missing or undecodable body does not abort the loop — it behaves like Python's get_body() raising inside each alternative's own try, so alternatives are still consumed in order.
3L40–46All alternatives failing leaves the body Null, and downstream .body.field accesses null-propagate. This is exactly why an unguarded ABI parse is silent on the C++ side: the prefix-check error is indistinguishable from "not this type", and the divergence only surfaces later as a diff against Python.

  • block-tree — the body cell handed to a parser is the base64 message content decoded by the loader — a missing content row is a parse-alternative failure, not an error
