Build programs — expressions, captures, host seam

Matching (matcher-runtime) answers "does this shape occur here" and hands back a set of captured blocks. A build program answers the second half: "what does it MEAN" — it turns those captures into the produced block's data dict, its failed/broken flags, and (for a switch matcher) its btype. After this chapter you can read any .mch build program and predict exactly what the engine does with it: which statements can reject a match, where a null quietly propagates and where it faults, what parse actually guarantees, when the engine calls out to a hand-written C++ host fn, and why the C++ and Python engines cannot drift apart on any of it. You will also be able to read the GENERATED C++ that the engine really runs — build programs are not interpreted in production; mch-codegen emits one straight-line BuildOutcome build_<n>(BuildEnv&) per matcher whose only job is to call the rt_* leaves documented here. The one thing this chapter does NOT cover is what happens to the produced block afterwards: merging into the tree is block-tree, serialization into Action rows is actions.

What a build program is

A .mch matcher has two halves separated by a blank line: a PATTERN (chapter 5) and, below it, a build program. The build program is a short imperative script over the captures the pattern bound. Its whole statement vocabulary is: parse CAP as T1|T2, let NAME = expr, reject when expr, failed when expr, broken when expr, out { field: expr }, and produces switch { when expr => BTYPE out {...} … else => … }.

Two properties make it tractable. It is STATELESS — nothing survives between runs, and the program is re-run from scratch for every matched anchor in the trace. And it is TOTAL in one direction only: every statement can reject the match, none can crash it. Any evaluation error anywhere (a missing object field, an un-orderable comparison, an unregistered lookup kind) becomes a clean rejection of this match, indistinguishable from the pattern not having matched at all.

The first excerpt is the whole language on one screen.

1L40–45The bridge between the two halves: @transfer / @internal are pattern capture names, and the build program addresses them as plain identifiers. There is no third namespace — a let name and a capture name live in the same scope, and shadowing a capture is a compile error on the Python frontend, not a runtime surprise.
2L46–47reject when is the only statement whose PURPOSE is to reject; every other statement can reject as a side effect of faulting. Here the intent is legacy parity: build_jetton_transfer_core asserts the wallet is non-null, and reject when is the containable spelling of that assert.
3L49–50?? is where the soft-parse contract pays off. If JettonInternalTransfer failed to parse, internal.body is Null, internal.body.amount null-propagates, and the ?? silently falls back to the outer transfer's amount. No error is raised anywhere on that path — which is exactly why an unguarded ABI-path parse is dangerous (parse-layer).

5L56The ternary is A if cond else B — Python's order, not C's. Worth internalising before you read the generated code, where it becomes an ordinary if/else and the source ordering is gone.

1L16produces A | B | C declares the switch up front so the IR (and the block-type registry) knows all three outcomes statically. The runtime picks one; the artifact still records the full set, which is what build_skip_reason and the btype prefilter reason about.

3L30name?: — an OPTIONAL key. The generated code is if (!v.is_null()) fs.emplace_back(...), so the key is ABSENT rather than null when the lookup misses. That distinction is observable: the dump renders a key set, and the Python twin's dict has to have the same keys. Mirrors legacy's conditional data['collection_address'] = ….

The execution model: stateless, per-matched-anchor, codegen'd

Nothing in this layer interprets a build program in production. mch-codegen --builds reads the IR artifact and emits one C++ function per matcher into the build tree; the engine holds a table of those function pointers keyed by artifact index. The generated code contains no policy — every operation is a call into BuildRuntime/ExprRuntime, so the interpreter path (ExprEval, used by the conformance vectors) and the production path cannot diverge on semantics.

The two structs below are the entire interface between generated code and the engine: BuildOutcome out, BuildEnv in.

parse: the statement, the expression, and the contract

parse CAP as T1|T2 is soft by design. Its inner half (soft_parse, first alternative that succeeds wins, all-fail ⇒ Null body) is excerpted in parse-layer; here is the outer half — what a parse statement does with the target it is given, and how .body reads the result back.

The key asymmetry to hold onto: an UNREGISTERED type name is a fault (broken spec), a failing PARSER is not (normal traffic). Everything else follows from that. And because a failed parse is silent, the op-guard rule from parse-layer is not optional discipline — it is the only thing standing between an ABI-path parse and a divergence that surfaces hundreds of lines away in a twin diff.

ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/BuildRuntime.cpp:51–81rt_parse — three target shapes, all softcpp173ea416
51EvalResult rt_parse(BuildEnv &env, const Value &target, const std::vector<std::string> &types) {
521 if (target.is_null()) {
53 return rt_ok(Value::null()); // absent optional capture: `.body` null-propagates
54 }
552 if (target.t == VType::List) {
56 for (const Value &el : *target.items) {
57 if (el.t != VType::Block || el.block == nullptr) {
58 continue; // null (gap) elements stay unparsed; non-blocks unreachable
59 }
60 Value body;
61 EvalResult r = soft_parse(el.block, types, body);
62 if (r.faulted) {
63 return r;
64 }
65 env.bodies[el.block] = std::move(body);
66 }
67 return rt_ok(Value::null());
68 }
69 if (target.t == VType::Block && target.block != nullptr) {
70 Value body;
71 EvalResult r = soft_parse(target.block, types, body);
72 if (r.faulted) {
73 return r;
74 }
75 env.bodies[target.block] = std::move(body);
76 return rt_ok(Value::null());
77 }
783 // Non-block target: Python's per-type try swallows the get_body attribute
79 // error, leaving the body unset for anything `.body` could reach — no-op.
80 return rt_ok(Value::null());
81}
1L52–54A null target is a NO-OP, not an error. An unbound optional capture (maybe op X @cap) therefore parses to nothing, and the later .body on it null-propagates through the whole expression. That is how internal.body.amount ?? transfer.body.amount degrades gracefully with no explicit null test in the spec.
2L55–68List targets parse element-wise and SKIP null gaps rather than erroring — but note the fault from soft_parse (unregistered type) short-circuits the whole loop. So a typo'd type name fails on the first element, not after silently parsing the rest.
3L78–80The most Python-shaped line in the file: a non-Block target is a no-op because Python's per-type try swallows the AttributeError from calling get_body() on something that has no such method. Reproducing the SHAPE of Python's exception handling, not its intent — a recurring theme in this port.

831EvalResult rt_parse_expr(BuildEnv &env, const Value &target,

852 (void)env; // stateless: no env.bodies store, unlike the statement form
86 // expr.py _eval_parse: a null target or a non-block target (no get_body)

2L85–90IR v1.1 (the W7 minify wave) added parse as an EXPRESSION, and it is soft-parse's mirror image on every axis: no env.bodies write (stateless), and a null-or-non-block target FAULTS where the statement form no-ops. env is taken only so all build-mode rt_* leaves share one signature.

That makes the expression form safe to use with an ABI-path parser without an op guard — the C++ error and the Python garbage-object both end up rejecting… but only if the Python twin also faults, which is why this form is still gated behind the same review rule.

Expressions: one runtime, two callers

Every operation a build expression performs — arithmetic, comparison, null propagation, attribute access, builtins, comprehensions — has exactly one implementation, in ExprRuntime. The tree-walking interpreter calls it recursively; the generated code calls the same functions in straight line. There is no second semantics to keep in sync, which is why the conformance-vector gates over the interpreter are evidence about the production path too.

Two builtins deserve individual attention because their behaviour is not what you would guess from the name.

ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/ExprRuntime.h:1–19The contract at the top of ExprRuntime.hcpp989c105f
1// Shared expression-runtime semantics for the MCH expression VM.
2//
3// This is the SINGLE implementation of every leaf operation an MCH expression
4// performs — builtins, arithmetic / comparison / negation, null propagation,
51// truthiness, attribute access, name resolution, lookup nodes. Both consumers
6// share it, so a codegen bug can never be masked by a subtly different runtime:
7// - the tree-walking interpreter (ExprEval) — reference / fallback path;
8// - the build-time C++ code generated from IR expressions (indexer frontend
9// module mch/cpp_expr_emit.py) — production path.
10//
112// Fault model (unchanged from stage 4a): a fault is a DISTINCT OUTCOME, never a
12// thrown exception. Every operation returns an EvalResult{faulted, value}. The
13// generated code threads these with straight-line early returns
14// (`if (r.faulted) return r;`); the interpreter does the same recursively.
153// Null propagation is baked into each op exactly as the Python reference does it
16// (arith null->null, ordering null->false, `==` structural null handling,
17// builtins null-strict), so call sites never need to special-case null except
18// for the lazy operators (`and`/`or`/`??`/ternary), which are control flow and
19// stay at the call site.
1L5–9"A codegen bug can never be masked by a subtly different runtime" is the actual design argument. The generated code is allowed to be wrong about STRUCTURE (which leaf, in what order); it cannot be wrong about SEMANTICS, because it has no semantics of its own.
2L11–14A fault is a value, not a throw. This is what lets the generated code be pure straight-line C++ with if (r.faulted) return r; and no unwinding — and it is why an unexpected C++ exception escaping a host fn is a categorically different event (it reaches the trace-level boundary in ClassifyCore, not the build rejection path).
3L15–19Null propagation is baked into each op, so call sites never null-check — EXCEPT the lazy operators (and, or, ??, ternary), which are control flow and stay inlined in the generated code. That is why you see if (!rt_is_null(v20)) { … } else { … } in the generated ?? rather than a runtime call.

2L491–497The trap. A Cell is serialised with td's BOC writer, whose byte output differs from pytoniq's on multi-ref trees — so the b64 text of a forward_payload is NOT comparable across engines. What IS equal is the cell it decodes back to. The layer's answer is at the render boundary, not here: render_value in BuildDriver.cpp routes known BOC-carrying field names through boc_field_cellhash, so the dumps compare root hashes instead of base64. See value for the field-name set and the hashing rule.

588EvalResult rt_quant(bool is_all, const Value &xs, const ElementFn &body) {
589 if (rt_is_null(xs)) return rt_ok(Value::null());
590 if (xs.t != VType::List) {
591 return rt_fault(std::string(is_all ? "all" : "any") + " comprehension expects a list, got " +
592 xs.describe());

596 EvalResult r = body(el);
597 if (r.faulted) return r;

599 if (b.faulted) return b;
600 if (!is_all && b.value.boolean) {
601 result = true;
602 break;
603 }
604 if (is_all && !b.value.boolean) {
605 result = false;
606 break;
607 }
608 }

4L598–599A quantifier body must return a Bool: any(xs as x => x.amount) faults rather than testing truthiness. Note the fault happens on the FIRST element, so it short-circuits before evaluating the rest — a fault and a true result are both early exits.

Lookups: why the build fn runs more than once

lookup kind(args) reaches outside the trace — jetton wallet interfaces, NFT items, pool records. In Python that is an inline async call. In C++ the fetch has to be batched (production issues one actor round per trace, prod-path), so the build fn is executed as a DRY pass against a table that records misses, the misses are fetched, and the fn is re-run against a filled table. The build program being stateless and side-effect-free is exactly what makes running it twice legal.

One subtlety forces a loop rather than a single dry pass: a lookup whose ARGUMENT comes from another lookup. On the first pass the inner lookup returns Null, the null-strict rule short-circuits the outer call, and the outer key never forms. So the collect pass is iterated to a fixpoint.

1L227–231The A2 fast path: no lookups and no host fns ⇒ zero possible misses ⇒ run once against an empty filled table. Byte-identical to the loop below by construction, not by measurement.
2L235–246Each round is a full re-execution with a FRESH env — bodies is per-run state, so re-parsing happens every round. That is cheap and, more importantly, keeps the passes independent: a round is not allowed to observe the previous round's leftovers.
3L247–254The non-convergence branch throws rather than proceeding with a partial table, and the comment says why: Python resolves arbitrary lookup depth inline, so a truncated fixpoint here is silent WRONGNESS, not a benign approximation. Today's artifacts have max depth 2 and converge in ≤2 rounds, so this is dead code whose value is that it can never become quiet.
4L256–258Only the FINAL pass's outcome is used. Any rejection or fault produced during a collect round is discarded — which is another reason build programs must be free of side effects: a dry pass that rejected still counted as a real execution.

The host seam: preds, fns, shapers

Some logic genuinely cannot be written declaratively — reconstructing roles from an unordered consumed set, walking a DeDust step chain, scanning for a per-hop event. Those stay as hand-written C++ registered in one of three name→function-pointer maps. The names are the PYTHON registry keys, so a .mch spec compiled by the Python frontend and executed by the C++ engine resolves the same identifier on both sides.

The three registries differ in when they run: predicates at match time (chapter 5), fns during the build program, shapers AFTER the produced block has merged its consumed set. And they share one consequence: an unregistered name is not a crash but a SKIP — the matcher is excluded from the run and the reason is reported, so the C++ engine can legitimately implement a subset of the artifact while the twins compute the identical subset.

54struct ShaperMatch {
55 std::map<std::string, Block *> captures; // capture name -> block (or absent)
56 std::vector<Block *> consumed; // match consumed set (`match.consumed`)
57 BlockArena *arena{nullptr}; // proxy-block allocation
58 
594 Block *capture(const std::string &name) const {
60 auto it = captures.find(name);
61 return it == captures.end() ? nullptr : it->second;
62 }
63};

65using HostShaperFn = void (*)(Block *produced, const ShaperMatch &m);

A spec calling a host fn must therefore expect it to be entered with nulls.
2L35–38Two ways to reject from a host fn, and they are not equivalent: a fault rejects the match unconditionally, while returning Null rejects only if the spec wrote reject when d == null. The hybrid specs use the second so that "no roles found" reads as data, not as an error. Note the signature takes BuildEnv& — that is how a host fn reaches env.lookups and participates in the two-phase fetch.
3L44–53The shaper contract, including its honesty note. Python's EmptyBlock() self-allocates; C++ blocks are arena-owned, so the arena has to ride along on ShaperMatch. 4L59–62Shapers address captures BY NAME, unlike build programs' slot indexing. They are hand-written C++ that predates the slot scheme and there are three of them, so the name map is cheaper than threading a slot table through.

52 static HostResult fault(std::string m) { return HostResult{Kind::Fault, {}, std::move(m)}; }

Long arrays truncated at the right margin. This is the C++ engine describing ITS OWN registries; the output is committed as twins/cpp_surface.json and the Python twins read the fn/pred/shaper/lookup lists from it to compute the identical included-matcher set. Nothing is hand-mirrored, so registering a host fn without regenerating this file makes the twins disagree — that is a gate failure, covered in gates.

What actually runs: the skip table

build_skip_reason is the function that turns "this C++ engine implements a subset" into a precise, comparable statement. It is computed once at startup per matcher from the artifact's declared references plus the four registries, and the Python twin computes the same string from the same artifact and the same cpp_surface.json. A matcher with an empty reason runs end-to-end; anything else is excluded from BOTH engines, so the A/B diff stays meaningful.

3L132–137Lookups are checked against FixtureLookupSource::kinds() — the OFFLINE source's kind set. That is why dedust_pool had to be listed there even though no matcher references it as a lookup node (a host fn fetches it): the honest kind set and the skip-gating set are the same set, so an omission would silently move a skip decision.

Check yourself

Four claims from this page, each testable in a couple of minutes.

**1 — Build programs really are compiled, not interpreted.** Pick any statement from a spec and find its C++ image; the first run below does it for let d = coffee_swap_data(consumed) in coffee_swap.mch. Then read the ~70 generated lines around the hit and match every one back to a spec line. If you can do that for one matcher you can do it for all 33.

**2 — The parse EXPRESSION is vector-only today.** grep -c rt_parse_expr returns 0 in builds_ir_generated.cpp and 3 in builds_vectors_generated.cpp. That is the coverage claim in the parse section, stated as a command rather than a promise — and it is why the mch_build_vectors ctest is the only thing exercising rt_parse_expr.

**3 — The surface is a projection, not a hand-mirrored list.** Regenerate twins/cpp_surface.json from the running binary and diff it against the committed copy (second run below; note the CRLF normalisation on Windows). A non-empty diff means someone registered a host binding without refreshing the file, and the Python twins are about to compute a different included-matcher set.

**4 — A rejection consumes nothing.** Worth doing once by hand: delete reject when wallet == null from specs_decl/jettons.mch, recompile the artifact, and diff the --classify dump. Predict first — the only change should be extra jetton_transfer actions whose wallet lookup missed. If a consumed set changes, or a downstream matcher gains or loses a block, your model of §10.7 is wrong.

From blocks to Action rows

By the end of build-programs a matcher has produced a Block carrying a data dict. This chapter is the last leg: how that block becomes an Action row with an id, a time window, a tx-hash set, an accounts set, eight directional columns and one protocol-specific composite. Two files do the work. ClassifyCore.cpp runs the post-pass stage — the host post-processors (post_process_dedust_liquidity, post_process_stonfi_v2_liquidity, unwind_deployments) that mutate the already-matched block set, plus the per-trace exception boundary that decides between "commit these actions" and "throw them all away and fall back to leaf actions". ActionBuild.{h,cpp} is the block_tree_serializer.py port: build_action fills the universal fields, fill_action dispatches on btype to one of 21 fill_* functions. Rendering is NOT in either — render_action stays harness-side in Classify.cpp, which is the whole point of the core/harness split. Two things will surprise you if you know the Python classifier from another branch: there is NO role system on this branch (action_accounts is role-less by design, not by omission), and the A/B twin gate compares FULL rendered rows, so every field you see below is byte-pinned against the real Python serializer over 148 fixtures.

The seam: a CoreAction is not a row

The core deliberately stops one step short of an Action. What the matcher loop collects is a CoreAction: four raw pointers into the caller's arena, no strings, no rendering, no schema. Everything that turns those pointers into text or into a row happens in an adapter — the CLI dump in Classify.cpp, or the production actor in prod-path.

That sounds like ceremony until you notice WHEN a CoreAction is collected versus when it is rendered. It is collected at fire time, mid-walk, while later matchers are still mutating the tree; it is rendered after the post-pass, from the block's FINAL state. Keeping the two apart is what lets a later merge rewrite produced->data and have the row reflect it.

ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/ClassifyCore.h:44–71CoreAction / ClassifyResult — the core's whole output vocabularycpp5c70ffae
44// One produced action, RENDERING-AGNOSTIC: raw block pointers + fire-time aux.
45// The adapter renders block_key(anchor)/data/consumed/aux or builds an Action
46// row from `produced`. Pointers reference the caller's arena (TraceContext),
47// valid for as long as the caller keeps it alive.
481struct CoreAction {
49 std::string matcher_name;
50 Block *anchor;
51 Block *produced;
522 std::vector<Block *> aux; // fire-time excess/bounce auto-append (anchor)
53};
54 
55// Buffered ATOMIC per-trace result: on a mid-trace throw the pipeline sets
563// `failure` (+ reason) and returns whatever was collected — NOTHING is emitted
57// by the core; the adapter decides (a dump reproduces today's TRACE_FAIL line,
58// production commits only on success).
59struct ClassifyResult {
60 std::vector<CoreAction> actions; // surviving post-pass, in fire order
61 bool failure = false;
62 std::string failure_reason;
63 // Trace-terminal failure category (additive telemetry; none unless `failure`).
64 FailureCategory failure_category = FailureCategory::none;
654 // Step 2c basic-actions fallback (try_classify_basic_actions): populated ONLY
66 // when `failure` — a fresh leaf-only classify (no matchers) + the
67 // post-processor chain, one CoreAction per surviving spine block of a basic
68 // btype (call_contract / contract_deploy / ton_transfer). Production commits
69 // these when classification fails. Ungated (corpus has no failing traces).
70 std::vector<CoreAction> fallback_actions;
71};
1L48–53anchor and produced are usually different blocks: the anchor is where the matcher's test_self hit (the block whose key the dump prints), produced is the new composite block the match built. On the fallback path they are deliberately the SAME pointer — a leaf block is its own anchor.
2L52aux is the one piece of fire-time state that cannot be recovered later. It is captured from the anchor's next_blocks at match time; by the time the post-pass has run, merges may have moved those siblings. Storing them as raw pointers (not rendered strings) is what keeps the core rendering-agnostic while still preserving the fire-time answer.
3L56–58"Buffered ATOMIC" is the contract that makes the failure fork possible: nothing is printed or inserted while the trace is being classified, so a throw halfway through can discard the whole trace's output without needing to un-emit anything. Python gets this for free by building a list; C++ has to promise it.
4L65–70Two separate action vectors, never both populated. fallback_actions is the Step 2c path and is UNGATED — no corpus trace fails, so the A/B twins never exercise it. Treat any behaviour you read in basic_classify_fallback as unproven-by-gate, unlike everything else on this page.

1L69–73Read from the ANCHOR's next_blocks, not the produced block's. The merge just consumed a set of blocks into produced, but the anchor's sibling list is untouched by that — so excess/bounce messages that trail the matched subtree are still visible here and only here.
2L74–76stable_sort by min_lt before scanning: the list is already in canonical order (block-tree), but the sort is re-asserted because aux order IS rendered and a merge earlier in this same walk could have appended out of order.
3L80–82Two hardcoded opcodes — 0xD53276DB (excess) and 0xFFFFFFFF (bounce) — gated per matcher by include_excess / include_bounces from the IR (ir-artifact). A matcher that opts out simply gets an empty aux list; the messages stay unconsumed in the tree.
4L87The only place a CoreAction is created on the normal path. Note what is NOT stored: no data snapshot, no rendered strings. produced->data is read later, after the post-pass may have rewritten it.

The post-pass stage: what survives becomes a row

After every matcher has walked, three host post-processors run over a freshly re-collected spine list. They are ports of blocks/liquidity.py and event_processing.py, and unlike matchers they are imperative surgery on the block graph: they merge two produced blocks into one, re-parent children, and delete blocks that already have a CoreAction pointing at them.

That last part is the mechanism to understand. A post-processor never touches pending; it inserts into a removed set, and the filter at the end of classify_trace is what actually drops the row. So "this matcher fired but produced no action" has exactly two causes on this branch: a clean rejection inside try_build (matcher-runtime), or a post-processor merging the produced block away here.

498 while (!q.empty()) {

1L495–504The spine is re-collected from scratch AFTER matching, not reused from the prefilter inventory at the top of the function. It has to be: matchers rewired next_blocks as they merged, so the pre-match BFS order is stale. Note the walk follows next_blocks only — children of produced composites are not on the spine.
2L506–508Order is load-bearing and mirrors event_processing.py exactly. post_process_stonfi_v2_liquidity pairs blocks that post_process_dedust_liquidity may already have merged; running them the other way round changes which pair survives. unwind_deployments last, and it is a no-op for the dumps (it only appends to the spine, which the dump never re-walks) — ported so the chain matches production, per prod-path.
3L509–511The whole survival rule in three lines, and it keys on produced, not anchor. A merged-away block's CoreAction disappears silently — there is no "merged" marker in the output, the row just isn't there. When a dump has fewer rows than you expect, this filter and try_build's clean rejection are the two places to look.

1L171–174contract_key deliberately uses describe() (the debug rendering) for anything that is not an Account. That is not sloppiness: the key only needs to group blocks, and Python groups by the raw object's equality. Using describe() gives a total, deterministic key for the Null / wrong-type cases without adding a branch per Value kind (value).
2L184–186Python logs a warning and skips merging when a deposit contract appears more than twice; C++ silently returns. The stdout channel is the A/B comparison channel, so a log line here would be a diff — warnings that Python prints to its logger have no C++ counterpart by design.
3L193–198combine_deposits signals its consistency failures by throwing, and the catch turns that into "leave the pair unmerged" — the net effect of a Python raise propagating out of the same call. Unreached over the corpus, so this is parity by construction rather than by gate.
4L199–209The merge itself: first is erased from the spine AND inserted into removed (two different jobs — the spine erase affects later passes, the removed insert kills the row), then its event nodes and children are folded into final_b and the lt window recomputed. The sort+unique on children_blocks is a pointer-value dedup, which means child order after a merge is ADDRESS order, not lt order — harmless only because emit_action sorts the rendered child keys.

302// event_processing.py unwind_deployments (3rd production post-processor, Step
303// 2b): promote ContractDeploy blocks nested in children up to the top-level
304// spine list. The Python `for block in blocks` loop SEES appends (it re-scans
3051// the promoted deploys), so the C++ index loop must too. NOTE: a no-op for the
306// classify/actions DUMP — the dump emits matcher-produced blocks (`pending`),
307// and this only appends to the spine, which the dump never walks; ported to
308// keep the post-processor chain aligned with production for Phase G.
309void unwind_deployments(std::vector<Block *> &blocks) {
310 std::set<Block *> visited;
3112 for (std::size_t i = 0; i < blocks.size(); i++) { // index loop: sees appends
312 std::deque<Block *> queue(blocks[i]->children_blocks.begin(),
313 blocks[i]->children_blocks.end());
314 while (!queue.empty()) {
315 Block *child = queue.front();
316 queue.pop_front();
3173 if (child->btype == "contract_deploy" && visited.count(child) == 0) {
318 blocks.push_back(child);
319 } else {
320 for (Block *c : child->children_blocks) queue.push_back(c);
321 }
322 visited.insert(child);
323 }

1L305–308The honesty note that matters: this pass is a no-op for both dumps. It appends promoted contract_deploy blocks to the spine, and the dump emits matcher-produced blocks from pending, never the spine. It exists so the pass chain is identical to production, where the spine IS the serialization input.
2L311An index loop, not a range-for, and the comment says why: Python's for block in blocks over a list being appended to re-scans the appended entries. A range-for (or a cached end()) would silently change the traversal — and because the pass is a dump no-op, the gate would not catch it.
3L317–322Note the else: a promoted deploy's own children are NOT queued. Promotion terminates the descent on that branch, so a deploy nested inside a deploy is reached on the outer loop's later pass over the appended entry, not here.

That equality is the cheapest sanity check that the ported fill set still covers the corpus.

The failure fork

classify_trace wraps the whole matcher loop and post-pass in one try/catch. This is the C++ image of event_processing.py's per-trace boundary: a trace that throws anywhere loses ALL its classified actions and is re-run through a leaf-only classification instead.

The FailureCategory enum next to it is newer and serves a different purpose — shadow-mode telemetry for prod-path. It is worth reading its comment carefully, because it documents as much by what it refuses to enumerate as by what it does.

ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/ClassifyCore.h:23–42FailureCategory — four members, and the argument for fourcppba4f1841
23// Failure/skip taxonomy (additive, Phase G slice 3 review). A shared vocabulary
24// for WHY a matcher/trace did not produce actions; used for shadow-mode
25// telemetry only — rendering-agnostic, no dump/twin sees it, existing gates stay
261// byte-stable. TRACE-TERMINAL reasons only:
27// - lookup_infra_fail: two-phase lookup did not converge (infra error).
28// - engine_fault: a mid-trace exception (Python's per-trace fallback).
29// - malformed_trace: the trace could not be loaded into an event tree
302// (schema map / empty tree) — set caller/actor-side.
31// Deliberately NOT enumerators: matcher_skip (a setup-level fact, read from
323// ClassifySetup.skips, never a per-trace outcome) and clean_reject / parse_null /
33// the per-lookup tier misses (per-(block, matcher, lookup) events on the hot
34// path — counted in ParsedBlockLookupSource::LookupStats, or left uncounted).
35// None of those can be the single trace-terminal value this field holds, so an
36// enumerator for them would be a state the type never reaches.
37enum class FailureCategory {
38 none,
39 lookup_infra_fail,
40 engine_fault,
41 malformed_trace,
42};
1L26–31"TRACE-TERMINAL reasons only" is the type invariant. The field holds ONE value for a whole trace, so anything that can happen many times per trace (a clean reject, a null parse, a lookup tier miss) cannot be a member without making the type lie.
2L30–31malformed_trace is the one member classify_trace never sets — the trace never reached it. It is set caller-side by whoever failed to build the event tree (block-tree), which is why you will not find it assigned anywhere in ClassifyCore.cpp.
3L32–36The deliberately-excluded list. matcher_skip is a SETUP fact (read from ClassifySetup.skips, same for every trace) and would be a category error here; the per-lookup misses are counted separately in LookupStats. This comment is the reason the enum shrank from a larger draft to four.
ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/ClassifyCore.cpp:512–531The catch and the discardcppa6ff2878
512 } catch (const std::exception &e) {

5161 // infra fault, distinct from a spec/parse engine fault. Everything else is
517 // a generic engine_fault (Python's per-trace fallback boundary).
518 result.failure_category =

520 ? FailureCategory::lookup_infra_fail

5222 } catch (...) {

1L516–521Categorisation by substring match on the exception message. Fragile-looking, and it is — the string "two-phase lookup did not converge" is thrown by the build driver and matched here by text. It survives because the category is telemetry only: getting it wrong mislabels a metric, it does not change a row. Anything else is engine_fault.
2L522–526The catch-all is NOT redundant. A parser tail can throw something that is neither a std::exception nor a vm::VmError (parse-layer covers the narrow catch list one level down); without this the throw would escape into the caller's loop and take the whole corpus run with it.
3L527–530actions.clear() is the atomicity promise being kept: a trace that failed at action 40 does not emit its first 39. Python does the same by letting the list go out of scope. The fallback is then computed from a FRESH block tree, not from the half-mutated one — see the next excerpt.
ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/ClassifyCore.cpp:327–367basic_classify_fallback — a second classification with no matcherscpp95df804c
327// try_classify_basic_actions (event_processing.py, Step 2c): a FRESH leaf-only
328// classify (init_block over the same event tree, NO matchers) + the
329// post-processor chain; one CoreAction per surviving spine block of a basic
330// btype. serialize_blocks skip conditions applied: skip root/empty, and
331// call_contract with a null source or destination. Throw-safe (Python's
332// fallback returns [] on any exception). Ungated (corpus has no failing traces).
333std::vector<CoreAction> basic_classify_fallback(TraceContext &ctx) {
334 std::vector<CoreAction> out;
335 try {
3361 Block *root = init_block(ctx.arena, ctx.tree.root);
337 Block *wrap = ctx.arena.make("root");
338 wrap->connect(root);
339 std::vector<Block *> spine;
340 {
341 std::deque<Block *> q{wrap};
342 while (!q.empty()) {
343 Block *cur = q.front();
344 q.pop_front();
345 spine.push_back(cur);
346 for (Block *n : cur->next_blocks) q.push_back(n);
347 }
348 }
3492 std::set<Block *> removed;
350 post_process_dedust_liquidity(spine, removed);
351 post_process_stonfi_v2_liquidity(spine, ctx.arena, removed);
352 unwind_deployments(spine);
3533 for (Block *b : spine) {
354 if (b->btype == "root" || b->btype == "empty" || removed.count(b) != 0) continue;
355 if (b->btype == "call_contract") {
356 if (pp_field(b->data, "source").is_null() ||
357 pp_field(b->data, "destination").is_null()) {
358 continue;
359 }
360 }
3614 out.push_back(CoreAction{"basic", b, b, {}});
362 }
363 } catch (...) {
364 out.clear(); // Python: fallback returns [] on any exception
365 }
366 return out;
367}
1L336–338init_block over ctx.tree.root again: a brand-new spine, allocated from the same arena, sharing nothing mutable with the tree the failed run mangled. That is the only safe thing to do — the failed run threw mid-merge, so the old spine may be half-rewired.
2L349–352The post-processor chain runs here too, over blocks no matcher ever touched. In practice they all no-op (there are no dedust/stonfi composite btypes without matchers), but the chain is kept verbatim because Python's try_classify_basic_actions calls it.
3L353–360The serialize_blocks skip conditions, inlined: root/empty wrappers out, and a call_contract with a null source OR destination out. That second rule is why a bounced-to-nowhere message never becomes a fallback row.
4L361–366CoreAction{"basic", b, b, {}} — anchor and produced are the same block, matcher_name is the literal "basic", aux is empty. Downstream build_action cannot tell the difference, which is exactly why the fallback rows render through the same code path. The catch-all out.clear() reproduces Python's "fallback returns [] on any exception": a failure to fall back yields no rows at all, never a partial set.

build_action: the fields every row gets

ActionBuild.{h,cpp} moved out of the harness in R1b so the production actor could call it without dragging stdout printing along. The code is byte-identical to what used to live in Classify.cpp — the twin dumps proved the move.

build_action fills what does not depend on btype: the action id, the lt/utime window, mc_seqno_end, tx_hashes, and accounts. Then it calls fill_action, and only if that succeeds does it assemble accounts — because accounts are derived from the directional fields the fill just wrote.

One honesty note about the demo trace used below (013-itRDy…): in PRODUCTION this trace is classified as coffee_staking_claim_rewards — the coffee staking protocol is NOT ported to mch specs, so the mch engine (both C++ and its Python twin, identically) classifies the ported jetton_transfer leg instead. The row is real and every column below is exactly what ActionBuild emits; it is just not what the production classifier stores for this trace. The twin gate proves C++ == Python-mch over PORTED specs — not C++ == the production event_classifier. See gates for the precise claim.

1L25THE divergence from the docs you may have read. accounts is a bare vector<string> with no parallel role map, because this branch has no role system: action_accounts in indexer/core/database.py is (action_id, trace_id, account) plus lt/utime denormalisation and NOTHING else, and role_assignment.py does not exist here. CLAUDE.md's ROLE_SENDER/ROLE_RECEIVER section describes a different branch. Verified in "Check yourself" below.
2L26–28Eight directional columns + amount/value/opcode, all typed Value rather than string/int64. That is not laziness: it gives "unset" a first-class representation (Null) distinct from empty-string, matching Python's None exactly, so a field the fill never touched renders as null on both sides.
3L29–32Fourteen composite columns, one per protocol family, plus extra. A new action type is supposed to REUSE one of these rather than add a column — fill_dedust_v2_claim_reward below is the worked example of that rule, and it is why the list has stayed this length.
ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/ActionBuild.cpp:556–594build_action head — id, time window, tx_hashescpp66b3dd28
556bool build_action(Block *b, Action &a) {
557 a.type = b->btype;
558 a.success = !b->failed;
559 // action_id: sha256(root_event_node msg_hash|tx_hash + btype), base64.
5601 const EventNode *root = nullptr;
561 for (const EventNode *n : b->event_nodes) {
562 if (root == nullptr || n->lt() < root->lt()) root = n;
563 }
564 std::string key;
565 if (root != nullptr) {
566 key = (root->msg != nullptr) ? root->msg->msg_hash : root->tx_hash();
567 }
568 key += b->btype;
569 std::string digest = td::sha256(td::Slice(key));
570 a.action_id = td::base64_encode(td::Slice(digest));
5712 // tx_hashes (base set, event_nodes only) + lt/utime ranges + mc_seqno_end.
572 std::set<std::string> ths;
573 std::int64_t maxlt = std::numeric_limits<std::int64_t>::min();
574 std::int64_t minu = std::numeric_limits<std::int64_t>::max();
575 std::int64_t maxu = std::numeric_limits<std::int64_t>::min();
576 std::int64_t seqmax = std::numeric_limits<std::int64_t>::min();
5773 for (const EventNode *n : b->event_nodes) {
578 ths.insert(n->tx_hash());
579 std::int64_t tlt = n->tx != nullptr ? n->tx->lt : 0;
580 maxlt = std::max(maxlt, tlt);
581 minu = std::min(minu, node_utime(n));
582 maxu = std::max(maxu, n->tx != nullptr ? n->tx->now : 0);
583 if (n->tx != nullptr) seqmax = std::max(seqmax, n->tx->mc_block_seqno);
584 }
5854 // tx_hashes extension by initiating_event_node (block_to_action, Step 2a).
586 if (b->initiating_event_node != nullptr) {
587 ths.insert(b->initiating_event_node->tx_hash());
588 }
589 a.tx_hashes.assign(ths.begin(), ths.end());
590 a.start_lt = b->min_lt;
591 a.end_lt = b->event_nodes.empty() ? 0 : maxlt;
592 a.start_utime = b->event_nodes.empty() ? 0 : minu;
593 a.end_utime = b->event_nodes.empty() ? 0 : maxu;
594 a.mc_seqno_end = b->event_nodes.empty() ? 0 : seqmax;
1L560–570The action id is base64(sha256(msg_hash_or_tx_hash + btype)) over the EARLIEST event node. The tie-break is load-bearing: n->lt() < root->lt() with strict < keeps the first minimum, which is what Python's min() returns. Flip it to <= and traces with two nodes at the same lt get a different id — a silent, data-dependent diff.
2L571–584end_lt / start_utime / end_utime / mc_seqno_end are recomputed here from event_nodes, whereas Python reads block.max_lt / min_utime / max_utime. They agree because Python's calculate_min_max_lt computes them from the same node set — but the C++ Block genuinely has no such fields (block-tree), so this is a re-derivation, not a read. node_utime (above, line 86) reproduces get_utime's three-way rule: tick_tock -> tx.now, created_lt set -> created_at, else tx.now.
3L577–583Every accumulator is null-guarded on n->tx. Python is not: max(n.message.transaction.lt ...) would raise on a tick_tock node and max(...) over an empty event_nodes raises ValueError. The guards below (event_nodes.empty() ? 0 : …) make the C++ total where Python would throw — unreachable for the ported btypes, but it means a bug here degrades to a zero rather than to a trace failure.
4L585–589The Step 2a extension: the block's initiating_event_node contributes its tx hash even though that node is not in event_nodes. std::set gives sorted-unique for free; Python uses set() and gets arbitrary order, which is why BOTH dumps sort tx_hashes before rendering. Do not read meaning into the order.

1L595Accounts are assembled AFTER the fill, and that ordering is required: three of the four sources below are the directional fields the fill just wrote. A fill that forgets to set source silently shrinks the accounts set — which is a missing action_accounts row in production, not a visibly wrong column.
2L602–608push_acc accepts only VType::Str. That works because av_addr has already converted every Account/Asset to a canonical string — a directional field still holding an Account would be silently dropped. The invariant "directional columns are Str or Null" is enforced by convention in the fills, not by the type.
3L611–614The is_ghost_block gate on destinations. On this branch the C++ substrate has no ghost nodes so the flag is always false (see BlockTree.h), meaning this branch is structurally dead — ported anyway because the Python serializer has it and a future ghost-producing matcher would need it.
4L615–621The initiating tx's account joins the set unless the node is tick_tock. Python logs a debug line when that account was not already present; C++ does not (stdout is the diff channel). sort+unique versus Python's list(set(...)): the CONTENTS are gated, the order is not — both dumps sort, and action_accounts is a set of rows anyway.

fill_action: dispatch, helpers, and two representative fills

Everything btype-specific lives in a fill_*. They all have the same shape: read block.data fields by name, run them through one of three converters, write directional columns and one composite dict. The converters are the interesting part — they are where the engine's rich Value types (value) collapse into the flat column types the DB expects.

One consequence worth internalising before reading any fill: render_value SORTS dict keys, so the order of f.emplace_back(...) calls is invisible to the A/B gate. The names and values are pinned; the emission order is not.

ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/ActionBuild.cpp:37–63The three converters every fill runs oncppa987a22a
371// _addr(): AccountId/Asset/None -> canonical address STRING (Str) or Null.
38// Composites and directional fields store addresses as plain strings (Python
39// _addr / .as_str()), so they render with the "str:" prefix on both sides.
40Value av_addr(const Value &v) {
41 if (v.is_null()) return Value::null();
42 if (v.t == VType::Asset) return v.has_jetton ? Value::make_str(v.str) : Value::null();
43 if (v.t == VType::Account) return v.addr_none ? Value::null() : Value::make_str(v.str);
44 return Value::null();
45}
46 
472// Amount.value / _value(): Amount -> its underlying Int (or Float / Null);
48// a plain Int (jvault/evaa/tgbtc raw amounts) passes through unchanged.
49Value av_amount(const Value &v) {
50 if (v.is_null()) return Value::null();
51 if (v.t == VType::Amount) {
52 if (v.amount_float) return Value::make_float(v.dnum);
53 return v.num.is_null() ? Value::null() : Value::make_int(v.num);
54 }
55 return v; // Int / Float passthrough
56}
57 
583// data field read (Dict/Obj); missing == Null.
59Value dg(const Value &d, const char *k) {
60 const Value *v = d.field(k);
61 return v != nullptr ? *v : Value::null();
62}
63bool has(const Value &d, const char *k) { return d.field(k) != nullptr; }
1L37–45av_addr is the whole reason directional columns render as str:0:ABC… and not asset:… or a raw Account. Note the two null-producing cases: an Asset with no jetton (i.e. TON) becomes Null, and an addr_none Account becomes Null. So "TON" and "no address" are indistinguishable in a column — a fill that needs to say "this leg was TON" has to encode it elsewhere (see fill_jetton_transfer's asset branch).
2L47–56av_amount unwraps Amount to its underlying Int (or Float for the NaN-ish cases), and passes a bare Int through untouched. That passthrough is what lets jvault/evaa/tgbtc fills, whose builders emit raw ints rather than Amounts, share the same converter. It also means you cannot tell from the row whether the builder produced an Amount.
3L58–63dg returns Null for a missing key, has distinguishes missing from present-and-null. Several fills need BOTH (has(d,"receiver_wallet") ? av_addr(...) : Null in the next excerpt) because the Python side reads the key conditionally — the same conditionally-present-key discipline as the parse layer (parse-layer), one level up.

1L101has(...) guarding a field that dg would already return Null for. It is not redundant in intent: it documents that Python reads receiver_wallet only when the builder set it. Since both branches produce Null here, this is one of the few places where the C++ is defensive beyond what the gate can prove.
2L103–104The TON-vs-jetton fork. A TON Asset becomes Null explicitly rather than by falling through av_addr — semantically the same result, written out because the reader needs to know that asset=null on a jetton_transfer row means TON, not "unknown".
3L105–113The composite. Seven keys, and two of them (custom_payload, forward_payload) are Cell-derived — they render as cellhash:HEX rather than as serialized BOC, which is the §12 root-hash bar that makes pytoniq-vs-td serialization differences invisible to the byte diff. comment goes through comment_value, which picks base64 for encrypted comments and UTF-8 backslashreplace otherwise.

1L286–288The T12.2 protocol from parse-layer, arriving at its final destination. Note what it does NOT do: set a.type. The row's type stays the raw btype dedust_v2_claim_reward — several other fills DO rewrite type (fill_dedust_deposit -> dex_deposit_liquidity, fill_ethena_deposit -> stake_deposit), so the btype and the rendered type are not interchangeable.
2L292–306A reward claim is modelled as a one-sided liquidity withdrawal: every side-2 key is explicitly Null rather than omitted. Emitting the nulls (instead of leaving keys out) is what keeps the composite's key SET constant across the btypes that share it — the DB composite is positional, so an absent key and a null key are not the same thing downstream.
3L304Worth a look before this reaches production: is_refund is emitted by both engines (Python's _fill_dedust_v2_claim_reward sets it too, so the A/B gate is satisfied), but the dex_withdraw_liquidity_details CompositeType declared in indexer/core/database.py has no such column. The gate proves the two engines agree on the dict; it says nothing about what Postgres stores.
4L307–309extra is the escape hatch for the one field that fits no existing composite. Preferring extra over a new column is a standing rule on this branch — a new composite type means a DDL migration on a table with billions of rows.

1L521–524An if/else-if chain on b->btype, matching Python's match block.btype. The Python version has ~90 cases; this has 21. The difference is not a porting backlog — it is the corpus: only btypes that FIRE in the fixture set can be A/B-gated, and an ungated fill is a liability.
2L524contract_deploy shares fill_call_contract, exactly as Python's case 'call_contract' | 'contract_deploy' does. Both are fallback-only here: the main dump's blocks are matcher-produced composites, never leaves.
3L535The only fill that takes a third argument. evaa_withdraw derives success from BOTH the data's is_success field and the block's failed flag — the one place where a row's success is not simply !b->failed.
4L546–551The named skip, and the honest reason: nft_purchase/dns_purchase have zero corpus coverage, so porting the fill would add untested code that the twin gate cannot check. Note the asymmetry this creates — the Python twin's PORTED_BTYPES set skips the same btypes, so the gate cannot detect a MISSING fill at all. Coverage of the fill set is a human responsibility, not a gated one.

This same fixture also produces a jetton_transfer row (the payout leg), which is why the grep filter is needed.

The render seam and the Python parity contract

render_action is the piece that did NOT move lib-side, and the split is exactly where you would want it: everything above produces an Action value; this turns one into a line of text for the A/B channel. Production never calls it — it binds the same Action to SQL instead (prod-path).

The parity contract is stronger than it is for any other layer in this engine. twins/py_actions.py does not reimplement the serializer — it calls the REAL block_tree_serializer.block_to_action and renders the result in this same column set. So a diff here is a diff against production Python, not against a twin's approximation.

1L66–67The row is rendered by building a Value Dict and handing it to the ordinary render_value. That is why an Action row and a block's data render with identical syntax — one renderer, so a str:/amount:/cellhash: prefix means the same thing everywhere in the dumps.
2L75–84tx_hashes and accounts are sorted HERE, at render time, not in build_action. The reason is Python: list(set(...)) gives hash order, so neither side has a meaningful order to compare. Sorting at the boundary keeps the diff stable without forcing an order the data model does not have.
3L85–92The eight directional columns pass through as raw Values — no conversion left to do, because av_addr already ran inside the fill. If one of these ever renders as asset:… or 0:ABC… (an Account) instead of str:0:ABC…, a fill skipped its converter.
4L68–74What is absent is as informative as what is present: no trace_id, no trace_end_lt/trace_*, no finality, and no roles. The trace-level fields are constant per fixture (the twin feeds a stub Trace), and roles do not exist on this branch — so neither is gated here, and neither should be inferred from this list.

1L177–185The failure line goes to stdout as a bare TRACE_FAIL while the REASON goes to stderr. That asymmetry is deliberate: stdout is the byte-compared channel, and exception messages are the one thing that will never match between a C++ and a Python engine.
2L186–193Fallback rows are tagged FALLBACK and only exist in --actions mode; --classify prints nothing after a TRACE_FAIL. Since no corpus trace fails, this entire block is dead in every gate run — which is precisely why the tag exists, so that if it ever fires it is unmistakable in a diff.
3L196–205The two modes share everything up to this point and differ only in the per-action render: build_action + render_action for --actions, emit_action (raw block data) for --classify. Note the continue on a false return — an unported btype is skipped SILENTLY, so --classify and --actions row counts can legitimately differ. Today they don't (199 = 199).

The gate this whole chapter rests on. Every field of every row above — ids, lt windows, sorted tx_hashes and accounts, every composite key — is byte-identical to what block_tree_serializer.block_to_action produces in the real Python classifier. The mechanics of the gate set (and the other five twins) are gates.

Check yourself

Four things worth doing before moving on to gates. The first has its captured output below; the other three you run yourself.

2. Prove that composite key ORDER is not gated. Swap any two adjacent f.emplace_back(...) lines inside fill_jetton_transfer (ActionBuild.cpp 105-113), rebuild ton-mch-engine, and re-run the twin diff from the previous section. It stays at 0, because render_value sorts keys. Then convince yourself why that is still dangerous: the DB composite in indexer/core/database.py is positional.

3. Prove that field VALUES are gated, hard. Swap a.source and a.destination in the same fill, rebuild, re-run the diff — you should see roughly 114 changed rows (one per jetton_transfer in the histogram above), and the ids will NOT change, because action_id is derived from the event node and the btype, never from the columns. That is worth seeing once: a corrupted row keeps its identity.

4. Read block_to_action's tail in indexer/indexer/events/blocks/utils/block_tree_serializer.py (lines 1519-1541) next to build_action's tail (ActionBuild.cpp 595-622) and check the four accounts sources line up: event-node tx accounts, source + source_secondary, destination pair gated on is_ghost_block, and the initiating tx's account gated on is_tick_tock. If you can also say why Python's list(set(...)) there forces both dumps to sort, you have the parity contract.

Gates and twins — verify everything yourself

Every claim in the previous eight chapters rests on one bar: run the C++ engine and the Python engine over the same corpus with the same artifact, and the two stdout streams must be byte-identical. Not "equivalent", not "same count" — Compare-Object returns zero lines. This chapter is the empowerment chapter: it shows the four kinds of gate (self-contained ctest modes, differential A/B twins, path-equivalence diffs, and generator repro guards), what each one actually proves, and the exact commands to run them. The twins are real Python — they import the production classifier (mch_ir engine, block_tree_serializer, the post-process passes), so a twin passing means the C++ engine agrees with the real Python mch runtime and serializer code — over the PORTED spec set. It does NOT mean agreement with the production event_classifier pipeline, whose old-engine matchers cover protocols mch has not ported (see the coffee-trace example in actions) today, not with a reimplementation of it. Two shared files keep the two sides from drifting silently: twins/cpp_surface.json (emitted by the engine itself) and twins/twin_registries.py (one factory list for all three twins). After this page you can check any number in this tutorial yourself, and you should — the numbers quoted in docs/mch-cpp-plan.md §1 are a dated snapshot and are already stale.

The twin philosophy: byte-diff-0, and why the dump is buffered

A twin is not a test fixture. It is a second implementation of a dump mode, written in Python, that imports the REAL classifier — indexer.events.mch_ir for the engine, block_tree_serializer.block_to_action for Action rows, post_process_dedust_liquidity / unwind_deployments for the host passes. So the gate is not "does C++ match a spec I wrote down" but "does C++ match the real Python mch engine and the serializer code it shares with production" — scoped, as always, to the PORTED spec set. That is why the twins were moved out of session scratchpads and committed: they encode gate semantics (canonical sorting, field-keyed cellhash renders, skip tables) that cost more to reconstruct than to keep.

Four twins, four engine modes, one comparison operator. Each twin's module docstring is the format contract from the Python side; the matching C++ header carries the same contract from the other side, and neither may change without the other.

The dump being byte-comparable at all depends on a property of the core: results are BUFFERED per trace and emitted only after the post-process passes have run. Nothing is printed mid-pipeline, so a trace that faults halfway does not leave half a dump behind — it emits exactly one TRACE_FAIL line on both sides. That atomicity is what makes the diff a clean signal instead of a cascade.

1L4–7"They import the REAL Python classifier" is the whole argument for this design. A twin that reimplemented the classifier would prove the two reimplementations agree; this one proves C++ agrees with the code the indexer actually runs. The price is that a twin must run from indexer/ with the project venv — it is not standalone.
2L11The asterisk matters when you copy-paste: py_msg_dump takes ONLY the traces dir (parsing does not depend on the IR artifact), the other three take the artifact path first. Getting this wrong gives a confusing "no such file" rather than a gate failure.
3L19The entire acceptance criterion in one line. Not a count, not a tolerance — Compare-Object must return an empty result. Any single character of divergence anywhere in the corpus is a red gate, which is what makes the gates useful as a refactoring net: you never have to judge whether a diff is benign.
4L21–23Build discipline lives here rather than in the C++ tree. build_mch.bat is the sanctioned entrypoint because the compile must run under vcvars64 AND be invoked from PowerShell — Bash/cmd.exe wrapping mangles the vcvars call (plan §0.9, first bullet). A SEPARATE rule in the same section: never run cmake *configure* under vcvars (libpqxx try_compile breaks); the bat only does --build, so it stays on the right side of both. If you are only running gates you do not need it — the exe is already built.

45// The adapter renders block_key(anchor)/data/consumed/aux or builds an Action

47// valid for as long as the caller keeps it alive.
48struct CoreAction {
49 std::string matcher_name;
50 Block *anchor;
51 Block *produced;
52 std::vector<Block *> aux; // fire-time excess/bounce auto-append (anchor)
53};

552// Buffered ATOMIC per-trace result: on a mid-trace throw the pipeline sets
56// `failure` (+ reason) and returns whatever was collected — NOTHING is emitted
57// by the core; the adapter decides (a dump reproduces today's TRACE_FAIL line,
58// production commits only on success).
59struct ClassifyResult {
60 std::vector<CoreAction> actions; // surviving post-pass, in fire order
61 bool failure = false;
62 std::string failure_reason;
63 // Trace-terminal failure category (additive telemetry; none unless `failure`).
64 FailureCategory failure_category = FailureCategory::none;
653 // Step 2c basic-actions fallback (try_classify_basic_actions): populated ONLY
66 // when `failure` — a fresh leaf-only classify (no matchers) + the
67 // post-processor chain, one CoreAction per surviving spine block of a basic
68 // btype (call_contract / contract_deploy / ton_transfer). Production commits
69 // these when classification fails. Ungated (corpus has no failing traces).
70 std::vector<CoreAction> fallback_actions;
71};
1L44–47"RENDERING-AGNOSTIC" is the split that makes multiple gates possible from one pipeline: the core hands back block POINTERS, and the adapter decides whether to render a --classify line, an --actions row, or (in production) a DB insert. --classify and --actions are therefore not two pipelines to keep in sync — they are two renderers over the same CoreAction list (actions).
2L55–58The atomicity guarantee. A mid-trace throw sets failure and returns what was collected; NOTHING has been printed yet. The Python twin mirrors this with a try/except around the whole matcher loop that prints a single TRACE_FAIL on stdout — so a fault is one comparable line on both sides rather than a diverging tail of partial output.
3L65–70fallback_actions is populated only on failure and is UNGATED — no corpus trace fails, so no twin ever exercises it. Worth knowing before you trust it: it is the one production behaviour on this page that byte-diff-0 does not cover (named as a gap in prod-design §7.2, see prod-path).

1// Match-phase dump runner (`--match` mode) for the MCH IR walker.
2//
31// DUMP FORMAT CONTRACT (must be reproduced byte-for-byte by the Python twin,
4// twins/py_match_dump.py):
5//
6// SKIP <matcher> reason=<reason> # once, at top, sorted by matcher name
7// ...
8// === <fixture-basename>
9// MATCH <matcher> anchor=<key> consumed=[<k>,<k>,...] captures={<n>=<v>,...}
10// ...
11// === <fixture-basename>
12// ...
13//
142// - SKIP lines: one per unrunnable matcher (pred / where_expr dependent), sorted
15// by matcher name, emitted ONCE before any fixture (the skip set is artifact-
16// global). `reason` is e.g. `pred:name1,name2` (sorted) or `where_expr`.
17// - Per fixture: a `=== <basename>` header, then MATCH lines for every
18// (block, matcher) that matches — blocks in BFS-from-root canonical order
19// (dedup by identity), matchers in priority order, gated by test_self.
20// - block key = `<btype>#<opcode-hex8>@<min_lt>` for a block with an opcode,
213// else `<btype>@<min_lt>`. Uses only substrate fields proven byte-identical
22// in the A/B substrate verification (btype, opcode, min_lt) — deliberately
23// NOT tx_hash, whose cross-language string form is unverified.
244// - consumed = SORTED list of block keys (set semantics per §7 — order-
25// independent). captures = per capture in slot declaration order,
26// `name=<val>`; a scalar val is a block key or `null`; a list val is
27// `[k,k,...]` in assembly order (`null` for gap-aligned None), NOT sorted.
28// - A fixture that fails to load prints `ERROR: <msg>` under its header.
1L3–4"must be reproduced byte-for-byte by the Python twin" — the header is the specification, not documentation of an implementation. When a dump format needs to change, this comment and the twin's docstring change in the same commit or the gate goes red immediately.
2L14–16SKIP lines are emitted ONCE before any fixture because the skip set is artifact-global, not per-trace. This is itself A/B'd: the twin computes runnability from the artifact independently (see skip_reason below), so the two engines' opinions about which matchers they can run are compared, not assumed.
3L21–23The block key uses only btype/opcode/min_lt — deliberately NOT tx_hash. Rule of thumb for adding anything to a dump: a field may appear only if its cross-language STRING form has itself been A/B-proven. A field that renders differently in Python and C++ turns every gate into noise.
4L24–27Sorted vs unsorted is semantic, not cosmetic. consumed is a SET (§7), so it is sorted to make the render canonical; captures is a list in assembly order and must NOT be sorted, because order there carries meaning (matcher-runtime). Sorting the wrong one would hide a real ordering bug.

One twin up close: py_classify.py

py_classify.py is 306 lines and worth reading end to end once; it is the shortest complete statement of what the C++ engine is supposed to do. Three parts carry all the subtlety: what it imports (nothing hand-mirrored), how it decides which matchers are runnable, and the loop — which deviates from event_processing.py in exactly one documented way.

The render functions in the middle of the file (render, _cellhash, _render_field) are the value-rendering contract from value restated in Python; the cellhash: treatment of BOC-container fields is the §12 root-hash bar, which exists so that a payload cell compares by its root hash rather than by a serializer-dependent byte encoding.

184def skip_reason(rec, nodes):
1851 preds = _preds(rec, nodes)
186 missing = preds - CPP_PREDS
187 if missing:
188 return "pred:" + ",".join(sorted(missing))
189 if rec["anchor"]["kind"] == "mixed" and preds:
190 return "mixed_anchor_preds"
191 if "build_program" not in rec:
192 return "builder" if "builder" in rec else "no_build_program"
1932 types, lookups, fns = _refs(rec)
194 parts = []
195 missing_t = sorted(t for t in types if t not in CPP_PARSERS)
196 missing_l = sorted(l for l in lookups if l not in CPP_LOOKUP_KINDS)
197 missing_f = sorted(f for f in fns if f not in CPP_FNS)
198 if missing_t:
199 parts.append("types:" + ",".join(missing_t))
200 if missing_l:
201 parts.append("lookups:" + ",".join(missing_l))
202 if missing_f:
203 parts.append("fns:" + ",".join(missing_f))
204 if "shape" in rec and rec["shape"] not in CPP_SHAPERS:
205 parts.append("shaper:" + rec["shape"])
2063 return ";".join(parts) or None
1L185–190Order is load-bearing: a missing PREDICATE short-circuits before anything else is examined, so the reason string is pred:a,b and never a mix. The C++ loader computes the same reasons in the same order, and the reasons are printed — so this function is a second implementation of IrLoader runnability that gets diffed, not a convenience.
2L193–203The three reference classes a build program can miss on — parse types, lookup kinds, host fns — checked against the sets loaded from cpp_surface.json. 2231 # Canonical-order BFS (T21 extension, DELIBERATE deviation from
224 # event_processing.bfs_iter&#39;s raw insertion order): the C++ substrate keeps
225 # next_blocks canonical (min_lt asc, stable) at all times, so the raw
226 # Python insertion order is not representable there. Both sides walk the
227 # canonical order; generator semantics (children read AFTER try_build ran
228 # on the parent) are preserved.
229 def bfs_canonical(start):
230 queue = [start]
231 while queue:
232 cur = queue.pop(0)
233 yield cur
234 queue.extend(sorted(cur.next_blocks, key=lambda x: x.min_lt))

240 # loop prints a single `TRACE_FAIL` line on stdout (the A/B channel), the
241 # detail on stderr. No corpus trace triggers this.
242 try:
2433 # Phase E: COLLECT produced actions during the matcher loop; the
244 # post-process passes (which merge/remove blocks) run AFTER, then the
245 # surviving actions are emitted from their FINAL state. aux is
246 # fire-time (unchanged by pairing); data/consumed are post-pass.
247 pending = [] # (matcher_name, anchor_key, produced, aux_s)
248 for m in included:
249 for b in bfs_canonical(root):
2504 if b.parent is not None:
251 continue

253 if not r:
254 continue

1L223–228The honest part of the twin. event_processing.bfs_iter walks next_blocks in raw insertion order; the C++ substrate keeps that list canonical (min_lt asc, stable) at ALL times, so raw insertion order is not even representable there. Rather than fake it, the twin walks canonical order too and says so. Generator semantics — children read AFTER try_build ran on the parent — are preserved, because THAT is what changes results.
2L236–241"No corpus trace triggers this." The per-trace exception boundary mirrors production's fallback-to-basic-actions behaviour, and it prints its detail on STDERR while stdout gets a bare TRACE_FAIL. Splitting the channels is what keeps a fault comparable: the message text (a Python exception repr) could never match C++, the fact of the fault must.
3L243–247Phase E in three lines of comment: COLLECT during the matcher loop, run the passes AFTER, emit from the FINAL state. aux is fire-time and never revised; data/consumed are read post-pass. Get this ordering wrong on either side and the diff shows up as a handful of actions with stale data on otherwise-identical traces.
4L250–251The parent is not None guard is the port of the outer loop's root-only rule — a block that has been absorbed into a parent is never offered to try_build again. It is a continue inside the BFS rather than a filter on the queue, so the traversal itself still descends through consumed blocks (matcher-runtime).

A pass that merges two deposit blocks into one removes the losers from the spine; every collected action whose produced block is gone is dropped from the dump. id() (not equality) because two structurally identical produced blocks are still two actions.

4L277–279The literal format contract. Compare this f-string against the ACTION line in the run above and against Classify.h's comment — three statements of one format, and the gate is what keeps them equal.

Two shared files: the surface and the registries

Both engines have to agree on facts that are not in the IR artifact: which message parsers exist, which host predicates and fns are registered, which lookup kinds are servable, which fields are BOC containers. The C++ side owns those registries. Rather than mirror them by hand in Python (the original design, which drifted), the engine emits them.

--surface prints the live registries as stable-sorted JSON; the committed twins/cpp_surface.json is that output, and twins/cpp_surface.py loads it into the CPP_* sets every twin imports. Drift is caught twice: output-affecting drift blows up the A/B gates, and benign-superset drift (which would slip past them) is caught by a pytest that runs --surface and compares.

On the Python side the mirror-image problem is the builder registries. twin_registries.py holds one factory list, merged last-wins, imported by all three IR twins.

663def combined_registries() -> Registries:

1L48–6027 factories, and the ORDER is preserved verbatim from the three twins this file replaced — because the merge is last-wins per dict key, reordering could silently change which builder a name resolves to. It looks like an arbitrarily ordered list; it is a pinned one.
2L62–63The eight registry dicts a protocol can contribute to. Five of them pair 1:1 with a --surface key — predicates↔preds, message_types↔parsers, lookups↔lookup_kinds, fns↔fns, shapers↔shapers. The other three have no surface entry: opcodes and block_types because the C++ engine reads those out of the IR artifact rather than a registry, and builders because a C++ builder is a generated build fn, not a registered row. The mapping also runs short the other way — the surface's boc_fields is a C++-only set with no Python registry behind it, which the twins import from cpp_surface.py for rendering.
3L66–72A fresh Registries per call, merged in factory order. Cheap enough to call per twin invocation, and building it fresh (rather than caching a module-level singleton) means a twin can never be affected by another twin's mutation in the same process.

Self-contained gates: vectors and ctest

The A/B twins need Python, the corpus, and a venv. The gates in this section need none of that — they are engine modes over version-controlled JSON documents, wired into CTest so ctest -R mch runs all eight in under a second. That is deliberate: the differential gates stay OUT of ctest precisely because they have external dependencies, and a test suite you cannot run from a cold checkout is a test suite people stop running.

The three vector families cover the three layers the twins cannot isolate. Expression vectors are run TWICE — once through the tree-walking interpreter and once through the generated C++ — against the same expectations, which is how the "one semantics" rule (interpreter and codegen call the same rt_* functions) is actually enforced rather than asserted. Build vectors do the same for statements, with expectations GENERATED by running the real Python BuildProgram.run rather than hand-authored. Message vectors are boundary cases emitted by the schema compiler next to the parsers it generates.

1L6–9"GENERATED by running the real Python BuildProgram.run … no hand-authored expectations" — the strongest sentence on this page. A hand-written expectation encodes what the author BELIEVED the semantics were; a generated one encodes what Python actually does. 2L9–12The C++ side runs the GENERATED build fns, and the table is permanently paired with its input document by suffix (gen_builds_vectors vs gen_builds_ir) plus a sha guard. Running vectors against a table built from a different document is a hard error, not a silent mismatch — see the CMake custom commands that emit both tables.
3L15–18The $block encoding carries a real BOC body, so parse inside a build program runs the real MsgParse dispatch rather than a stub. That is what makes these vectors cover the parse seam of parse-layer without needing a trace fixture.

Repro guards: nothing generated is hand-edited

Three of the artifacts these gates depend on are generated: the IR artifact (Python ir_emit), the message-parser TU plus its vectors (Python msgs_gen), and the ton-abi C++ pairs (ton-abi-gen). A generated file that someone "just tweaked" would make every downstream gate lie — it would still be green, and it would be green about the wrong thing.

So each generator has a byte-repro guard: regenerate into memory or a temp dir, compare bytes with the committed copy, fail on any difference. Same discipline, three places. The --surface mirror gets the same treatment for the same reason.

1L34–35The manifest, not the specs directory: emit_manifest.json pins the spec files AND their registration order, so the artifact is reproducible even as new .mch files land in the specs dir (conformance-only specs are deliberately excluded from the prod artifact). Emitting from the directory would silently change matcher priority ordering (ir-artifact).
2L40–41render_json(...).encode("utf-8") == committed.read_bytes() — bytes, not parsed-JSON equality. Key order, separators and float formatting are all part of the contract, because the C++ side pairs its generated build tables to the artifact by SHA of the file.

Path-equivalence gates: engine vs engine

The twins prove the C++ pipeline matches Python. They cannot prove that the PRODUCTION entry into that pipeline — a trace arriving as schema::Transactions from the indexer, and interfaces arriving from an in-block map plus a DB/kvrocks fallback — reproduces the fixture-driven entry the twins exercise. That needs a different comparison: the same engine, two input paths, diffed against itself.

SchemaGate.cpp is that harness. It re-routes each fixture through msgpack -> our structs -> schema -> SchemaTraceLoader -> our structs and classifies the result, so a diff against plain --classify isolates the loader. The -prod variants go further and swap the lookup source too. Because both sides are the same binary, a zero diff here is a statement about the ADAPTERS only — which is exactly the claim prod-path needs.

1L1–6"path B" vs "path A": the loader is proven by ROUND-TRIPPING the fixture through the production schema types and re-classifying. Note what this does NOT prove — that the indexer's real schema rows look like the synthesized ones. It proves the loader is lossless for everything the classifier reads, which is the part a fixture can speak to.
2L15–19The prod variants add ParsedBlockLookupSource with its two tiers: a synthesized in-block account_interfaces_ map (tier 1) and a fixture-backed fallback (tier 2). Diff-0 here means the tiering reproduces the fixture source's shapes exactly — the interesting failure mode being a tier-1 hit that returns a subtly different shape than the tier-2 answer would have.
3L23–26The --actions-* twins of these modes exist because the Action render exercises fields the classify dump does not: the raw-account leak into the accounts set, and aborted flipping success/failed. A gate that only diffed --classify would miss both (actions).
