The gate table, and why you should not trust its numbers

indexer/docs/mch-cpp-plan.md §1 is the canonical list: twelve rows, each a gate with an exact command and a Pass column. It covers the Python suites, the two expression-vector paths, build vectors, the shape/self tests plus ctest, the four A/B twins (msg parsing, match walker, classify, action rows), the schema-loader and prod-path equivalence gates, and codegen determinism. Its ground rules are equally load-bearing: run the full set before starting a task and again after finishing; a task is not done while any gate is red; Python is ground truth; and when codegen disagrees with the interpreter, codegen is wrong.

What you should NOT take from that table is its numbers. It is dated 2026-07-11 and says 147 fixtures, 196 classify actions, 196 Action rows, 97 expression vectors, 35 build vectors, ctest 5/5. Every one of those has moved: the corpus is 148 fixtures, classify and actions are 199 each, expression vectors 115, build vectors 38, message vectors 44, ctest 8/8 for mch plus 2/2 for ton-abi. All verified by the runs above, on this checkout, today. The commands in the table are stable; the counts are a snapshot, and the habit worth forming is to re-derive them rather than quote them.

One more honest gap, restated: the corpus contains no failing trace, so ClassifyResult::fallback_actions and the TRACE_FAIL path are exercised by neither twin. Byte-diff-0 is a very strong claim about the paths the corpus reaches, and says nothing about the ones it does not.

Check yourself

Four things to do before you consider this tutorial verified. Each is a real command; each either reproduces a number quoted somewhere in these ten chapters or tells you the tutorial has drifted.

1. RUN THE FAST GATE. cd to ton-index-worker/cmake-build-debug-visual-studio/ton-mch-engine and run ctest -R mch. You should get 8/8 in well under a second. Then cd ../ton-abi and run ctest for 2/2. If any of the ten fails on an unmodified checkout, nothing else on this page is trustworthy.

2. REPRODUCE THE HEADLINE DIFF YOURSELF. Copy the first runs block in this chapter verbatim. Confirm diff lines : 0, and confirm the fixture/action counts match what this chapter and actions claim (148 / 199). Then break it on purpose: open twins/py_classify.py, change sorted(produced.data) on line 275 to produced.data, re-run, and watch the diff count explode. That is what a real regression looks like, and it is worth seeing once so you recognise it.

3. PROVE THE SURFACE FILE IS NOT DECORATIVE. Run ton-mch-engine --surface and diff it against twins/cpp_surface.json — Compare-Object (gc twins/cpp_surface.json) (& $EXE --surface), expect 0. Then run python -m pytest tests/mch/test_cpp_surface.py -q from indexer/ and confirm it passes for the same reason. Now reason it through: if you deleted a row from abi_message_parsers() without regenerating the mirror, which of the two catches it first, and what would the failure message actually tell you?

4. READ ONE TWIN AGAINST ITS C++ CONTRACT. Open twins/py_match_dump.py and src/MatchRunner.h side by side. The header's DUMP FORMAT CONTRACT block and the twin's emission code should read as the same sentence in two languages. Any place where you cannot map one onto the other is either a comment that has drifted or a piece of the format that is not actually gated — both are worth reporting.

Connected scopes
  • actions — --actions is the second renderer over the same CoreAction list; its extra fields (accounts, cellhash renders, aborted) are why a separate twin exists
  • prod-path — --classify-prod / --actions-prod are the evidence that the schema loader and the two-tier lookup adapter are lossless
  • parse-layer — --parse-dump vs py_msg_dump is the parity gate behind every pytoniq-quirk claim there; --abi-bridge-test covers the third parser source
  • ir-artifact — the artifact's byte-repro guard (emit_manifest) is what lets generated build tables be sha-paired to it
  • build-programs — expr vectors run twice (interpreter + generated) to enforce the one-semantics rule that page depends on
Not annotated in this scope — read directly
  • ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/twins/py_classify.py — PARTIAL: header, skip_reason, the loop and the emit are excerpted. The remainder is the value-rendering half (render, _cellhash, _render_field, block_key) — the Python statement of the §12 render contract already covered from the C++ side in value (~306 LOC total)

10 · The production path (Phase G) — shadow mode, and what it does not yet prove

Everything so far ran the engine over .lz4 fixtures from a CLI. This chapter is the other end: the same library TUs running inside ton-index-postgres, on real ParsedBlock data, once per masterchain seqno. Three adapters make that possible — SchemaTraceLoader (production schema::Transaction -> the engine's own Trace structs), ParsedBlockLookupSource (the pipeline's in-block interface map -> lookup kind(key)), and MchClassifierActor (a thin td::actor gluing them to ClassifyCore). Nothing downstream changed: to_tree, init_block, MsgParse and classify_trace are byte-for-byte the code the gates already proved. The mode is SHADOW: fire-and-forget, log-only, zero DB writes, zero effect on the pipeline's promises. The offline proof that the adapters are faithful is a fourth gate pair, --classify-prod / --actions-prod, which diffs the full production path against the fixture path over the whole corpus — with one honestly-named hole (the nft family) that fixture floats make un-gatable offline. By the end you should know exactly which claims about production are proven, which are proven-by-construction, and which are still waiting on a remote shadow run.

Shadow mode: the contract

Phase G's rollout decision was made up front and it shapes every file on this page: the C++ engine runs BESIDE the authoritative classifier, not instead of it. It reads the ParsedBlock the interfaces stage just produced, classifies, and prints. It writes nothing, returns nothing, and cannot fail a seqno.

That constraint is what makes the wiring boring on purpose. There is no promise, no batch, no insert path, no _classifier_tasks bookkeeping — those all belong to the flip, not to shadow. Everything genuinely interesting in this chapter is therefore about FAITHFULNESS of the input adapters, not about output.

The library boundary was drawn one wave earlier: mch-classify is a static lib containing the pipeline TUs (loader, block tree, Value, IR, walker, host fns, build runtime, ActionBuild, ClassifyCore, parsers, the ABI pairs) plus the three Phase G adapters. The CLI exe links it and adds the harness TUs — dumps, vector runners, SchemaGate, main.cpp. ton-index-postgres links the lib only, so no harness code can reach production even by accident.

SchemaTraceLoader — production structs in, engine Trace out

The fixture loader (block-tree) reads msgpack into Trace / Transaction / Message / MsgContent. Production has a different shape entirely: schema::Transaction objects hanging off a ParsedBlock, with schema::Trace alongside. The obvious plan — walk schema::Trace — turns out to be wrong, and the header says why in its first paragraph.

schema::Trace carries only edges, no transaction list. And the engine's to_tree never used edges: it rebuilds the EventNode tree purely by message-hash linking (an out-msg hash of the parent tx equals the in-msg hash of the child). So the loader takes a plain std::vector<schema::Transaction> and the edges are simply unused. That single finding is what kept to_tree / init_block single-sourced and untouched.

What remains is a field-by-field map with three subtleties worth internalising: where aborted lives, why account strings get re-cased, and why message bodies are copied as already-serialized BOC strings.

ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/src/SchemaTraceLoader.cpp:38–64descr_info — the trap the --actions-prod gate exists to catchcpp1b68f6a3
38// TransactionDescr variant -> descr string + compute exit code + aborted. The
39// engine consumes the descr TYPE (tick_tock vs ord), the compute exit code (msg
401// .exit_code envelope) AND aborted (BlockTree is_leaf_failed reads tx->aborted;
41// also exposed as msg.transaction.aborted) — aborted lives INSIDE the schema
42// variant, unlike path A's flat top-level field. Non-ord/tick_tock descrs are
43// rare (storage/split/merge) and map to "other" (never matched as tick_tock).
44DescrInfo descr_info(const schema::TransactionDescr &d) {
45 DescrInfo r;
462 auto exit_of = [](const schema::TrComputePhase &cp) -> std::optional<std::int64_t> {
47 if (const auto *vm = std::get_if<schema::TrComputePhase_vm>(&cp)) {
48 return static_cast<std::int64_t>(vm->exit_code);
49 }
50 return std::nullopt; // skipped compute phase -> no exit code
51 };
52 if (const auto *ord = std::get_if<schema::TransactionDescr_ord>(&d)) {
53 r.descr = "ord";
54 r.exit_code = exit_of(ord->compute_ph);
55 r.aborted = ord->aborted;
563 } else if (const auto *tt = std::get_if<schema::TransactionDescr_tick_tock>(&d)) {
57 r.descr = "tick_tock";
58 r.exit_code = exit_of(tt->compute_ph);
59 r.aborted = tt->aborted;
60 } else {
61 r.descr = "other";
62 }
63 return r;
64}
1L40–43aborted lives INSIDE the TransactionDescr variant here, where the fixture path had it as a flat top-level field. It is read by is_leaf_failed in the block tree and it flips an action's success/failed rendering — so a missed aborted would not crash anything, it would quietly mislabel actions. This is exactly the class of bug an A/B row diff catches and a unit test does not.
2L46–51A skipped compute phase yields nullopt, NOT 0. Matcher predicates distinguish "no compute phase" from "exit code 0" (matcher-runtime), so collapsing them would change which matchers fire.
3L56–62Storage/split/merge descrs collapse to "other" and can never be matched as tick_tock. The engine only ever asks ord-vs-tick_tock, so "other" is a safe sink rather than a lossy one — but note it also leaves aborted false for those transactions.

91 // re-serialization, ClassifyCore untouched.

1L66–71The schema separates in_msg from out_msgs structurally; the engine wants one flat list with a direction string, because that is what the EventNode builder and every msg.direction expression read. The tag is supplied by the caller, not inferred.
2L76–81A null grams becomes nullopt, not 0 — same rule as the exit code. has_extra_currencies is derived from a non-empty vector, matching how the Python side computes it; the currencies themselves are never modelled.
3L86–87bounce is a plain bool but bounced is optional in the schema and defaults to false. Anything else would flip bounce-handling matchers on production data while the fixture corpus stayed green.
4L88–95The single best decision in this file: the already-serialized body_boc string is copied verbatim instead of re-serializing a cell. The engine carries bodies as base64 BOC and renders cells by HASH, so any pytoniq-vs-td byte-layout difference is invisible in output — which is why parse-layer needed exactly zero changes to run in production.

ParsedBlockLookupSource — two tiers, one of them still a stub

lookup kind(key) is the engine's only way to ask about on-chain state it cannot see in the trace (build-programs). Offline it is served by FixtureLookupSource, reading the interfaces dict bundled in the .lz4. Production has to serve it from the pipeline.

The honest complication, answered by the lead's Q2 investigation: ParsedBlock.account_interfaces_ only covers accounts TOUCHED in this seqno, while the Python classifier's interface_repository reads DB/kvrocks and can resolve an interface detected months ago — a counterparty jetton wallet that this block never touched, say. The fixtures happen to bundle exactly such historical data, so the offline corpus does not expose the gap. Hence a two-tier design: tier 1 is the in-block map, tier 2 is an injectable hook for a DB/kvrocks round.

Read the class header (lines 1-21, not excerpted) for the per-kind table. The short version: five kinds resolve from tier 1 (jetton_wallet, nft_item, nft_sale, nft_auction, dedust_pool), and two are TIER-2-ONLY — nominator_pool has no V2 interface variant at all, and jvault_assets needs raw account-state cells plus chained reads that live in account_states_, not in the interface map. In production today the tier-2 hook is unset. That is the largest remaining gap before flip, and the telemetry below exists to size it.

This is the strongest argument for the prod gate existing at all.

133Value ParsedBlockLookupSource::fetch(const std::string &kind, const std::vector<Value> &args) const {
1341 // FixtureLookupSource parity guard: every registered lookup passes exactly one
135 // Str address; anything else is a null result on both sources.
136 if (args.size() != 1 || args[0].t != VType::Str) {
137 return Value::null();
138 }
1392 // Tier 1 resolves from account_interfaces_; a miss falls through to tier 2.
140 // No kind whitelist here: tier1() self-gates (every branch tests `kind ==`,
141 // an unhandled kind falls through to null), so a second hand-kept kind list
142 // could only drift out of sync with it.
1433 Value v = tier1(kind, args[0].str);
144 if (!v.is_null()) {
145 stats_.tier1_hits++;
146 return v;
147 }
1484 // Tier-2-only kinds (nominator_pool, jvault_assets) and every tier-1 miss.
149 Value r = tier2_ ? tier2_(kind, args) : Value::null();
150 if (!r.is_null()) {
151 stats_.tier2_hits++;
152 } else {
153 stats_.misses++;
154 }
155 return r;
156}
1L134–137Arity/type guard mirroring the fixture source exactly: one Str address or null. Keeping the two sources bug-compatible at the boundary is what lets the prod gate diff at 0 instead of needing an allowance list.
2L139–142No kind whitelist here, and the comment explains the reasoning: tier1() self-gates because every branch tests kind ==. A second hand-kept list could only drift. Consequence: an unrecognised kind silently routes to tier 2 and then to null.
3L143–147"Non-null == tier-1 hit" is the attribution rule, and it has a known imprecision: a lookup that legitimately resolves to null is indistinguishable from a miss, so misses over-counts by however many genuine nulls the corpus contains. Fine for a hit-RATE, wrong if you read it as an error count.
4L148–155The two tier-2-only kinds land here on every single call. With the hook unset in production, nominator_pool and jvault_assets are permanently null in shadow mode — i.e. those matchers effectively do not fire, and their absence in a shadow diff means nothing until the fallback lands.

MchClassifierActor — startup prep, per-trace run, failure taxonomy

The actor itself is thin by construction: group, load, classify, log, stop. Two things in it deserve real attention — where the engine's startup checks happen (this is also where the ABI bridge rows enter the production path), and how transactions are grouped into traces.

load_engine_prep is the embedding entry point, called once from main.cpp before the scheduler runs. It performs the same advisory registry validation the CLI does, loads the IR artifact, and builds the ClassifySetup (runnable matchers, skip table, generated build-fn map, referenced lookup kinds). A table/fn mismatch is returned as an error so the caller can be startup-fatal.

That validate_registries() call is the only place the ABI/tolk toolchain touches this chapter: the three parser sources (hand, schema-generated, ABI) merge into one flat name space, and a duplicate key must stop the process rather than resolve to whichever source enumerated first. The mechanism is covered in parse-layer; the tolk side — declarations, generated from_slice, the value-universe split — gets its own tutorial and is deliberately out of scope here.

The --mch-shadow flag (ton-index-postgres)

The indexer-side change is deliberately tiny: one optional flag, one setter, one conditional spawn. Note the environment caveat up front — ton-index-postgres does NOT build on this Windows workstation (a pre-existing protobuf/MSVC failure unrelated to mch; the build directory contains no exe, only CMake scaffolding). Production builds are Linux-remote, so everything in this section is REMOTE-VERIFY only: the code below has been reviewed and links against mch-classify, but no local run exercises it. Every other claim in this chapter is locally reproducible.

2L345–349"fire-and-forget": create_actor(...).release() detaches the actor and no promise is created. Contrast every other stage in this file, which is promise-chained and calls handle_seqno_failure -> reschedule_seqno on error. The shadow classifier structurally cannot delay, fail, or requeue a seqno — that is the whole safety argument for enabling it on a live indexer.
3L350–352parsed_block is COPIED here (shared_ptr) and only moved into ActionDetector further down. So a slow shadow run keeps the block alive a little longer but never blocks the insert path — and the guard means an indexer started without the flag runs exactly today's code.

The offline proof: --classify-prod / --actions-prod

None of the above can be gated by running the indexer, so the harness fakes the production input instead. SchemaGate.cpp loads a fixture the normal way (path A), SYNTHESIZES schema::Transaction objects back out of the loaded structs, feeds them through SchemaTraceLoader (path B), and — for the -prod variants — also synthesizes an account_interfaces_ map of real BlockchainInterfaceV2 structs and serves lookups through a real ParsedBlockLookupSource. Both paths then share run_dump's rendering and engine loop verbatim, so any difference in the diff is the adapter's.

The reverse synthesis is harness-only scaffolding and lives nowhere near the lib. The tier-2 hook in the gate is wired to a FixtureLookupSource over the same fixture interfaces (GateProdLookupSource, lines 256-286) — that is the gate standing in for the DB/kvrocks round production has yet to implement.

Four modes exist: --classify-schema / --actions-schema vary only the trace loader; --classify-prod / --actions-prod vary the loader AND the lookup source. Diffed against --classify / --actions the expectation is exact zero, and it holds across the whole corpus.

132// so path B is byte-comparable with path A and BOTH dumps (classify + actions)
133// route through it. The interfaces map (lookup data) is carried from path A
134// unchanged — it is the LookupSource's concern, not part of trace->tree.

138 TRY_RESULT(trace_b, schema_to_trace(ctx_a.trace.trace_id, schema_txs));
139 TraceContext ctx_b;

143 if (ctx_b.tree.root == nullptr) {
144 return td::Status::Error("empty event tree (path B)");
145 }
146 ctx_b.root = init_block(ctx_b.arena, ctx_b.tree.root);

1L129–134The injected-loader shape is what makes the diff meaningful: run_dump supplies the identical rendering and engine loop for A and B, so the only variable is how the TraceContext was acquired. A gate that re-implemented printing would prove much less.
2L136–138This reverse synthesis (engine structs -> schema::Transaction) is HARNESS-ONLY and never runs in production — production feeds real schema objects from ParsedBlock. It is the price of gating a production adapter without a live indexer, and it is deliberately lossy: storage/credit/action phases are dropped because the loader reads only descr-type, exit code and aborted.
3L141The interfaces map is carried over from path A UNCHANGED, so this gate isolates one variable — trace shape. The -prod variants then swap the second variable (lookups) on top of it. Two gates, two axes; a single combined gate would not tell you which adapter broke.

What remains before the flip

Shadow mode is wired, gated offline, and never run against live data. The worklist that stands between here and writing rows, in rough order of weight:

1. A REMOTE SHADOW RUN on a bounded dev seqno range — the only thing that produces real numbers for the tier-2 hit rate, the failure-category mix, and the cross-seqno fragmentation described above. Nothing offline can substitute for it. 2. The tier-2 lookup fallback (DB/kvrocks). Until it exists, nominator_pool and jvault_assets never resolve and historical interfaces are invisible; a shadow diff against Python-written rows will show deficits that are this, not the engine. 3. Trace gathering across seqnos — decide whether the actor waits for trace completion or the caller gathers. 4. Persistence itself: ClassifyResult.actions -> InsertBatchPostgres with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, plus cleanup-on-reprocess by trace_id, plus the _classifier_tasks bookkeeping inventory. ActionBuild already produces the rows (actions); nothing calls it from the actor. 5. Explicit matcher priorities in the specs (the artifact currently leans on file-name ordering) and the nft_purchase fill, which is blocked on corpus coverage.

Also worth carrying forward: the basic-actions fallback (ClassifyResult.fallback_actions) is ported but DORMANT — no corpus trace fails, so it is ungated. Shadow mode on live data is where it first gets real input, which is another reason the remote run is the gating item.

Check yourself

Four things you can verify in a few minutes, each testing a claim this page makes rather than re-reading the code.

1. Re-run the prod-gate diffs from the previous section and confirm both read 0 at 148 fixtures / 199 rows. Then break it on purpose: change "owner" to "owner_" in ParsedBlockLookupSource.cpp's jetton_wallet branch, rebuild the engine, and watch --classify-prod diverge from --classify while --classify itself stays green. That is the failure mode the gate is for — and it is exactly the failure mode the nft branches are NOT protected against.

2. Prove the shadow actor cannot write anything (run below).

3. Prove the offline gate synthesizes only two of the five tier-1 interface variants (run below), then read SchemaGate.cpp lines 205-224 for the reason.

4. Confirm the environment caveat yourself: ls S:/Dev/ton-indexer-clear/ton-index-worker/cmake-build-debug-visual-studio/ton-index-postgres contains only CMakeFiles and cmake_install.cmake — no executable, no object files. The --mch-shadow wiring has never been compiled on this machine; treat that section as reviewed-not-run.
